records.introduction_objective: Many diabetes risk scores including the ADA’s risk assessment tool incorporate self-reported physical activity, which is prone to bias and coarse categorization. We evaluated whether objectively measured, wearable-derived moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) predicts incidence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) in the All of Us (AoU) cohort.
records.methods: We analyzed AoU participants with linked EHR and Fitbit data. Weekly MVPA was derived from the first year of Fitbit wear among participants with ≥180 valid wear days (>100 steps/day). Incidence of T2D was identified using validated ICD-10 codes (E11) over a 10-year follow-up period. Weekly MVPA was computed using Fitbit-derived daily values. Multivariable logistic regression estimated odds ratios (ORs) for T2D adjusting for sex, race (White vs non-White), ethnicity, hypertension history, age (per 10 years), and BMI (per 5 kg/m²). Model’s T2D prediction performance was assessed using area under the ROC curve (AUROC).
records.results: 13,482 participants (51±16 years; 72% female; 79% White) without a history of T2D were analyzed, of whom 189 developed T2D over the 10-year follow-up. The cohort had 327±50 days of wearable data and 249±207 minutes of weekly MVPA. In adjusted models, every additional hour of weekly MVPA was associated with 6% lower odds of T2D (OR:0.94, 95%CI 0.89-1.00, p=.046). Traditional risk factors remained significant, including male sex (OR 1.94, p<.001), non-White race (OR 1.84, p=.005), hypertension history (OR 1.54, p=.02), older age (OR 1.22 per 10 years, p=.002), and higher BMI (OR 1.52 per 5 kg/m², p<.001). The model achieved an AUROC of 0.75 (95% CI 0.69-0.80) for 10-year T2D risk prediction.
records.conclusion: In a large national cohort, objective wearable-derived weekly MVPA was independently associated with lower odds of T2D after adjustment for well-known risk factors. These findings support the potential value of wearable-derived activity to complement or refine self-reported measures in diabetes risk scores.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Many diabetes risk scores including the ADA’s risk assessment tool incorporate self-reported physical activity, which is prone to bias and coarse categorization. We evaluated whether objectively measured, wearable-derived moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) predicts incidence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) in the All of Us (AoU) cohort.

Methods: We analyzed AoU participants with linked EHR and Fitbit data. Weekly MVPA was derived from the first year of Fitbit wear among participants with ≥180 valid wear days (>100 steps/day). Incidence of T2D was identified using validated ICD-10 codes (E11) over a 10-year follow-up period. Weekly MVPA was computed using Fitbit-derived daily values. Multivariable logistic regression estimated odds ratios (ORs) for T2D adjusting for sex, race (White vs non-White), ethnicity, hypertension history, age (per 10 years), and BMI (per 5 kg/m²). Model’s T2D prediction performance was assessed using area under the ROC curve (AUROC).

Results: 13,482 participants (51±16 years; 72% female; 79% White) without a history of T2D were analyzed, of whom 189 developed T2D over the 10-year follow-up. The cohort had 327±50 days of wearable data and 249±207 minutes of weekly MVPA. In adjusted models, every additional hour of weekly MVPA was associated with 6% lower odds of T2D (OR:0.94, 95%CI 0.89-1.00, p=.046). Traditional risk factors remained significant, including male sex (OR 1.94, p<.001), non-White race (OR 1.84, p=.005), hypertension history (OR 1.54, p=.02), older age (OR 1.22 per 10 years, p=.002), and higher BMI (OR 1.52 per 5 kg/m², p<.001). The model achieved an AUROC of 0.75 (95% CI 0.69-0.80) for 10-year T2D risk prediction.

Conclusion: In a large national cohort, objective wearable-derived weekly MVPA was independently associated with lower odds of T2D after adjustment for well-known risk factors. These findings support the potential value of wearable-derived activity to complement or refine self-reported measures in diabetes risk scores.

records.introduction_objective: Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA) shares features of both type 1 (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D), leading to frequent misdiagnosis with current tools. This study aimed to determine whether T-cell and B-cell receptor (TCR/BCR) repertoire profiling could serve as a clinically actionable biomarker to accurately distinguish LADA
records.methods: We performed deep TCR and BCR sequencing on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) samples from patients with LADA (n = 20), T1D (n = 20), T2D (n = 15), and healthy donors (HD, n = 20), with an independent validation cohort comprising 15 LADA and 15 T1D patients. Associations between TCR/BCR repertoires and clinical/cytokine profiles were analyzed. Machine learning models were built using repertoire features to discriminate LADA from T1D.
records.results: LADA patients exhibited a distinct immune repertoire signature, characterized by significantly higher TCRα/β and BCR (particularly IgM and IgG) repertoire diversity, and the lowest clonal dominance compared to T1D, T2D, and HD (all P<0.0001). This hyper-diverse, less clonal immune state in LADA was associated with a unique cytokine profile, featuring the highest levels of IL-2 and IFN-γ and the lowest IL-6 (all P<0.0001). Significant correlations were found between repertoire features and key metabolic biomarkers, autoantibody titters, and cytokines. Machine learning models integrating TCR/BCR repertoire features achieved superior performance (AUC = 0.889) in distinguishing LADA from T1D in both training and validation sets, outperforming models based solely on conventional autoantibodies (AUC = 0.667) or clinical indicators (AUC = 0.680).
records.conclusion: TCR/BCR repertoire profiling is a highly accurate and novel diagnostic tool that can effectively differentiate LADA from T1D, offering a direct path to more precise patient classification and personalized management in clinical practice.

Methods: We performed deep TCR and BCR sequencing on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) samples from patients with LADA (n = 20), T1D (n = 20), T2D (n = 15), and healthy donors (HD, n = 20), with an independent validation cohort comprising 15 LADA and 15 T1D patients. Associations between TCR/BCR repertoires and clinical/cytokine profiles were analyzed. Machine learning models were built using repertoire features to discriminate LADA from T1D.

Results: LADA patients exhibited a distinct immune repertoire signature, characterized by significantly higher TCRα/β and BCR (particularly IgM and IgG) repertoire diversity, and the lowest clonal dominance compared to T1D, T2D, and HD (all P<0.0001). This hyper-diverse, less clonal immune state in LADA was associated with a unique cytokine profile, featuring the highest levels of IL-2 and IFN-γ and the lowest IL-6 (all P<0.0001). Significant correlations were found between repertoire features and key metabolic biomarkers, autoantibody titters, and cytokines. Machine learning models integrating TCR/BCR repertoire features achieved superior performance (AUC = 0.889) in distinguishing LADA from T1D in both training and validation sets, outperforming models based solely on conventional autoantibodies (AUC = 0.667) or clinical indicators (AUC = 0.680).

Conclusion: TCR/BCR repertoire profiling is a highly accurate and novel diagnostic tool that can effectively differentiate LADA from T1D, offering a direct path to more precise patient classification and personalized management in clinical practice.

records.introduction_objective: Pancreatic islet function is closely related to cell-cell communication and paracrine signaling, suggesting that the spatial arrangement of endocrine cells could play a critical role in islet physiology. However, quantitative analyses linking islet spatial organization to functional outcomes are limited. This study systematically characterized the distribution and spatial arrangement of endocrine cells and their relationship to islet function.
records.methods: We analyzed the phenotyping data of isolated human islets from 578 organ donors without diabetes obtained through Integrated Islet Distribution Program (IIDP) and Human Pancreas Analysis Program (HPAP), representing different age, sex, BMI, and race/ethnicity. Immunofluorescence images of islet histological sections were processed with machine learning-based pipelines to annotate cell types and extract spatial organization features from 54,974 islets (diameter ≥ 50 μm). Statistical modeling and graph-based deep learning identified associations between cell organization and secretory function.
records.results: Endocrine cell organization was non-random, with significant enrichment of homotypic (i.e., α-α, β-β, and δ-δ cell) contacts (p<10-100). The enrichment level varied substantially between donors (p<10-100). Deep learning models demonstrated that the spatial arrangement of α, β, and δ cells provided predictive power for hormone secretion beyond endocrine cell composition alone. Despite being the smallest of the three endocrine cell types, δ cells showed the strongest associations with stimulated insulin secretion. Both higher δ cell number (p<0.001) and larger per-δ-cell cytoplasmic area (p<0.01) correlated with reduced insulin secretory responses.
records.conclusion: The spatial organization of endocrine cells in human islets exhibits substantial inter-donor heterogeneity yet follows non-random patterns. Neighborhood relationships among endocrine cells, particularly δ cells, are key determinants of human islet function in vitro.

Immunofluorescence images of islet histological sections were processed with machine learning-based pipelines to annotate cell types and extract spatial organization features from 54,974 islets (diameter ≥ 50 μm). Statistical modeling and graph-based deep learning identified associations between cell organization and secretory function.

Conclusion: The spatial organization of endocrine cells in human islets exhibits substantial inter-donor heterogeneity yet follows non-random patterns. Neighborhood relationships among endocrine cells, particularly δ cells, are key determinants of human islet function in vitro.

records.introduction_objective: Effective obesity management requires identifying non-responders early to prevent therapeutic inertia. We aimed to: (1) compare the predictive accuracy of baseline profiling versus early dynamic weight loss markers; and (2) validate a clinical decision rule for escalating treatment to GLP-1 RAs or ketogenic diets (VLCKD).
records.methods: We analyzed a retrospective cohort of 8,450 adults with obesity prescribed a Mediterranean diet (ICANS). We modeled 24-month trajectories using Joint Latent Class Models to account for attrition. XGBoost models predicted non-response using baseline characteristics versus 1-month weight loss velocity. The rule was validated in an independent cohort (N=573) using Target Trial Emulation to compare 12-month outcomes of Standard Care versus Early Intensification.
records.results: Modeling identified a dominant “Early Attrition” phenotype (69%). Baseline profiling (demographics, HOMA-IR, lipids, psychometrics) failed to identify these patients (AUC 0.57). Conversely, incorporating 1-month weight loss velocity achieved high accuracy (AUC 0.91). A practical cutoff of <1.5% weight loss/month achieved >90% sensitivity. In validation, high-risk patients on Standard Care achieved a median 12-month weight loss of only 1.4%. Those switched to Intensified Therapy achieved 7.9% loss (Cohen’s d=1.08, p<0.01). Low-risk patients achieved clinically meaningful loss (10.2%) on Standard Care.
records.conclusion: Baseline profiles are insufficient for predicting dietary success. However, the physiological response at 1 month effectively integrates biological complexity to predict outcomes. A dynamic monitoring strategy using a 1.5% monthly weight loss threshold reliably identifies non-responders who benefit from early escalation.
records.abstract_text:

Methods: We analyzed a retrospective cohort of 8,450 adults with obesity prescribed a Mediterranean diet (ICANS). We modeled 24-month trajectories using Joint Latent Class Models to account for attrition. XGBoost models predicted non-response using baseline characteristics versus 1-month weight loss velocity. The rule was validated in an independent cohort (N=573) using Target Trial Emulation to compare 12-month outcomes of Standard Care versus Early Intensification.

Results: Modeling identified a dominant “Early Attrition” phenotype (69%). Baseline profiling (demographics, HOMA-IR, lipids, psychometrics) failed to identify these patients (AUC 0.57). Conversely, incorporating 1-month weight loss velocity achieved high accuracy (AUC 0.91). A practical cutoff of <1.5% weight loss/month achieved >90% sensitivity. In validation, high-risk patients on Standard Care achieved a median 12-month weight loss of only 1.4%. Those switched to Intensified Therapy achieved 7.9% loss (Cohen’s d=1.08, p<0.01). Low-risk patients achieved clinically meaningful loss (10.2%) on Standard Care.

Conclusion: Baseline profiles are insufficient for predicting dietary success. However, the physiological response at 1 month effectively integrates biological complexity to predict outcomes. A dynamic monitoring strategy using a 1.5% monthly weight loss threshold reliably identifies non-responders who benefit from early escalation.

records.introduction_objective: Digital health platforms generate rich engagement data, yet real-world evidence remains limited on which features are most strongly associated with clinically meaningful glycemic improvement. Understanding these relationships is critical for optimizing personalization and program design. This study used the Dario digital health platform to identify engagement features most strongly associated with reductions in average blood glucose (BG) through enhanced feature engineering and correlation analysis in a real-world diabetes population.
records.methods: A retrospective analysis of members who joined the Dario digital health platform in 2025 with baseline average BG above target (>154 mg/dL; estimated HbA1c (eA1c) >7.0%) examined engagement across integrated app features. A feature-engineering pipeline derived metrics capturing longitudinal trends, timing (early vs late engagement), and frequency across domains. Pearson correlations were calculated between each engagement feature and the decrease in average BG. A random forest model (500 trees) predicted BG reduction, with feature importance assessed.
records.results: In a cohort of 8,056 members, 44.8% achieved a clinically meaningful eA1c reduction of ≥1%. Among those with high-risk baseline BG levels (>183 mg/dL; eA1c >8.0), average BG decreased significantly by 35 mg/dL at month12 (p<0.001). Increasing total engagement over time showed the strongest correlation with glucose improvement (r=0.09, p<0.001). Food tracking trend, physical activity trend, and statistics viewing trend were significantly associated with BG reduction (r= 0.05-0.07, p<0.01). Random forest models identified total engagement consistency as the strongest predictor of glucose improvement.
records.conclusion: In this real-world digital diabetes cohort, consistent, longitudinal engagement rather than a single interaction was strongly linked to glycemic improvement, supporting the use of sustained engagement metrics to guide personalization and optimize digital diabetes care.

records.summary: Deep learning-based multi-omics integration effectively identifies clinically distinct T2D subtypes, outperforming single-omics models. This approach provides a comprehensive insight into T2D heterogeneity, supporting personalized management.
records.introduction_objective: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is highly heterogeneous; accurate stratification is essential for understanding its pathophysiology and advancing precision medicine. We developed a deep learning-based framework to integrate multi-omics data and identify subtypes reflecting molecular and lifestyle factors.
records.methods: In this observational study of 670 T2D patients from the Seoul National University Hospital cohort, we integrated genetic, proteomic, metabolomic, and longitudinal clinical data with a deep learning model. Subtypes were identified via K-means clustering in a clinically informed latent space. Feature importance was assessed using Integrated Gradients, with validation in the UK Biobank cohort.
records.results: Among 670 patients (median age 65 years; mean duration 11.9 years), four distinct subtypes were identified. The subtypes showed high concordance with Ahlqvist et al. subtypes (Adjusted Rand Index [ARI] 0.78), with the multi-omics model outperforming the best single-omics (proteomics) model (mean ARI 0.67 vs. 0.46). Proteomic and metabolomic patterns were major discriminators, while genetic variation provided weak background risk. Omics attribution varied: proteomics was dominant in Mild Age-Related Diabetes (MARD; 82%) but less prominent in Severe Insulin-Resistant Diabetes (SIRD; 28%). Key markers included decreased APOM in SIRD, increased LEP in Mild Obesity-Related Diabetes (MOD), and decreased FABP4 in MARD. Complication prevalence differed significantly (p < 0.05); SIRD was most associated with CKD, while Severe Insulin-Deficient Diabetes (SIDD) showed the highest diabetic retinopathy prevalence. Findings were replicated in the UK Biobank.
records.conclusion: Deep learning-based multi-omics integration effectively identifies clinically distinct T2D subtypes, outperforming single-omics models. This approach provides a comprehensive insight into T2D heterogeneity, supporting personalized management.

records.introduction_objective: Sarcopenia in type 2 diabetes (T2D) is accelerated by anabolic resistance and glucotoxicity. We evaluated whether a 'triple-stack' of leucine-enriched essential amino acids (EAA), creatine HCl, and calcium-HMB, combined with AI-driven 'Digital Twin' metabolic coaching, improves appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASMM) and glycemic markers compared with placebo.
records.methods: In this 12-week double-blind trial, adults with T2D (HbA1c 6.5-8.5%) and confirmed sarcopenia were randomized to: (A) Active supplement (15g EAA with 4g leucine, 3g creatine HCl, 3g Ca-HMB) + BiOS AI app; or (B) Placebo + sham app. The BiOS AI app provided real-time metabolic 'action plans' based on Digital Twin glucose predictions. The primary outcome was ASMM change (DXA). Secondary outcomes included grip strength and Triglyceride-Glucose (TyG) index.
records.results: Ninety participants (mean age 64±6 y) completed the study. The intervention increased ASMM (+1.4±0.3 kg vs +0.2±0.2 kg; P<0.01) and grip strength (+12% vs +1%; P<0.05) compared with control. The TyG index, a marker of lipotoxicity, decreased significantly in the intervention arm (-18% vs -3%; P<0.05). Adherence was 92% in the app-guided group. No renal adverse events occurred.
records.conclusion: A targeted anabolic nutrient stack combined with Digital Twin coaching reverses sarcopenic muscle loss and improves metabolic quality in T2D. This 'nutrition + digital' model offers a scalable strategy to combat diabetic frailty.

records.introduction_objective: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) is a key driver of insulin resistance (IR), but it’s unclear if insulin secretory capacity modulates this link. It also remains an open question, if primary hyperinsulinemia—high β-cell output before dysglycemia—is permissive or causal for IR. Longitudinal models predicted M-value change (ΔM) from baseline VAT, ΔVAT, baseline BCF and interactions.
records.results: In cross-sectional analyses adjusted for sex, BMI and diabetes type, higher VAT was tightly associated with lower M-value (each SD increase in VAT: β=−0.54 SD log-M, p<0.001), whereas SAT was weakly associated with M-value (β=−0.14, p=0.012). Introduction and Objective: Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) is a key driver of insulin resistance (IR), but it’s unclear if insulin secretory capacity modulates this link. It also remains an open question, if primary hyperinsulinemia—high β-cell output before dysglycemia—is permissive or causal for IR. Since surrogate indices do not allow assessing insulin secretion independently of insulin sensitivity, we used independent tests to examine whether β-cell function (BCF) modifies VAT-associated IR in the German Diabetes Study (GDS).

Methods: We analyzed 1,641 GDS participants with normal glucose tolerance (NGT), type 1 (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D), with baseline MRI-measured VAT and subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) volumes, clamp-derived insulin sensitivity (M-value), and glucagon-stimulated 6-min C-peptide measurements. Repeated measures were available in 640 participants. Cross-sectional analyses used multivariable linear models with interactions. Longitudinal models predicted M-value change (ΔM) from baseline VAT, ΔVAT, baseline BCF and interactions.

Results: In cross-sectional analyses adjusted for sex, BMI and diabetes type, higher VAT was tightly associated with lower M-value (each SD increase in VAT: β=−0.54 SD log-M, p<0.001), whereas SAT was weakly associated with M-value (β=−0.14, p=0.012). Higher BCF associated with higher M-value (β=0.13, p=0.018). However, higher BCF strengthened the inverse VAT association with M-value (VAT×BCF interaction: β=−0.19, p<0.001). The association of VAT with M-value was present in NGT/T2D (ß<-1.22, p<0.001), but weak in T1D (β=−0.57, p=0.054). Longitudinally, increases in VAT related to decreased M-value only in those with higher baseline BCF (ΔVAT×BCF: β=−6.53×10−4, p=0.018).

Conclusion: BCF modifies the association of VAT with IR across cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses, indicating that VAT-related IR is strongest with preserved BCF and consistent with insulin hypersecretion contributing to the development of IR.

records.conclusion: This DAG-based framework provides a foundation for future machine learning analysis, identifying key baseline determinants of ITx outcome, including era, centre, IR and IS.

Participants were stratified into four subgroups using a 2×2 framework based on predicted risks of progression to diabetes and CVD.

Results: In internal validation, T-PDM-CVD achieved AUCs of 0.72 (95% CI: 0.70-0.73) for T2D and 0.64 (95% CI: 0.63-0.65) for CVD. In external validation, AUCs improved to 0.80 (95% CI: 0.79-0.81) for T2D and 0.75 (95% CI: 0.74-0.76) for CVD.Compared to the low T2D-CVD risk group, the isolated high-T2D subgroup had the highest risk of developing diabetes (HR 3.31, 95% CI 3.13-3.50), and the isolated high-CVD subgroup had the highest cardiovascular risk (HR 1.93, 95% CI 1.77-2.10). Conclusion: The T-PDM-CVD model enables simultaneous prediction of T2D and CVD risks in prediabetes, providing enhanced risk stratification to inform personalized prevention strategies.

records.introduction_objective: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are chronic, slow-healing wounds characterized by unresolved inflammation affecting a significant proportion of patients with diabetes. Dysregulated NLRP3 inflammasome activation in diabetic wounds contributes to chronic inflammation, impeding tissue repair and promoting ulcer chronicity. NLRP3 expression is significantly upregulated in patients with DFUs compared to healthy controls.
records.methods: THP-1 derived macrophages and primary cells were used to evaluate compound activity in vitro. Selectivity was assessed by testing against other inflammasomes and a 44-panel safety assay. Hyperglycemia was induced in mice with STZ and a full-thickness wound created on the dorsal skin. Efficacy was assessed by wound closure rate.
records.results: Using our AI-based drug discovery platforms, we developed ISM5059, a peripherally restricted NLRP3 inhibitor with nanomolar inhibition potency of IL-1β (IC50 10.2 nM) and IL-18 (IC50 9.1 nM) release in THP-1-derived macrophages. ISM5059 showed similar activity in primary human monocytes and mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages. ISM5059 displays high selectivity, with no inhibitory activity on AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1 inflammasomes, and a clean safety profile in a 44-panel screen. In vivo efficacy evaluated in an STZ-induced diabetic foot ulcer mouse model found ISM5059 accelerated wound healing in a dose-dependent fashion; at 6 mg/kg, its effect was comparable to the positive control, dapagliflozin. Combined treatment with dapagliflozin further accelerated wound closure, achieving healing rates similar to those observed in non-diabetic, healthy mice. ISM5059 exhibited favorable drug-like properties, including optimal in vitro ADMET profiles, strong in vivo exposure and clearance, and excellent oral bioavailability across multiple preclinical species.
records.conclusion: These findings establish ISM5059 as an effective and selective peripheral NLRP3 inhibitor with robust efficacy and a promising safety margin for potential treatment of diabetic foot ulcers.

records.introduction_objective: In GO MOMs, early pregnancy OGTT did not sufficiently improve prediction of gestational diabetes (GDM) or large-for-gestational age birthweight (LGA) beyond clinical factors to warrant universal first-trimester screening. This secondary analysis evaluated if early metabolic or lipid measures improved predictions of these outcomes.
records.methods: Singleton gravidas without preexisting diabetes from 9 US centers had 75g OGTT, metabolic measures [Matsuda insulin sensitivity (IS), β-cell function (βCF)] and fasting lipids [free fatty acids (FFA), triglycerides (TG)] at 10-14 weeks gestation. Logistic regression models evaluated addition of IS and βCF to clinical factors (age, BMI, history of GDM or macrosomia) and OGTT values for prediction of GDM at 24-28 weeks using Carpenter-Coustan criteria. For prediction of LGA, FFA and TG were added to the models. Binary variable cutoffs maximized area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) in a training data set (4 centers), with results validated in remaining centers.
records.results: Of 2178 GO MOMs participants, 91% completed OGTTs (15% GDM) and 96% had live births (11% LGA). Neither IS nor βCF improved predictive accuracy compared to models with clinical factors or clinical factors + OGTT for GDM. For LGA, neither metabolic measures nor lipids improved prediction (Figures).
records.conclusion: Metabolic or lipid measures in early pregnancy do not improve prediction of GDM or LGA over clinical factors + OGTT.

records.introduction_objective: Translating genetic and molecular biomarkers into clinically actionable T2D risk prediction models is challenged by uncertain incremental value beyond standard clinical factors in real-world populations. We assessed metabolomic risk score (MRS) and a polygenic risk score (PRS) for incident T2D prediction in a diverse healthcare system.
records.methods: We studied 36,352 adults free of diabetes at metabolite assessment in the Mass General Brigham Biobank and followed for care for ~6 years. We derived the MRS using elastic net regression in UK Biobank (N=233K; 10,707 incident cases; follow-up: ~13 years) profiled on the Nightingale platform, and a PRS constructed from T2D GWAS summary statistics. Cox models to predict incident T2D were sequentially adjusted from demographics to established clinical risk scores (BMI, blood pressure, family history, and lipids), random glucose and HbA1c to mimic varying levels of clinical data availability.
records.results: Both MRS and PRS were associated with incident T2D and improved discrimination in all models including those adjusted for HbA1c (P < 10-10, iC-index 0.01). Each standard deviation increase in MRS was associated with a threefold risk (age/sex adjusted model: HR 3.0, 95% CI 2.8-3.2, C-index 0.83; fully adjusted model: HR 1.7, 1.4-2.0, 0.84). Associations were stronger at higher BMI and among GLP-1 receptor agonist users (P interaction < 10⁻⁴) adjusting for clinical factors including BMI. Absolute risk estimation showed marked stratification: individuals with high MRS and PRS had ~30% 10-year T2D risk by age 40 and >50% by age 60 whereas lower risk profiles were <3% in all BMI categories. Higher MRS was also associated with increased risk of incident chronic kidney disease among individuals with T2D.
records.conclusion: MRS and PRS provide complementary, clinically meaningful prediction of T2D beyond HbA1c and BMI supporting the integration of molecular profiling with standard clinical risk factors for targeted T2D prevention and risk reduction.

Cox models to predict incident T2D were sequentially adjusted from demographics to established clinical risk scores (BMI, blood pressure, family history, and lipids), random glucose and HbA1c to mimic varying levels of clinical data availability.

Results: Both MRS and PRS were associated with incident T2D and improved discrimination in all models including those adjusted for HbA1c (P < 10-10, iC-index 0.01). Higher MRS was also associated with increased risk of incident chronic kidney disease among individuals with T2D.

Conclusion: MRS and PRS provide complementary, clinically meaningful prediction of T2D beyond HbA1c and BMI supporting the integration of molecular profiling with standard clinical risk factors for targeted T2D prevention and risk reduction.

records.introduction_objective: We examined the association between a composite social determinant of health (SDOH) score and incident coronary heart disease (CHD), adjusting for genetic susceptibility to CHD and traditional risk factors, among adults with T2D.

Missing SDOH survey items were imputed using random forests with predictive mean matching. A weighted, standardized SDOH-CHD score was developed using an elastic-net model. records.authors: WEI THING SZE, DANIEL LANE, RYOHEI NAKADA, KAYO WAKI, Tokyo, Japan, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, Japan, Bunkyo-ku, Japan
records.trigger_snippet: 1286-OR - FiberMore: A Generative AI-Enabled Behavior Change Intervention to Improve Dietary Fiber Intake and Glycemic Management in Individuals with Type 2 Diabetes Introduction and Objective: A high intake of dietary fiber has been shown to imp
records.summary: A generative AI-powered, app-based intervention led to a significant increase in dietary fiber intake and a corresponding reduction in HbA1c.
records.introduction_objective: A high intake of dietary fiber has been shown to improve glycemic management in individuals living with Type 2 diabetes (T2D). We developed FiberMore, a generative AI-based mobile app grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior, to address inadequate fiber intake in individuals with T2D, and assessed its efficacy in increasing fiber intake and reducing HbA1c levels.
records.methods: This is a single-blinded randomized controlled trial targeting 70 adults with T2D from two hospitals in Tokyo with a 12-week intervention and 12-week observation. The intervention group used FiberMore, which employs a fine-tuned GPT-4o model to analyze meal nutrients and provides personalized, real-time feedback on fiber. An AI chatbot embedded in FiberMore delivers personalized goal setting, barrier/coping-strategy setting, emotional attitude assessment, and education. The control group received sham salt-reduction education and recorded daily salt-reduction efforts in a diary.
records.results: The intervention group showed a greater fiber increase from run-in to Week 12 than the control group (+7.3 g vs -0.9 g), with a significant between-group difference of +8.2 g (P < 0.001) representing a 64% increase. HbA1c decreased by 0.35% in the intervention group and by 0.14% in the control group, resulting in a not-significant between-group difference of 0.21% after baseline adjustment (P = 0.170, 95% CI −0.52 to −0.092), which was consistent with prediction from a published fiber dose-response relationship (estimated −0.27%, 95% CI −0.55 to 0.00) for a 64% increase in fiber. Higher engagement with AI-delivered behavior change strategies, including goal setting, barrier/coping-strategy setting, and emotional attitude assessment, were significantly associated with greater dietary fiber intake (P < 0.05).
records.conclusion: A generative AI-powered, app-based intervention led to a significant increase in dietary fiber intake and a corresponding reduction in HbA1c.

records.introduction_objective: While diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) prediction models have been successfully developed using electronic health record (EHR) data, incorporating continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) metrics may further improve risk stratification. To explore this possibility, we examined the association between CGM metrics and DKA events in adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D).
records.methods: We identified adults with T1D treated in our health system between 1/1/2017 - 3/20/2025 by adapting the SUPREME-DM and Klompas algorithms to our EHR. We identified DKA events using the ADA 2024 Consensus criteria. We included those whose Dexcom CGM data was retrievable from Dexcom Clarity prior to DKA-related hospitalization. For these individuals, we extracted pre-DKA data (i.e., all available CGM data from the 90-day window preceding each DKA event) and non-DKA data (i.e., all available CGM data, up to 450 days, separated ≥90 days from any DKA event). We used mixed-effects models to compare CGM metrics (e.g., time-in-range, variability, Glycemia Risk Index) between pre-DKA periods and matched non-DKA periods across four prespecified time windows (1, 7, 30, and 89 days before DKA).
records.results: Thirteen adults (mean age 56.5 ± 19.2 years, 46% female) experienced 28 DKA-related hospitalizations. On the day immediately preceding DKA, mean glucose was markedly elevated compared with 1-day non-DKA periods (263 vs. 199 mg/dL, p<0.001), time >250 mg/dL doubled (50% vs. 24%, p<0.001), and time-in-range was halved (24% vs. 49%, p<0.001). Glycemic variability was increased in the 7-day pre-DKA window (mean amplitude of glycemic excursions [MAGE] 180 vs. 157, p=0.006). In the 30- and 89-day pre-DKA windows, the Hypoglycemia Component of the Glycemia Risk Index was significantly reduced (0.4 vs. 1.0 at 30 days, p=0.012; 0.3 vs. 0.8 at 89 days, p=0.008).
records.conclusion: CGM metrics were associated with DKA across time windows from 1 to 89 days. Future work will integrate CGM-derived metrics into our EHR-based DKA prediction model to enhance risk stratification.

On the day immediately preceding DKA, mean glucose was markedly elevated compared with 1-day non-DKA periods (263 vs. 199 mg/dL, p<0.001), time >250 mg/dL doubled (50% vs. 24%, p<0.001), and time-in-range was halved (24% vs. 49%, p<0.001). Glycemic variability was increased in the 7-day pre-DKA window (mean amplitude of glycemic excursions [MAGE] 180 vs. 157, p=0.006). In the 30- and 89-day pre-DKA windows, the Hypoglycemia Component of the Glycemia Risk Index was significantly reduced (0.4 vs. 1.0 at 30 days, p=0.012; 0.3 vs. 0.8 at 89 days, p=0.008).

Conclusion: CGM metrics were associated with DKA across time windows from 1 to 89 days. Future work will integrate CGM-derived metrics into our EHR-based DKA prediction model to enhance risk stratification.

Introduction and Objective: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived pancreatic β-like cells (hPSC-β cells) represent a promising cell source for diabetes therapy. However, their clinical translation is hampered by time- and cost-intensive differentiation protocols. Establishing a scalable expansion system for hPSC-derived pancreatic endoderm (progenitor) cells (hPSC-PEs) would enable accessible regenerative therapies.

Methods: To identify the mechanisms limiting their expansion, we performed single-nucleus multi-omics analysis, machine learning approach, and chemical compound screening for hPSC-PEs.

Conclusion: These findings elucidate fundamental mechanisms constraining progenitor cell expansion and establish a robust expansion system, thereby paving the way for scalable transplantation therapies.

Introduction and Objective: MASLD is a common polygenic condition, but current GWASs have only identified 14 loci due to a lack of scalable, clinically relevant phenotypes.

Methods: Using machine learning on four UKBB data modalities (MRI, DXA, plasma metabolites, blood biomarkers; n=25,474 to 262,927), we predicted liver fat (LF) and adipose tissue volume (ATV), increasing statistical power. A GWAS of LF, adjusting for ATV, identified liver-specific genes. Liver-targeted siRNAs validated key targets in vitro and in vivo in mice and monkeys.

Results: GWAS identified 480 loci linked to LF accumulation, showing strong genetic correlation with predicted LF (R2 = 0.79-0.97), and MASLD (R2 = 0.73-0.87). Novel de novo lipogenesis (DNL) genes were found, with IRS1 being the strongest association (p = 2 x 10-82) and supported across all four modalities. A potent, selective liver-targeted siRNA against IRS1 (IC50~0.04 nM) suppressed lipid accumulation in human hepatocytes. In DIO mice a single dose (0.3-10 mg/kg) reduced hepatic IRS1 expression (85%), DNL (59%) and triglycerides (45%) after one month, significantly improving NAS score (2.2 ± 0.2 vs. vehicle 4.3 ± 0.2, p = 0.0002). Cynomolgus monkeys (3 and 10 mg/kg) showed sustained hepatic IRS1 reduction for 28 days without affecting glucose homeostasis.

Conclusion: Liver-targeted siRNA effectively targets IRS1, showing efficacy and tolerability in preclinical MASLD models.

records.introduction_objective: In-hospital hypoglycemia increases the risk of mortality, but there is a lack of risk-stratification tools to identify those at risk of hypoglycemia-related adverse events. We aimed to develop a prognostic model to estimate mortality risk within 24 hours of resolution of in-hospital hypoglycemia in people living with diabetes (PLwD).
records.methods: All in-hospital hypoglycemic episodes (glucose <3.9mmol/l) in PLwD between January 2023 and December 2024 were extracted from a multi-centre (11 hospitals) NHS trust dataset in England. A derivation model was developed using a multiple logistic regression, with collinearity, performance and calibration being assessed. Discrimination was assessed using the Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC), and the magnitude of individual predictors was assessed using odds ratios (OR). Internal validation was performed using bootstrapping.
records.results: 2160 hypoglycaemic episodes were included in the dataset. 7.0% were associated with mortality within 24 hours of resolution. Type 2 diabetes (OR 2.1 compared to type 1 diabetes), Charlson Comorbidity Index score (OR 1.1 per unit score increase), IHSG level 2 or 3 (OR 4.4 Level 2 and OR 10.1 Level 3 compared to Level 1) and precipitating factors (OR 2.0 for fasting/missing a meal and OR 2.1 for multiple factors vs unclear cause) were included in the final model. The model demonstrated moderate discrimination (AUROC: 0.74), good calibration, and high stability in internal validation (AUROC 0.73 after optimisation).
records.conclusion: We successfully developed and internally validated a prognostic model to predict mortality within 24 hours of hypoglycaemia in PLwD in acute settings. This tool could support early risk stratification and clinical decision-making in acute settings.

records.introduction_objective: Inpatient hypoglycemia remains a challenge and is associated with increased complications and mortality. Our institution’s improvement efforts include a hypoglycemia prediction alert developed in 2012 and integrated into the electronic health record (EHR) in 2023. We aimed to enhance the model’s predictive performance by utilizing a machine learning model.
records.methods: An XGBoost binary classification model was trained on four years of adult inpatient EHR data to identify real‑time hypoglycemia risk. Eligible encounters included non‑ICU, non-pregnant, adult inpatients receiving insulin; insulin infusions were excluded. The outcome was blood glucose (BG) <70 mg/dL occurring ≥12 hours after admission. Data were randomly split 70% for training and 30% for validation. Features included 24‑hour glucose trends, lab values, 24‑hour insulin doses by type, demographics, length of stay, renal replacement therapy, prior severe hypoglycemia, and diabetes type.
records.results: Among 133,392 encounters, ~11% (14,615) experienced BG <70 mg/dL. The model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.89. Top features ranked highest-to lowest included creatinine clearance, A1c, length of stay, weight, minimum 24‑hour BG, albumin, basal and rapid‑acting insulin totals, most recent BG, and age. A score threshold of 0.35 balanced performance: F1‑score 45%, precision (PPV) 30%, recall (sensitivity) 84%, NPV 97%, specificity 76%, accuracy 77%. Performance improved markedly over the 2012 model, which had lower precision (16%), F1‑score (25%), and recall (70%).
records.conclusion: The optimized model demonstrated substantially improved predictive performance over the previous version within acceptable tolerance for clinical decision support use.

records.introduction_objective: Obesity is associated with elevated urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR), but bidirectional relationships and hormone-mediated effects remain unclear. We examined obesity-ACR bidirectionality and cortisol’s role in non-diabetic/non-hypertensive individuals.
records.methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study of 2,724 participants without diabetes or hypertension. Obesity indices included body mass index (BMI), visceral fat level (VFL), body fat percentage (PBF), and waist-hip ratio (WHR). The primary outcome was ACR positivity (≥30 mg/g). Spearman correlation, multivariate logistic regression and stratified analysis were used to assess associations, adjusted for demographics and metabolic factors.
records.results: Compared with normal-weight participants, severely obese individuals had a 5.56-fold higher risk of ACR positivity (95%CI: 3.48-8.87, P<0.001). VFL showed the strongest correlation with ACR (r=0.32, P<0.001), and cortisol mediated 31.3% of this association. Gender differences were observed: VFL was an independent risk factor in males (OR=1.14, 95%CI: 1.10-1.18, P<0.001), while PBF was critical in females (OR=1.07, 95%CI: 1.04-1.10, P<0.001). The ACR positivity prediction model had an AUC of 0.836 (95%CI: 0.802-0.870).
records.conclusion: Central obesity and ACR have bidirectional links, with cortisol as key mediator and gender-specific effects. VFL and cortisol aid obesity-related renal injury risk stratification, supporting targeted visceral fat reduction.

records.introduction_objective: Cathepsin L (CTSL) is a lysosomal cysteine protease that promotes tubular inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and renal fibrosis in diabetic kidney disease (DKD). Although CTSL is a validated therapeutic target, the lack of clinically actionable inhibitors remains a major translational barrier. This study aimed to establish a deep learning-enabled discovery framework to identify CTSL inhibitors from natural products and evaluate their therapeutic potential in DKD-relevant models.
records.methods: An integrated pipeline combining deep learning-based activity prediction, structure-informed molecular docking, and multidimensional ranking was used to prioritize CTSL inhibitor candidates from a curated natural product library. Two hundred compounds were selected for experimental validation. CTSL enzymatic inhibition was assessed in vitro, followed by cytotoxicity screening in human renal tubular HK-2 cells. Lead compounds were evaluated in metabolically stressed DKD cellular models. Enzyme kinetic analyses and molecular dynamics simulations were performed to characterize inhibition mechanisms and target engagement.
records.results: Nine compounds showed reproducible, concentration-dependent CTSL inhibition. Kuwanon G, Iberverin, and Wighteone achieved greater than 50% inhibition at non-cytotoxic concentrations. Kuwanon G emerged as the lead compound, significantly reducing inflammatory signaling and fibrotic marker expression under high-glucose and high-lipid conditions. Kinetic analyses identified Kuwanon G as a competitive CTSL inhibitor, while molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated stable binding within the catalytic pocket.
records.conclusion: Deep learning-enabled drug discovery effectively accelerates CTSL inhibitor identification and overcomes key translational barriers in DKD. Kuwanon G represents a promising CTSL-targeted therapeutic candidate for further development.

Methods: An integrated pipeline combining deep learning-based activity prediction, structure-informed molecular docking, and multidimensional ranking was used to prioritize CTSL inhibitor candidates from a curated natural product library. Two hundred compounds were selected for experimental validation. CTSL enzymatic inhibition was assessed in vitro, followed by cytotoxicity screening in human renal tubular HK-2 cells. Lead compounds were evaluated in metabolically stressed DKD cellular models. Kinetic analyses identified Kuwanon G as a competitive CTSL inhibitor, while molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated stable binding within the catalytic pocket.

Conclusion: Deep learning-enabled drug discovery effectively accelerates CTSL inhibitor identification and overcomes key translational barriers in DKD. Kuwanon G represents a promising CTSL-targeted therapeutic candidate for further development.

AI-derived retinal biomarkers enable non-invasive vascular phenotyping and may complement circulating markers for CVD risk assessment. Adding Lp(a) to Dr Noon CVD improved discrimination (C-index 0.6490 to 0.6515; Δ0.0024; P = 0.001).
records.conclusion: Elevated Lp(a) was associated with higher incident CVD risk, primarily among individuals with elevated retinal risk. Integrating Lp(a) with retinal biomarkers may improve CVD risk assessment.

Simple cutpoint (TG/HDL >3.5) identifies high-risk patients despite optimal glycemic control. records.introduction_objective: The Steno T1 Risk Engine (ST1RE) is a prediction model for estimating the risk of the first fatal or nonfatal cardiovascular (CV) event and is recommended to assess CV risk in people living with type 1 diabetes (T1D). However, it does not include lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)], a recognized independent CV risk factor. We aimed to evaluate the impact of Lp(a) on CV risk category reclassification compared to ST1RE estimates.
records.methods: The InLipoDiab1 is a longitudinal observational study of adults with newly diagnosed T1D (NCT02306005). We studied 122 adults (82 men and 40 women) with T1D and no prior cardiovascular disease (CVD). ST1RE 5‑ and 10‑year risks were calculated and categorized as low (<10%), moderate (10-20%) and high (≥20%). Lp(a) was measured using immunoturbidimetry and results were stated in nmol/L. Lp(a)-based CV risk categories were classified as low (<75 nmol/L), moderate (75-125 nmol/L), and high (>125 nmol/L). Reclassification (upward, downward, or unchanged) was quantified, and symmetry was assessed using Bowker’s test.
records.results: Median age was 32 [28-37] years and diabetes duration was 7 [4,25-8] years. After considering Lp(a), the 5-year CVD risk category estimated with ST1RE moved up for 18% of individuals. For the 10-year CVD risk category estimation, 18% moved up and 4.9% moved down (overall 23% changed category). Bowker’s test indicated significant asymmetry for 10‑year reclassification (χ²=16.00, df=3, p=0.00113), mainly due to transitions from low ST1RE to high Lp(a) category.
records.conclusion: In adults with T1D without prior CVD, incorporating Lp(a) alters CV risk stratification. These data support including Lp(a) in routine CV risk assessment to refine prevention strategies in T1D.

records.introduction_objective: Adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1D) require contextually-aware, evidence-based self-management support. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) lack integration with systematically synthesized and appraised evidence or contextual tailoring. This study aimed to construct and evaluate T1DiaBot, a knowledge graph-grounded agent designed for adolescents with T1D.
records.methods: A self-developed “Evidence-to-Performance” (E2P) framework was followed: 1) Knowledge Graph Construction: The Diabetes Self-Management Knowledge Graph (DSM-KG) was constructed through synthesizing clinical guidelines and reviews, followed by contextual adaptation. 2) Agent Development: T1DiaBot was developed using LangChain, employing a Graph-RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) approach where the DSM-KG serves as the authoritative grounding source. 3) Validation: Clinical validity was assessed via a two-round Delphi experts panel (N=10); usability and safety via a one-month beta-test (N=20 users). 4) Benchmarking: Performance was compared against four general-purpose LLMs (DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi, Doubao) using 81 real-world queries, blindly rated by clinical experts (N=6) and a youth advisory panel (N=27 users).
records.results: The DSM-KG comprises six sub-graphs (e.g., non-familial setting management, insulin adjustment, parent-child communication, psychosocial support). T1DiaBot achieved high expert consensus (Kendall’s W=0.48-0.63), excellent usability (mean System Usability Scale score: 86.5/100), and no adverse events. It outperformed the four general LLMs in Content Accuracy and Adolescent Scenario Suitability (all P<0.001) and showed consistent superiority over one benchmark (Kimi) in all user experience dimensions (p>0.05).
records.conclusion: T1DiaBot is a clinically accurate and culturally tailored AI tool for supporting T1D self-management. The E2P framework provides a rigorous methodology for creating evidence-based AI agents in chronic disease care.

records.introduction_objective: Glucokinase (GK) is a central regulator of glucose homeostasis, with dysfunction closely linked to T2DM. As GK activators enter clinical practice, efficient and accurate knowledge transfer is required to support clinical decision-making and individualized therapy. However, GK biology spans complex multi-organ networks (pancreas-liver, gut-pancreas, and pancreas-brain), exceeding the capacity of conventional manual curation.
records.methods: We developed GK Charger, an intelligent interactive platform integrating large language models (LLMs) with a structured knowledge base (GK Brain). The system includes: (1) a curated, modular GK knowledge base derived from literature, clinical guidelines, expert consensus, and drug information; (2) an LLM-enabled knowledge graph capturing entities and semantic relationships; and (3) attention-based embedding models enabling semantic association, reasoning, and identification of users’ knowledge gaps. Natural language interaction supports physician education, pharmaceutical training, and patient consultation. All outputs undergo periodic expert review to ensure scientific accuracy.
records.results: Pilot implementation demonstrated enhanced clinical teams’ efficiency and depth of understanding of GK-mediated glucose regulation. Literature-linked outputs improved scientific rigor, while semantic simplification translated complex mechanisms into patient-comprehensible information, supporting clinical management adherence. User interaction-driven learning enabled automated identification of knowledge gaps and iterative optimization of the knowledge base, establishing a closed-loop knowledge management system.
records.conclusion: GK Charger illustrates a scalable and reproducible paradigm integrating artificial intelligence with authoritative medical knowledge, supporting precision education and digital healthcare delivery in T2DM.

records.introduction_objective: Dietary management for type 2 diabetes is based on evidence demonstrating improvements in surrogate outcomes such as blood glucose, blood pressure, and serum lipids. However, there is limited evidence using the onset of complications themselves as an outcome. Furthermore, as nutrients and dietary patterns are intricately interrelated, conventional statistical analysis methods have limitations. This study aimed to identify nutrients associated with the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) in a cohort of type 2 diabetes patients through the use of AI.
records.methods: We analyzed male patients with type 2 diabetes enrolled in the JDCS and J-EDIT cohorts, among whom 59 coronary heart disease (CHD) events were observed. Using a subgroup detection approach incorporating principal component analysis (PCA), linear regression, and Wilcoxon’s rank‑sum test, we identified a latent subgroup characterized by an association between nutrient intake and CHD risk. PCA was subsequently reapplied to this subgroup to define a high‑risk population. Finally, CHD incidence was compared between the high‑ and low‑risk groups using Kaplan-Meier survival curves, the log‑rank test, and hazard ratios (HRs).
records.results: A subgroup characterized by insufficient intake of potassium, vitamin B6, etc. was identified. Within this subgroup, excessive intake of protein, vitamin B1, etc. was associated with an elevated risk of CHD. The high‑risk group demonstrated a significantly higher incidence of CHD events (P = 0.024; HR = 4.90; 95% CI, 1.06-22.66).
records.conclusion: Analysis using artificial intelligence has facilitated the identification of high-risk groups through complex combinations of conditions. In men with type 2 diabetes who are deficient in potassium, vitamin B6, and other nutrients, excessive intake of protein and vitamin B1 may be associated with an increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD).

records.introduction_objective: Implementing lifestyle interventions guided by continuous glucose monitor (CGM) data can potentially prevent progression and reduce risk of prediabetes and type 2 diabetes (T2D). Maintaining healthy behaviors is particularly difficult in high-stress work environments like health care workers (HCWs). Sutter Health created a Metabolic Wellness Program (MWP) to educate on interpreting CGM data to help make personalized and sustainable lifestyle changes. We sought to understand the experience and impact of MWP for HCWs in-depth.
records.methods: At least three months after participating in MWP, two researchers conducted semi-structured interviews that were audio-recorded and transcribed. De-identified transcripts were uploaded into Databricks, and we used Open AI’s GPT OSS 120b to generate initial themes and supporting quotations. Themes were validated, refined, and finalized by human qualitative experts.
records.results: We interviewed 29 participants (7 metabolically healthy, 11 with pre-diabetes, 11 with T2D). Many participants mentioned their main motivations for joining MWP were family history and/or currently had prediabetes/T2D. Many said that they felt these sessions were better than primary care as they received “more in-depth” and specific information than general advice of “manage weight and exercise.” Participants reported mixed feelings about CGMs, with some expressing benefit from directly seeing impact of food and exercise while others noted additional “anxiety” from “spikes” and “alarms.” Sustained behavior changes months after MWP were also mixed, with some making “lasting changes” through increased exercise after meals and “eating carbs last” while others missed “accountability” from MWP or not having additional CGMs.
records.conclusion: The findings suggest that MWP may help to improve metabolic health and provide some sustained behavior change to potentially decrease the risk of diabetes and pre-diabetes in HCWs.

We leveraged the mySugr app database (over 5 million downloads) to measure the impact of digital engagement on glycemic outcomes. records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Despite the indisputable benefits of tight glycemic control and well defined clinical targets, real-world goal attainment remains hard to achieve.
We leveraged the mySugr app database (over 5 million downloads) to measure the impact of digital engagement on glycemic outcomes. Our goal was to apply machine learning to this real-world data to automatically detect complex behavioural interactions driving success, avoiding the need to explicitly hypothesize and model these terms as required in standard linear regression.

Methods: We analyzed glycemic and non-glycemic outcomes after 90 days of app use. Unlike traditional linear modeling, which assumes additive effects unless interactions are manually specified, we employed non-linear machine learning models paired with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). This methodology allowed us to automatically discover and quantify non-linear synergies between user characteristics and behaviors that drive goal achievement variability.

Results: Baseline glycemic status was the strongest predictor of outcome. SHAP interaction plots revealed that the relationship between engagement and outcome was non-linear: increased digital engagement (specifically session counts, tagging, and logging) correlated with improved glycemic control, but this benefit was significantly amplified in users with a baseline blood glucose >200 mg/dL. Subgroup analysis further identified distinct behavioural drivers: for Type 1 DM, irregular meal timing (specifically dinner) hindered improvement, while for Type 2 DM, overall BG irregularity was the primary predictor of poorer outcomes.

Conclusion: In summary, this work highlights the pivotal role of mobile health apps in diabetes management. Furthermore, it demonstrates the utility of explainable AI in decoding intricate, high-order interactions between behaviour and glycemic control that would likely remain hidden under the constraints of linear assumptions.

records.introduction_objective: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) often co-occurs with multiple chronic conditions. In our study, we analyzed comorbidities and their associated burden on self-rated general health in adults with T2D to corroborate the strongest predictors of poor health.
records.methods: We analyzed 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) data for adults with T2D who reported general health as excellent/very good/good (good) or poor; respondents reporting fair health were excluded, giving us a cohort of 7,619 individuals. Analyses incorporated survey weights and complex design. Chi-square tests compared comorbidity prevalence. Multivariable logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for poor vs good health. Random forest approaches were used to corroborate predictor importance for poor health classification.
records.results: Poor health was reported by 15.91% (n=1,212/7,619) of adults with T2D. Compared to good health, poor health was associated with higher prevalence of depressive disorder (45.67% vs 17.16%) and blindness/vision difficulty (21.56% vs 5.80%), as well as stroke, coronary heart disease (CHD), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), kidney disease, asthma, feet sores, hearing loss, arthritis, and cancer. In adjusted models, stroke had the strongest association with poor health (OR 3.684, 95% CI 2.501-5.425), followed by CHD (OR 3.553, 2.428-5.199), COPD (OR 2.563, 1.831-3.587), kidney disease (OR 2.459, 1.695-3.568), asthma (OR 2.170, 1.583-2.977), and vision difficulty (OR 2.416, 1.612-3.622). In random forest analyses, COPD and CHD were the most important comorbid predictors of poor health.
records.conclusion: Self-rated poor health in adults with T2D marks a high-risk group characterized by substantial vascular and pulmonary comorbidity and frequent visual, mental health, and physical health complications. Incorporating general health status into routine assessment may enable practical risk stratification and trigger integrating screening and prevention strategies to reduce avoidable complications.

Introduction and Objective: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) often co-occurs with multiple chronic conditions. In our study, we analyzed comorbidities and their associated burden on self-rated general health in adults with T2D to corroborate the strongest predictors of poor health.

Methods: We analyzed 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) data for adults with T2D who reported general health as excellent/very good/good (good) or poor; respondents reporting fair health were excluded, giving us a cohort of 7,619 individuals. Analyses incorporated survey weights and complex design. Chi-square tests compared comorbidity prevalence. Multivariable logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for poor vs good health. Random forest approaches were used to corroborate predictor importance for poor health classification.

Results: Poor health was reported by 15.91% (n=1,212/7,619) of adults with T2D. Compared to good health, poor health was associated with higher prevalence of depressive disorder (45.67% vs 17.16%) and blindness/vision difficulty (21.56% vs 5.80%), as well as stroke, coronary heart disease (CHD), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), kidney disease, asthma, feet sores, hearing loss, arthritis, and cancer. In adjusted models, stroke had the strongest association with poor health (OR 3.684, 95% CI 2.501-5.425), followed by CHD (OR 3.553, 2.428-5.199), COPD (OR 2.563, 1.831-3.587), kidney disease (OR 2.459, 1.695-3.568), asthma (OR 2.170, 1.583-2.977), and vision difficulty (OR 2.416, 1.612-3.622). In random forest analyses, COPD and CHD were the most important comorbid predictors of poor health.

Conclusion: Self-rated poor health in adults with T2D marks a high-risk group characterized by substantial vascular and pulmonary comorbidity and frequent visual, mental health, and physical health complications. Incorporating general health status into routine assessment may enable practical risk stratification and trigger integrating screening and prevention strategies to reduce avoidable complications.

records.introduction_objective: ASC37 is an oral GLP-1R/GIPR/GCGR triple agonist peptide, discovered and developed in-house at Ascletis. Peptide Oral Transport ENhancement Technology (POTENT) is a proprietary technology of Ascletis for oral peptides. POTENT technology impedes enzymatic degradation of peptides and increases gastrointestinal permeability of peptides.
records.methods: ASC37 oral tablets were developed utilizing Ascletis’ POTENT technology. The absolute oral bioavailability and drug exposure of ASC37 tablets were evaluated in non-human primate (NHP) models. ASC37 in vitro activity was also evaluated.
records.results: ASC37, a GLP-1R, GIPR, and GCGR triple agonist peptide, was discovered and optimized in-house utilizing Ascletis’ Artificial Intelligence-assisted Structure-Based Drug Discovery (AISBDD). ASC37 oral tablets achieved an average absolute oral bioavailability of 4.2%, approximately 9-, 30-, and 60-fold higher than semaglutide, tirzepatide, and retatrutide in the oral SNAC formulation, respectively, in head-to-head non-human primate (NHP) studies. ASC37 oral tablets’ drug exposure, as measured by the area under curve (AUC), was approximately 57-fold of retatrutide’s drug exposure in head-to-head NHP studies. Average observed half-life (as measured by time to 50% Cmax) of ASC37 oral tablets was approximately 56 hours in NHP studies, supporting once daily and less frequent oral dosing. ASC37 in vitro activity was approximately 5-, 4- and 4-fold more potent than retatrutide for GLP-1R, GIPR and GCGR, respectively.
records.conclusion: ASC37 is a promising oral GLP-1R/GIPR/GCGR triple agonist peptide for clinical development

Introduction and Objective: ASC37 is an oral GLP-1R/GIPR/GCGR triple agonist peptide, discovered and developed in-house at Ascletis. Peptide Oral Transport ENhancement Technology (POTENT) is a proprietary technology of Ascletis for oral peptides. Methods: ASC37 oral tablets were developed utilizing Ascletis’ POTENT technology. The absolute oral bioavailability and drug exposure of ASC37 tablets were evaluated in non-human primate (NHP) models. ASC37 in vitro activity was also evaluated.

Results: ASC37, a GLP-1R, GIPR, and GCGR triple agonist peptide, was discovered and optimized in-house utilizing Ascletis’ Artificial Intelligence-assisted Structure-Based Drug Discovery (AISBDD). ASC37 oral tablets achieved an average absolute oral bioavailability of 4.2%, approximately 9-, 30-, and 60-fold higher than semaglutide, tirzepatide, and retatrutide in the oral SNAC formulation, respectively, in head-to-head non-human primate (NHP) studies. ASC37 oral tablets’ drug exposure, as measured by the area under curve (AUC), was approximately 57-fold of retatrutide’s drug exposure in head-to-head NHP studies. Average observed half-life (as measured by time to 50% Cmax) of ASC37 oral tablets was approximately 56 hours in NHP studies, supporting once daily and less frequent oral dosing. ASC37 in vitro activity was approximately 5-, 4- and 4-fold more potent than retatrutide for GLP-1R, GIPR and GCGR, respectively.

Conclusion: ASC37 is a promising oral GLP-1R/GIPR/GCGR triple agonist peptide for clinical development

records.introduction_objective: This post hoc analysis identified patients (pts) at high risk of glycemic progression (GP) using baseline (BL) clinical and proteomic data and evaluated their risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).
records.methods: Pts receiving placebo (n=6578) in SELECT with complete 2-yr HbA1c profiles and BL proteomics were included. Pts receiving glucose-lowering rescue therapy during the 2-yr period were defined as clinical progressors (CP). Temporal clustering (TC) identified HbA1c (%) trajectories in the remaining pts. A validated random forest classifier identified BL clinical and proteomic factors predicting HbA1c progression. High-power predictive proteins were chosen. MACE risk was evaluated.
records.results: TC revealed 3 clusters with stable glycemia and 1 with metabolic progression (MP) (Fig. A). Four BL variables (HbA1c %, leptin/adiponectin, TG/HDL, GGT) and 31 proteins (covering insulin sensitivity and liver function signaling pathways) identified pts with GP (CP + MP) from those without (Fig. B). The model predicted GP with 81.8% sensitivity, 87.1% specificity, and 84.9% precision, outperforming HbA1c cutoffs of 5.7% and 6.0% (94.4% and 66.3% sensitivity, 54.8% and 95.5% specificity). Pts with GP had higher odds of ≥1 MACE within 4 yrs vs all other clusters combined (OR = 1.63 [95% CI 1.36, 1.94]; p<0.001; Fig. C).
records.conclusion: Pts with GP have increased MACE risk and can be identified with high precision using BL clinical and proteomic data.

Introduction and Objective: This post hoc analysis identified patients (pts) at high risk of glycemic progression (GP) using baseline (BL) clinical and proteomic data and evaluated their risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

Methods: Pts receiving placebo (n=6578) in SELECT with complete 2-yr HbA1c profiles and BL proteomics were included. Pts receiving glucose-lowering rescue therapy during the 2-yr period were defined as clinical progressors (CP). Temporal clustering (TC) identified HbA1c (%) trajectories in the remaining pts. A validated random forest classifier identified BL clinical and proteomic factors predicting HbA1c progression. High-power predictive proteins were chosen. MACE risk was evaluated.

Results: TC revealed 3 clusters with stable glycemia and 1 with metabolic progression (MP) (Fig. A). Four BL variables (HbA1c %, leptin/adiponectin, TG/HDL, GGT) and 31 proteins (covering insulin sensitivity and liver function signaling pathways) identified pts with GP (CP + MP) from those without (Fig. B). The model predicted GP with 81.8% sensitivity, 87.1% specificity, and 84.9% precision, outperforming HbA1c cutoffs of 5.7% and 6.0% (94.4% and 66.3% sensitivity, 54.8% and 95.5% specificity). Pts with GP had higher odds of ≥1 MACE within 4 yrs vs all other clusters combined (OR = 1.63 [95% CI 1.36, 1.94]; p<0.001; Fig. C).

Conclusion: Pts with GP have increased MACE risk and can be identified with high precision using BL clinical and proteomic data.

records.introduction_objective: Precision medicine approaches can optimise type 2 diabetes management by identifying the best treatment for a specific individual. We previously developed and validated a clinical prediction model using nine routinely available features (such as age, BMI, eGFR and sex) to estimate individual glycaemic responses to five major type 2 diabetes drug classes (n=100,107 initiations). Here, we extend the model to predict glycaemic response to both oral and subcutaneous semaglutide.
records.methods: We used UK routine primary care data (CPRD Aurum) for non-insulin-treated individuals initiating semaglutide up to June 2024. The primary outcome was the 12-month change in HbA1c. We assessed the model’s calibration by comparing predicted versus observed HbA1c measures against other GLP-1RAs in the original model (liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide prolonged-release), informing necessary adjustments. External validation was conducted using Scottish primary care data (Scottish Diabetes Research Network, SDRN).
records.results: In CPRD, there were 3,056 oral and 6,969 subcutaneous semaglutide initiations (mean [SD] baseline characteristics: HbA1c 74[13] mmol/mol, age 59[11] years, BMI 36[7] kg/m2, eGFR 93[18] ml/min/1.73m2, 55% male) with complete predictor and 12-month HbA1c outcome data on stable therapy. Oral semaglutide responses were consistent with model predictions for other GLP-1RAs, requiring no adjustment. Differential treatment responses with subcutaneous semaglutide were consistent with model predictions, although requiring intercept adjustment to accommodate a mean 7.0 (95% CI 6.2-7.6) mmol/mol greater overall HbA1c response compared to other GLP-1RAs. records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Precision medicine approaches can optimise type 2 diabetes management by identifying the best treatment for a specific individual. We previously developed and validated a clinical prediction model using nine routinely available features (such as age, BMI, eGFR and sex) to estimate individual glycaemic responses to five major type 2 diabetes drug classes (n=100,107 initiations). Here, we extend the model to predict glycaemic response to both oral and subcutaneous semaglutide.

Methods: We used UK routine primary care data (CPRD Aurum) for non-insulin-treated individuals initiating semaglutide up to June 2024. The primary outcome was the 12-month change in HbA1c. We assessed the model’s calibration by comparing predicted versus observed HbA1c measures against other GLP-1RAs in the original model (liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide prolonged-release), informing necessary adjustments. External validation was conducted using Scottish primary care data (Scottish Diabetes Research Network, SDRN).

Results: In CPRD, there were 3,056 oral and 6,969 subcutaneous semaglutide initiations (mean [SD] baseline characteristics: HbA1c 74[13] mmol/mol, age 59[11] years, BMI 36[7] kg/m2, eGFR 93[18] ml/min/1.73m2, 55% male) with complete predictor and 12-month HbA1c outcome data on stable therapy. Oral semaglutide responses were consistent with model predictions for other GLP-1RAs, requiring no adjustment. Differential treatment responses with subcutaneous semaglutide were consistent with model predictions, although requiring intercept adjustment to accommodate a mean 7.0 (95% CI 6.2-7.6) mmol/mol greater overall HbA1c response compared to other GLP-1RAs. The updated model displayed excellent calibration in SDRN external validation (n=2,951 initiations).

Conclusion: An updated five-drug class model accurately predicts glucose-lowering responses to oral and subcutaneous semaglutide. External validation supports model generalisability and its potential for routine clinical application.

Categorical variables were binarized. Univariate analysis (p<0.05) was used to preselect features prior to Gradient Boosting model development. Model optimization was achieved using GridSearchCV and evaluated using a stratified train/test split (75/25%), confusion matrix metrics, ROC-AUC, precision-recall indices, and learning-curve stability.

The most influential predictors were age at diagnosis, ketoacidosis at presentation, sedentary lifestyle, and type of initial antidiabetic treatment.

Conclusion: A Gradient Boosting-based model can accurately predict future insulin use using routinely collected clinical and lifestyle data in patients with T2D. Its excellent performance suggests potential utility for early therapeutic stratification and anticipatory diabetes care planning in clinical practice.

records.introduction_objective: Large language models (LLMs) show limited subspecialty accuracy in type 2 diabetes (T2D) management. Current cloud-based medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have privacy concerns and lack subspecialty expertise. We developed OLYMPUS (On-premise Local LLM for Medical Practice Under Secure environment), a privacy-preserving framework enabling knowledge distillation from expert teacher models to deployable student models using guideline-based synthetic data.
records.methods: Sophia (Llama 70B) was fine-tuned on the clinical data of 80 subjects with T2D to create an expert teacher model. Chiron generated 744 synthetic T2D cases, and fine-tuned Sophia generated expert-level solutions for all 744 cases. One endocrinologist validated each case-solution pair. Asclepius, a Qwen 14B model, was fine-tuned via low-rank adaptation on these 744 validated pairs using consumer hardware (Mac mini M4 Pro, 64GB RAM) with complete local processing. Performance was compared with GPT-4o through blinded evaluation of 40 randomly selected cases by three independent endocrinologists for treatment appropriateness, quality, guideline adherence, and clinical reasoning.
records.results: Asclepius significantly outperformed GPT-4o (4.08±1.00 vs 3.88±1.00, p=0.002), showing 5.3% improvement. Asclepius consistently exceeded GPT-4o across all domains: treatment appropriateness (+5.4%), treatment quality (+5.5%), guideline adherence (+4.2%), and clinical reasoning (+5.9%). All three evaluators independently rated Asclepius higher.
records.conclusion: In conclusion, knowledge distillation from expert teacher to deployable student model using guideline-based synthetic data achieved superior performance compared to state-of-the-art general medical AI while maintaining complete patient privacy through local processing.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Large language models (LLMs) show limited subspecialty accuracy in type 2 diabetes (T2D) management. Current cloud-based medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have privacy concerns and lack subspecialty expertise. We developed OLYMPUS (On-premise Local LLM for Medical Practice Under Secure environment), a privacy-preserving framework enabling knowledge distillation from expert teacher models to deployable student models using guideline-based synthetic data.

Methods: Sophia (Llama 70B) was fine-tuned on the clinical data of 80 subjects with T2D to create an expert teacher model. Chiron generated 744 synthetic T2D cases, and fine-tuned Sophia generated expert-level solutions for all 744 cases. One endocrinologist validated each case-solution pair. Asclepius, a Qwen 14B model, was fine-tuned via low-rank adaptation on these 744 validated pairs using consumer hardware (Mac mini M4 Pro, 64GB RAM) with complete local processing. Performance was compared with GPT-4o through blinded evaluation of 40 randomly selected cases by three independent endocrinologists for treatment appropriateness, quality, guideline adherence, and clinical reasoning.

Results: Asclepius significantly outperformed GPT-4o (4.08±1.00 vs 3.88±1.00, p=0.002), showing 5.3% improvement. Asclepius consistently exceeded GPT-4o across all domains: treatment appropriateness (+5.4%), treatment quality (+5.5%), guideline adherence (+4.2%), and clinical reasoning (+5.9%). All three evaluators independently rated Asclepius higher.

Conclusion: In conclusion, knowledge distillation from expert teacher to deployable student model using guideline-based synthetic data achieved superior performance compared to state-of-the-art general medical AI while maintaining complete patient privacy through local processing.

Methods: Data from a double-blind, randomized, two-period crossover trial (NCT05057819) were used. Model parameters, including Th and insulin sensitivity (IS), were estimated from plasma glucose and UGE data, with plasma insulin and CGM used as inputs.

Results: Fasting glucose levels were lower in E vs P (88.3 [84.7, 91.9] vs. 92.8 [86.5, 96.4] mg/dl, p=0.002), while incremental area under the glucose curve was similar (5.3 [3.1, 7.5] vs. 5.0 [3.0, 8.3] g/dl·min). Conclusion: The proposed model provides a quantitative, individualized estimate of empagliflozin's effect on UGE, which mechanistically explains the observed reduction in fasting glucose and can be used to dynamically assess treatment response over time.

We compared the two systems in terms of time in range (TIR) and glucose management indicator (GMI)

Methods: Weekly trend in GMI and TIR was assessed for 4 weeks after AID initiation in an endocrine clinic. AID and CGM device data downloads were analysed. 8 patients on conventional AID and 8 patients on AID with autonomous bolusing option were studied. Independent and paired t test analysis used

Results: There was no significant difference between the baseline GMI/TIR between the two groups. No significant intergroup differences in GMI / TIR seen at 4 weeks. Intragroup analysis showed no significant GMI / TIR change at 4 weeks compared to baseline within user-programmable AID. The AID with autonomous bolusing demonstrated significant GMI / TIR reduction (p value = 0.003) at 4 weeks

Conclusion: In this real world comparison, the AID system with autonomous bolusing using AI based adaptive algorithm with limited user input and lower user burden showed greater intragroup improvement in GMI and TIR within the first week.
