records.introduction_objective: While Transformer architectures have revolutionized language processing, their application to physiological time-series remains underexplored. This pilot study investigates whether a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) can autonomously extract personalized, invariant insulin sensitivity factors (ISF) and insulin-to-carbohydrate ratios (ICR) from Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) data without explicit physiological constraints or hand-tuned heuristics.
records.methods: We trained a TFT model on 2-4 years of retrospective Nightscout data (continuous glucose monitor, insulin, and carbohydrate records) from a pilot T1D subject. To interrogate the physiological relationships learned by the model, we implemented a synthetic validation pipeline, injecting synthetic insulin and carbohydrate impulses onto stable baselines at varying noise levels to measure predicted glucose excursions and reverse-engineer physiological parameters. We then evaluated this approach in a cohort of 5 additional T1D subjects (3 pediatric, 2 adult) to assess generalization.
records.results: For the pilot subject, the model converged on robust invariant values (ISF 92.8 ± 2.1 mg/dL/U; ICR 6.41 ± 0.15 g/U) once training noise exceeded a critical threshold (≥6.0). Low-noise baselines systematically underestimated sensitivity. In the 5-subject validation cohort, convergence was achieved for all individuals, with high parameter stability (mean variance 5.8% ± 3.9%). Extracted parameters differed substantially between subjects (e.g., ISF range 38.6-122.2 mg/dL/U), indicating subject-specific physiological learning rather than population averaging.
records.conclusion: Transformer-based attention mechanisms can learn individualized glucose-insulin dynamics directly from routine CGM and pump data. Synthetic probing of trained models enables stable extraction of personalized insulin delivery parameters, suggesting a pathway toward fully automated, data-driven pump setting personalization beyond static heuristic approaches.

records.introduction_objective: Carb estimating for meal insulin dosing is challenging and often error-prone in daily life with T1D. Large language models (LLMs) can be leveraged but accuracy is unknown. Small language models (SLMs) can run directly on mobile devices but perform worse than LLMs. We assessed carb counting accuracy of a LLM and 2 SLMs before and after fine-tuning.
records.methods: We used 6518 self-reported meal phrases with nutritionist carb estimates from the Type 1 Diabetes EXercise Initiative study from 337 participants and an LLM (GPT4.1) to generate 456260 chat-based queries asking for carb amounts across 7 different categories ranging from more to less detailed descriptions. SLMs were fine-tuned with Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on 5518 meals (386260 questions) using Chain-of-Thought reasoning. We evaluated accuracy on a subset of 7000 questions not used for fine-tuning.

From Tukey’s fences (k=3), all models yielded extreme outliers of AE>61 g - GPT 0.6%, Qwen 1.8% and SmolLM 2% of all estimates.

records.introduction_objective: Hypoglycemia is one of the clinical features of adrenal insufficiency (AI). Patients with AI require lifelong glucocorticoid replacement. However, whether glucocorticoid replacement therapy can restore physiological glycemic fluctuations in patients with AI remains unclear. We aimed to investigate the glucose fluctuation pattern in the patients with AI by Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and explore the association between CGM features and glucocorticoid administration.
records.methods: A total of 27 patients with a stable dose of glucocorticoids were enrolled. Fifty-four normal controls (NC) without known glucometabolic disorders were matched by age, sex, and BMI from a database of healthy volunteers. CGM was conducted in AI and NC with a blinded method for 14 days. The glucocorticoid regimen and adverse events during CGM were recorded.
records.results: The mean age of the AI group was 59.53±8.51 years, including 15 male. Compared with NC, the patients with AI had increased time below range (TBR, glucose <3.9 and <3.0 mmol/L), and decreased time in range (TIR, glucose within 3.9-7.8 mmol/L) during 24h, diurnal, and nocturnal periods. Time above range (TAR, glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L) during the lunch and dinner period were increased. The indicators representing glucose fluctuation were also increased. The patients taking glucocorticoid once per day had higher TAR during the lunch period than those with medication twice daily. Patients receiving hydrocortisone had a higher TAR during the breakfast and lunch periods than those taking prednisone. Patients with immune checkpoint inhibitors induced AI had higher glucose levels and fluctuation during the breakfast and dinner periods than those of the other etiology.
records.conclusion: Patients with AI undergoing glucocorticoid replacement therapy exhibited more asymptomatic hypoglycemia and larger glucose fluctuation. CGM may provide valuable information in determination of proper glucocorticoid administration of AI.

records.introduction_objective: Traditional food logging in diabetes care relies on manual self-reporting, limiting adherence and clinical utility. Image-based logging improves usability, but its impact depends on converting logs into personalized, actionable insights. This study evaluates an AI-driven food intelligence model that transforms food images into personalized dietary insights and assesses its effect on glycemic outcomes in people with diabetes.
records.methods: AI model was developed using over 100,000 real-world food logs from people with diabetes, integrating user persona, biomarkers, lifestyle, comorbidities, dietary preferences, and cultural eating patterns. The model evaluates composite meals per eating occasions to generate personalized food scores, healthier alternatives, and predicts post-prandial glucose impact. Glycemic outcomes were assessed over a 14-day CGM period, with Week 1 (W1) as baseline exposure to AI insights and Week 2 (W2) as continued engagement, comparing active meal loggers with non-loggers.
records.results: Over 14 days, active meal loggers (n=8,421) demonstrated greater percentage improvements in glycemic metrics compared with non-loggers (n=10,282). From W1 to W2, active loggers showed a 30.04% increase in TIR, a 14.45% reduction in TBR, and a 12.08% reduction in TAR (all p < 0.001). Introduction and Objective: Traditional food logging in diabetes care relies on manual self-reporting, limiting adherence and clinical utility. Image-based logging improves usability, but its impact depends on converting logs into personalized, actionable insights. In contrast, non-loggers exhibited a smaller 3.32% increase in TIR (p < 0.001), a substantial upward shift in TBR (21.53%; p < 0.001), and a modest upward shift in TAR (4.57%; p < 0.001).

Conclusion: This study shows that active food logging also improved food scores by 10.25% compared to the first week, contributing to improved glycemic control in the second week through enhanced meal-level awareness and timely dietary adjustments, and reinforcing its role in personalized dietary management, with potential added benefits from meal-specific glycemic index and glycemic load estimation.

records.introduction_objective: Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) generates complex time-series data often reduced to summaries (e.g., Time-in-Range). These metrics fail to capture the distributional shape of glycemic dynamics. This study applied Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and Wasserstein distances to identify intrinsic phenotypes of glycemic magnitude and evaluated their clinical relevance.
records.methods: We analyzed Dexcom G6 CGM data from 1,049 participants in the AI-READI dataset. We computed the pairwise Wasserstein Distance (mg/dL) between the glucose probability distributions of all participants. Hierarchical clustering was applied to the distance matrix to identify distinct subgroups. Clinical characteristics (HbA1c) and standard variability metrics (Coefficient of Variation) were compared across clusters using Kruskal-Wallis tests.
records.results: Topological clustering identified four distinct phenotypes with highly significant differences in clinical control (HbA1c p<0.0001). Cluster 1 (Mean Glucose: 342.4 ± 20.3 mg/dL) represented a saturated phenotype with the highest HbA1c (10.0% ± 3.4%) but low variability (CV: 16.4% ± 5.0%), reflecting sustained hyperglycemia near the sensor limit. In contrast, Cluster 2 (Mean: 260.6 ± 16.6 mg/dL; HbA1c: 9.3% ± 1.4%) represented an erratic phenotype with the cohort's highest variability (CV: 23.6% ± 4.6%), distinct from the saturated group. Cluster 3 identified a moderate-variable phenotype (HbA1c: 6.7% ± 1.1%; CV: 22.8% ± 6.0%), while Cluster 4 represented tight control (HbA1c: 5.6% ± 0.7%; TIR: 96.0% ± 7.4%).
records.conclusion: Topological phenotyping effectively disentangles glucose level severity from instability. Specifically, it distinguishes patients with saturated, unvarying hyperglycemia from those with chaotic, high-amplitude fluctuations; distinct clinical states that standard HbA1c metrics often conflate. This approach offers a precise framework for stratifying type 2 diabetes phenotypes beyond averages.

Accurate prediction of TIR and identification of important predictors can inform individualized treatment decisions. Introduction and Objective: In routine practice, CGM adherence is often summarized as % days worn, ignoring whether wear is continuous or intermittent. We assessed whether longitudinal CGM wear patterns are associated with 12-month changes in CGM outcomes.

Methods: One-year CGM readings were linked to health records (EHR) for 2,351 U.S. Veterans. We quantified similarity between year-long CGM wear patterns with a novel optimal-transport-based metric that accounts for timing, gaps, and pattern complexity. We used spectral clustering to identify use phenotypes. Using double machine learning with EHR covariates, we estimated adjusted 12-month changes in time-in-range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL).

Results: Three phenotypes were identified: Consistent, Fluctuating, and Low-engagement. Compared with Consistent users, Fluctuating users had worse glycemic outcomes (change in TIR -3.6 percentage points), yet 73.2% met the conventional >=80% days-covered threshold. There was dose-response across use patterns, with Low-users deteriorating the most (change in TIR -7.0 points). Consistent wear related to larger favorable changes in TIR over 12 months among insulin pump users and those prescribed glucagon (Fig).

Conclusion: Glycemic benefit from real-world CGM is tied to CGM use patterns that are not captured by standard time of wear assessments. These results highlight the need for more sophisticated CGM use assessment and of tailoring patient education to improve individualized adherence goals.

records.introduction_objective: Accurate short-term glucose prediction is key to preventing hypoglycemia and post-meal spikes, but CGM-only models have notable gaps. This study developed a multimodal ML model within the Lillia Care digital diabetes management that integrates wearable, dietary, and medication data to forecast glucose 60-180 minutes ahead in adults with Type 2 Diabetes.
records.methods: Data were prospectively collected from 73 adults (64 M) with T2DM (mean age 50 years; BMI 28.9; HbA1c 7.5%; diabetes duration 12.3 years), each contributing complete CGM cycles. Alongside CGM, body composition parameters were recorded, and over a 4 week period data were paired with smartwatch metrics (heart rate, steps, sleep), food logs, and medication adherence. A NeuralProphet deep time-series model was trained with extensive hyperparameter tuning using a 60/20/20 train-validation-test split to ensure stable and accurate 1-hour glucose forecasts.
records.results: The multimodal model showed better performance than CGM-only baselines, delivering strong and consistent accuracy across all prediction horizons. For 1-hour forecasts, the model achieved an RMSE of 14.47+3.18 mg/dL, with individual errors ranging from 8.2 to 22.38 mg/dL. Predictive reliability remained stable as the horizon extended, with 2-hour and 3-hour RMSEs of 15.03+3.40 mg/dL (range 7.1-22.55) and 15.44+3.35 mg/dL (range 8.4-23.04), respectively. These well-bounded error distributions indicate robust performance across diverse glycemic profiles. Feature-importance analysis further showed that variables such as time since last steps, cumulative calories burned, daily stress levels, and oxygen-desaturation events significantly enhanced forecasting accuracy, underscoring the value of incorporating behavioral and physiological context into glucose prediction models.
records.conclusion: Integrating CGM with wearable, dietary, and medication signals enables reliable, clinically meaningful short-term glucose forecasting in people with T2DM, maintaining accuracy even as prediction windows extend to 3 hours.

records.introduction_objective: CGM patterns inform diabetes management, but manual detection is labor-intensive. Whether LLMs can match expert performance and how input modality affects detection remains unexplored. This study evaluates LLM against expert curated labels to determine if LLMs achieve clinically acceptable accuracy and whether input modality significantly impacts performance.
records.methods: We compared GPT-4o-mini predictions against expert labels for five CGM patterns (afternoon spike, dawn phenomenon, morning hyperglycemia, nocturnal hypoglycemia, overnight compression). Three independent clinical experts (RDN, CDCES, and BC-ADM) reviewed 7-day CGM tracings and labeled patterns. We evaluated three modalities: (1) raw—timestamped individual readings; (2) image—visual time-series plots; and (3) aggregate—3-hour statistical summaries. Ground truth was established via majority vote from 111 triple-labeled instances. We calculated precision, recall, F1 score, and accuracy, and assessed inter-rater reliability via perfect agreement rates.
records.results: Inter-rater perfect agreement ranged from 0% (overnight compression) to 49% (morning hyperglycemia). Raw data points achieved the highest F1 of 80.7% (recall 96.1%), while image and aggregate achieved 77.0% and 76.9%, respectively. Pattern-specific results revealed modality dependencies: nocturnal hypoglycemia was detected exclusively by raw/text (F1 88.0%), while afternoon spike and morning hyperglycemia performed well across modalities (F1 >85%). Overnight compression failed across all modalities (0% F1).
records.conclusion: Pattern-specific prompts with strategic modality selection achieved F1 scores of 76.9-80.7% (66% improvement over baseline). Raw/text modality offers practical clinical deployment with high recall, though modality impact varies by pattern. These findings demonstrate that prompt engineering and modality selection are essential for accurate CGM pattern detection.

records.introduction_objective: Annual eye examinations for diabetes (EEDs) are essential for early detection of diabetic retinopathy, yet adherence remains suboptimal, particularly in rural communities where access to eye care is limited. Autonomous AI systems offer a scalable approach to expand patient access at the point of care. We evaluated the real-world impact of LumineticsCore™, an FDA-cleared autonomous AI diagnostic system for EEDs, deployed across rural and urban clinics within SSM Health (SSM).
records.methods: This retrospective observational study assessed adult patients with diabetes receiving care at SSM clinics before and after LumineticsCore implementation. Clinics were classified as rural or urban using Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes based on clinic ZIP codes. The primary outcome was change in adherence to annual EEDs, defined as completion of a documented eye exam by LumineticsCore or an eyecare provider within the measurement year. Adherence rates before and after implementation were stratified by rural versus urban clinic designation.
records.results: A total of 52 clinics (rural: 13; urban: 39) were included, representing 43,344 patients for the calendar year pre-implementation, and 48,607 for the calendar year post-implementation. Following implementation, adherence to annual EEDs increased significantly from 58.3% (25,288/43,344) in the pre-period, to 65.1% (31,652/48,607) in the post-period (p<0.001). Comparable improvements were observed across settings, with adherence increasing in urban clinics from 60.4% (18,941/31,360) to 67.3% (23,231/34,508) and in rural clinics from 53.0% (6,347/11,984) to 59.7% (8,421/14,099). The magnitude of improvement was similar between rural and urban clinics, with no significant difference between settings (p=0.40).
records.conclusion: Adoption of an autonomous AI diagnostic system resulted in equivalent improvements in EED adherence across rural and urban clinical settings. These findings suggest autonomous AI can support scalable access to EEDs and help close longstanding rural care gaps.

records.introduction_objective: Current medical AI benchmarks rely on single-best-answer exam accuracy (e.g. USMLE), but real-world type 2 diabetes (T2D) care involves context-dependent clinical decisions with acceptable practice variability. To discriminate real-world clinical effectiveness of AI systems, we aimed to develop a diabetologist-validated framework in T2D management.
records.methods: We devised a Donabedian model-based framework to assess AI clinical decision capability by evaluating clinical reasoning for patient triage/problem list, medication recommendation, treatment strategy, dose adjustment, and monitoring/education. Meta-evaluation items embedded at the end of each phase assessed the framework’s ability to discriminate the clinical effectiveness of AI systems. Reviewers rated comprehensiveness (coverage of required elements in T2D care) and clarity (unambiguous interpretation and application) on a 4-point scale, and provided free-text feedback to inform between-round revisions. 12 diabetologists completed two initial Delphi rounds; 3 senior diabetologists led the final consensus review.
records.results: Delphi rounds 1-2 generated 102 item-level revision comments spanning validity, clarity, coverage, feasibility, and traceability. Iterative revisions streamlined the framework from 56 to 29 evaluation items by removing redundancy and sharpening workflow-aligned criteria, while increasing content validity index from 64.4%/51.1% (comprehensiveness/clarity) in the initial round to 100%/100% in the final round.
records.conclusion: This diabetologist consensus-validated framework provides explicit standards to systematically assess AI-generated T2D treatment recommendations across reasoning reliability, clinical utility, and real-world feasibility. The framework demonstrates potential to serve as an evaluative benchmark for distinguishing AI systems that effectively support diabetologists' treatment decision-making.

Results: Delphi rounds 1-2 generated 102 item-level revision comments spanning validity, clarity, coverage, feasibility, and traceability. Iterative revisions streamlined the framework from 56 to 29 evaluation items by removing redundancy and sharpening workflow-aligned criteria, while increasing content validity index from 64.4%/51.1% (comprehensiveness/clarity) in the initial round to 100%/100% in the final round.

Conclusion: This diabetologist consensus-validated framework provides explicit standards to systematically assess AI-generated T2D treatment recommendations across reasoning reliability, clinical utility, and real-world feasibility. The framework demonstrates potential to serve as an evaluative benchmark for distinguishing AI systems that effectively support diabetologists' treatment decision-making.

Model-derived Diabetes Complexity Score (DCS) stratified patients into low (DCS<30, 12% complications), moderate (DCS 30-60, 48% complications), and high-risk (DCS>60, 82% complications) categories, enabling precision intervention. Early achievement of targets within 5 years reduced DCS by 45 points and complication probability from 68% to 18% (NNT=2).

records.introduction_objective: Diabetes represents a growing health burden with disproportionately higher prevalence, mortality and morbidity in the rural South, relative to urban counties in the U.S.. In rural areas, access to specialized diabetes care, as well as technological advances, are often inadequate. The objective of this project was to identify region-specific diabetes challenges and develop effective technological solutions for rural communities in the Southeastern U.S. Artificial intelligence and other health technological solutions were used to meet a critical need in rural areas.
records.methods: A diabetes problem discovery workshop was organized, based on human-centered design and community-based participatory principles. A Steering Committee of rural health leaders helped recruit subject matter experts (SMEs) representing medicine, nursing, pharmacy, nutrition, mental health, public health, laboratory science, and information technology. Participants refined 25 challenges faced by patients and other stakeholders in rural Georgia into ten priority diabetes-focused problems. Technological innovations were then co-developed by computer science students and rural health stakeholders, culminating in a 'DiaTech' demonstration day.
records.results: The problems reflected gaps in clinical practice, systemic care delivery, medication access and adherence, and nutrition and lifestyle support. The need for offline functionality, digital literacy support, and relation-based care was emphasized. Mobile health applications were developed for nutritional guidance, including an AI powered chat-bot that uses food pantry and refrigerator inventory to customize healthy meal planning. Other mobile health applications engaged users with comic-like visuals and interactive guidance on diabetes self-management and culturally tailored education on medications.
records.conclusion: This community-based, problem-focused approach represents a model for driving contextually appropriate and innovative health technologies for low-resource settings.

records.introduction_objective: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) requires protocolised management, yet real-world adherence is often inconsistent beyond initial stabilisation. We assessed the association between dynamic adherence to local DKA protocol and hospital length of stay (LOS) and examined the impact of DKA severity and specialist involvement (Endocrinology and ICU)).
records.methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults admitted with DKA at Barwon Health between November 2024 and October 2025. An Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based auditing tool retrospectively evaluated adherence across the first seven protocol decision points. The primary outcome was hospital length of stay (LOS).
records.results: A total of 82 admissions were included; 92.7% were patients with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus. Correct initial insulin dosing occurred in 100% and prompt initiation in 89% of cases. Patients without prompt initiation had a longer mean LOS (9.4 vs 3.7 days). DKA severity was distributed as mild (32.9%), moderate (26.8%) and severe (29.3%) with increasing severity associated with longer LOS (3.1, 3.5 and 5.6 days, respectively). Greater protocol adherence correlated with shorter LOS (r = -0.43). Patients with complete adherence had a mean LOS of 1.7 days (n = 25) compared with 5.5 days in those with any deviation (n = 57). Specialist involvement was common and was associated with longer LOS, consistent with higher clinical complexity.
records.conclusion: In this retrospective cohort, strict dynamic adherence to DKA protocol steps was strongly associated with a significantly shorter hospital LOS. Delays following initial stabilisation were dominant contributors to prolonged hospitalisations. Specialist involvement did not reduce LOS, likely reflecting confounding by indication. AI-enabled auditing tools may provide a scalable approach to improving protocol reliability and support earlier corrective intervention in DKA management.

records.introduction_objective: Diabetes is associated with high rates of acute care utilization (ACU), posing a substantial burden on healthcare systems. Timely identification of individuals at higher risk for ACU can enable proactive interventions and improve resource allocation. The objective of this study was to develop and evaluate machine learning models to predict ACU within 365 days by people with diabetes.
records.methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using electronic health record (EHR) data from 23,052 patients with diabetes in an urban academic health system. EHR data included encounter history, demographics, vital signs, diagnoses, medications, and laboratory results. ACU during the most recent 365-day period was encoded as a binary outcome variable. Machine learning models spanning 15 different algorithms, including XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, were trained on the training set using 8-fold cross-validation with hyperparameter tuning. Model performance was evaluated on the test set using the macro F1 score, accuracy, and AUROC.
records.results: Among the evaluated models, LightGBM achieved the best overall performance, with a macro F1 score of 0.69, an accuracy of 74.91%, and an AUROC of 0.78. CatBoost and XGBoost demonstrated comparable performance, yielding similarly strong predictive accuracy. Analysis with permutation importance and SHAP from the top-performing model identified prior healthcare utilization, selected laboratory values, and demographic characteristics as key predictors of ACU.
records.conclusion: These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of ML models for predicting ACU among people with diabetes. While integrating multimodal EHR data is valuable, our results suggest that comparable predictive performance can be achieved using a targeted subset of high-impact features, enabling efficient and scalable risk stratification in clinical settings.

records.introduction_objective: HbA1c outcomes in diabetes vary widely due to differences in clinical characteristics and real-world adherence. This study aimed to develop and validate machine-learning models to predict HbA1c at 120 days using demographic, clinical, and behavioral adherence data from a digital diabetes platform.
records.methods: Data from 507 participants enrolled in the Lillia Care digital diabetes management platform were analyzed. The cohort had a mean age of 47 years, mean BMI of 26.7 kg/m², and mean diabetes duration of 6.2 years. Mean HbA1c improved from 8.74% at baseline to 7.31% at follow-up (mean reduction: 1.43%). Predictors included demographic and clinical variables, comorbidities, lifestyle factors, and adherence scores for nutrition, exercise, medication use, and platform engagement. Nutrition and exercise adherence varied widely, while medication adherence was consistently high (mean 96.3%). Multiple regression models were evaluated using cross-validation and held-out testing, with performance assessed using mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE).
records.results: Among all evaluated models, a Gradient Boosting regressor incorporating adherence metrics demonstrated the strongest predictive performance of HbA1c, achieving a cross-validation MAE of 0.62, test MAE of 0.63, and RMSE of 0.98. Tree-based ensemble models consistently outperformed linear, kernel-based, and neural-network approaches, highlighting nonlinear relationships between adherence behaviours and glycemic outcomes.
records.conclusion: Machine-learning models leveraging real-world adherence data can accurately forecast short-term HbA1c outcomes and support personalized diabetes care. Beyond risk stratification, the proposed model can serve as a motivational and educational tool by visually demonstrating adherence-driven glycemic outcomes, reinforcing the impact of improved nutrition, physical activity, and medication adherence on HbA1c trajectories and encouraging sustained behavior change.

records.authors: EUNSOL YANG, SEJUNG HWANG, XING LUU, MOLLY L. TANENBAUM, PATRICK PHILLIPS, RADA SAVIC, SHYLAJA SRINIVASAN, San Francisco, CA, Stanford, CA
records.trigger_snippet: 2087-P - Predictive Modeling of HbA1c Progression for Use in Synthetic Controls in Youth-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Introduction and Objective: Youth-onset type 2 diabetes (T2D) is highly heterogeneous, complicating trial evaluation and requir
records.summary: Our HbA1c progression model in youth has the potential to create synthetic controls for trials and support risk-stratified strategies from diagnosis. It will be prospectively evaluated as a digital twin intervention in a clinical trial to project individual trajectories and guide behavioral changes.
records.introduction_objective: Youth-onset type 2 diabetes (T2D) is highly heterogeneous, complicating trial evaluation and requiring individualized management. We developed a predictive model of HbA1c trajectories to generate patient-matched synthetic controls (digital twins) using routine clinical features.
records.methods: We modeled 12,970 HbA1c measurements over a median 4.5 yr from 699 youth (median age 14 yr) in the TODAY study using a nonlinear mixed effects approach. The model was used to simulate HbA1c trajectories for 1,555 real-world youth from the SEARCH study and the UC Health Data Warehouse using patient-level baseline data under weight and dietary scenarios.
records.results: A progression model on HbA1c formation best described the data (individual-level fit R2=0.81). Elevated triglycerides, lower AST/ALT ratio, longer T2D duration, and Tanner stage 1-3 at baseline, plus higher BMI Z-score and carbohydrate (carb) intake during treatment, predicted rapid HbA1c progression (P<0.01). Simulations showed distinct progression by baseline risk (median 1-yr HbA1c 5.4-7.5%), with weight loss and low-carb intake reducing 1-yr HbA1c by 0.2% vs. weight gain and high intake.

Introduction and Objective: Youth-onset type 2 diabetes (T2D) is highly heterogeneous, complicating trial evaluation and requiring individualized management. We developed a predictive model of HbA1c trajectories to generate patient-matched synthetic controls (digital twins) using routine clinical features.

Methods: We modeled 12,970 HbA1c measurements over a median 4.5 yr from 699 youth (median age 14 yr) in the TODAY study using a nonlinear mixed effects approach. The model was used to simulate HbA1c trajectories for 1,555 real-world youth from the SEARCH study and the UC Health Data Warehouse using patient-level baseline data under weight and dietary scenarios.

Results: A progression model on HbA1c formation best described the data (individual-level fit R2=0.81). Elevated triglycerides, lower AST/ALT ratio, longer T2D duration, and Tanner stage 1-3 at baseline, plus higher BMI Z-score and carbohydrate (carb) intake during treatment, predicted rapid HbA1c progression (P<0.01). Simulations showed distinct progression by baseline risk (median 1-yr HbA1c 5.4-7.5%), with weight loss and low-carb intake reducing 1-yr HbA1c by 0.2% vs. weight gain and high intake.

Conclusion: Our HbA1c progression model in youth has the potential to create synthetic controls for trials and support risk-stratified strategies from diagnosis. It will be prospectively evaluated as a digital twin intervention in a clinical trial to project individual trajectories and guide behavioral changes.

records.introduction_objective: Elevated blood pressure (BP) is a common but underrecognized contributor to vascular complications in children with type 1 diabetes (T1D). We aimed to characterize BP patterns and kidney function trajectories in pediatric T1D and to identify clinical, immune, and genetic predictors of elevated BP.
records.methods: We examined longitudinal patterns of BP and eGFR in 2,395 children with T1D from the Utah Diabetes Database. In parallel, predictive modelling was performed in 289 ADDAM Biobank participants followed at Montreal Children’s Hospital to evaluate the clinical, immune, and genetic contributors to elevated BP during childhood using machine-learning approaches.
records.results: In UDDb, pediatric T1D patients showed BP variability and heterogeneous eGFR trajectories. Rapid eGFR decline was linked to older age at diagnosis, higher median systolic BP, and more BP measurements. In the ADDAM cohort, 48 children (16%) had elevated BP. Predictive performance was modest (best model: XGBoost, ROC AUC ≈0.69). Age at BP measurement and GAD65 autoantibody titers were key predictors, while BMI, hemoglobin A1C, and genetic risk score accounted for only some cases.
records.conclusion: Elevated BP and adverse kidney patterns are common in pediatric T1D and not fully explained by metabolic risk factors. Immune markers and BP trajectories may help identify children at higher vascular risk and support earlier kidney and cardiovascular assessment.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Elevated blood pressure (BP) is a common but underrecognized contributor to vascular complications in children with type 1 diabetes (T1D). We aimed to characterize BP patterns and kidney function trajectories in pediatric T1D and to identify clinical, immune, and genetic predictors of elevated BP.

Methods: We examined longitudinal patterns of BP and eGFR in 2,395 children with T1D from the Utah Diabetes Database. In parallel, predictive modelling was performed in 289 ADDAM Biobank participants followed at Montreal Children’s Hospital to evaluate the clinical, immune, and genetic contributors to elevated BP during childhood using machine-learning approaches.

Results: In UDDb, pediatric T1D patients showed BP variability and heterogeneous eGFR trajectories. Rapid eGFR decline was linked to older age at diagnosis, higher median systolic BP, and more BP measurements. In the ADDAM cohort, 48 children (16%) had elevated BP. Predictive performance was modest (best model: XGBoost, ROC AUC ≈0.69). Age at BP measurement and GAD65 autoantibody titers were key predictors, while BMI, hemoglobin A1C, and genetic risk score accounted for only some cases.

Conclusion: Elevated BP and adverse kidney patterns are common in pediatric T1D and not fully explained by metabolic risk factors. Immune markers and BP trajectories may help identify children at higher vascular risk and support earlier kidney and cardiovascular assessment.

records.introduction_objective: Severe hypoglycemia (SH) is a life-threatening complication of type 1 diabetes (T1D), making accurate risk identification essential. We used artificial intelligence (AI)-based chart review to improve identification of factors associated with SH in children with T1D.
records.methods: We studied children (<18y) with T1D seen in endocrinology clinics at a large tertiary health center between April 2020 and April 2025 (n = 4,018). Clinicians were required to screen for SH at each visit using questionnaires built into the medical chart. Data scientists employed a hybrid AI-assisted and traditional approach to extract clinical, socioeconomic, and CGM data using PySpark transformations, ChatGPT 5.1 within Palantir Foundry, and custom Python scripts. Groups with and without SH were compared using Fisher's exact, χ² and Mann-Whitney tests. Select multivariate regressions were performed.
records.results: Clinician-documented SH occurred in 5% of patients (206/4018). Table 1 presents group comparisons. Controlling for insurance type, Black race was no longer significantly associated with SH (p=0.07).
records.conclusion: AI-assisted analyses of SH reflect established disparities in glycemic control and diabetes technology use, possibly associated with insurance coverage. Future AI-generated predictive models may improve risk assessment and guide focused interventions.

records.introduction_objective: Women with type 2 diabetes have suboptimal pregnancy outcomes, including high risks of miscarriage, stillbirth and perinatal death. Optimizing pre-pregnancy glycemia to achieve HbA1c <48 mmol/mol (6.5%) can improve outcomes. Insulin therapy preconception is widely recommended, but can cause weight gain and is often unappealing to patients, suggesting that alternative glucose-lowering agents may have a role. We aimed to identify optimal alternative therapies to improve glycemic control in women with early onset type 2 diabetes using a recently validated model which predicts individual glycemic responses to five major glucose-lowering drug classes using routine clinical features.
records.methods: We analyzed UK routine primary care data (Clinical Practice Research Datalink) for adult women 18-40 years old initiating one of 5 major glucose-lowering therapies post 1st-line metformin, up to December 2023. We excluded patients already treated with insulin. We assessed the model’s calibration of overall benefit drug pair comparisons in model-concordant and model-discordant patients.
records.results: We identified 6,533 therapy initiations (mean [SD] baseline characteristics: HbA1c 76[14] mmol/mol, age 35[4] years, BMI 37[9] kg/m2, diabetes duration 5[4] years and 66%, 24% and 6% self-identified as White, South Asian and Black ethnicities). Mean observed HbA1c reductions with initiation of SGLT2i, GLP-1RA, DPP4i, SU and TZDs were 13[17], 9[15], 3[16], 8[17] and 10[17] mmol/mol, respectively. Using the 5-drug class model, the best single agent was predicted to be SGLT2i in 61% and GLP-1RA in 32% of cases. Receiving model predicted optimal therapy was associated with a mean overall benefit of 5.7 (95% CI 4.6-7.0) mmol/mol, and model predictions were well-calibrated with observed responses.
records.conclusion: Optimal alternative treatments for women with early onset type 2 diabetes are SGLT2i or GLP1RAs to optimize glycemia in preparation for pregnancy. SGLT2is and GLP1RAs should be stopped 4-8 weeks before discontinuing contraception.

records.introduction_objective: The Triglyceride-Glucose (TyG) index and the Triglyceride-to-HDL cholesterol (TG/HDL) ratio are simple, cost-effective markers of insulin resistance. However, their prognostic value in quantifying long-term cardiovascular risk is not fully established. This study aims to compare the predictive accuracy of these markers against the 10-year Framingham Risk Score and establish clinical cutoffs.
records.methods: Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2017-2020 was analyzed. Adults aged 20-79 years with complete data for calculating the TyG index, TG/HDL ratio, and FRS were included. High cardiovascular risk was defined as an FRS ≥ 20%. Logistic regression and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis were used to assess the association and predictive performance.
records.results: Both TyG index (ρ = 0.33, p < 0.001) and TG/HDL ratio (ρ = 0.30, p < 0.001) showed moderate positive correlation with the FRS. Both markers were significantly associated with high cardiovascular risk (TyG: OR = 2.20; 95% CI: 1.78-2.72; TG/HDL: OR = 1.35; 95% CI: 1.22-1.50; p < 0.001 for both). The TG/HDL ratio had a slightly higher predictive performance (AUC = 0.659, optimal cutoff: 1.75) compared to the TyG index (AUC = 0.645, optimal cutoff: 8.52).
records.conclusion: These findings suggest that both the TyG index and TG/HDL ratio have moderate discrimination in identifying individuals at high 10-year cardiovascular risk.

records.introduction_objective: While retinal AI enables non-invasive cardiovascular disease (CVD) screening, its utility for monitoring longitudinal changes remains unverified. We validated a retinal AI score (Dr. Noon CVD) in a Korean population and verified progression patterns using the UK Biobank (UKBB).
records.methods: We analyzed data from the GreenCross (GC) checkup center (Korea, 2022-2024) and the UKBB. Participants free of baseline CVD with ≥2 fundus exams (≥30 days interval) were included. In GC, missing smoking data were imputed as non-smoker if absent across all visits, or the recorded status otherwise. We assessed AI score’s accuracy for high risk (PREVENT score ≥7.5%) and the correlation between changes in AI and PREVENT scores in GC. Annual progression rates were verified in both datasets.
records.results: 18,084 (GC) and 1,745 (UKBB) participants were included. Dr. Noon CVD achieved an AUROC of 0.950, and longitudinal score changes correlated strongly with PREVENT changes (r=0.67, p<0.001) in GC. Median annual progression in low-risk (<31) groups was 1.21 [IQR -0.49-3.81] (GC) and 2.03 [1.02-3.62] points/year (UKBB). Rapid progression cutoffs (top 5%) were 16.70 and 5.37 points/year, respectively.
records.conclusion: Dr. Noon CVD accurately identifies high-risk individuals and effectively tracks dynamic risk changes. The longitudinal progression patterns, verified across Korean and UK populations, support its utility for non-invasive risk monitoring.

records.introduction_objective: Misclassification of T1D as T2D is common in adults, potentially leading to ineffective treatment and adverse outcomes. This study prospectively validates an AI algorithm trained to identify adults with misclassified T1D from EMR data, integrating it into clinical workflows at two US health systems via the HSX health information exchange (HIE). records.methods: The algorithm was run on HSX data to flag patients at high risk for misclassified T1D at the two sites. records.introduction_objective: Early identification of individuals at high risk for progressing to Stage 3 (clinically diagnosed) Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is essential for designing prevention trials and recommending disease modifying therapies. Existing risk models often rely on limited data types and struggle to capture variability in complex data, limiting predictive accuracy. Using a novel algorithm designed to capture patterns in complex data, we developed a machine learning (ML) model to predict 2-year progression to Stage 3 T1D among TrialNet Pathway to Prevention (PTP) participants with ≥2 T1D-associated autoantibodies (AAb).
records.methods: Demographic, immunologic, metabolic, and genetic data for participants with ≥2 AAbs were divided into five stratified subsets for feature selection and model training via cross-validation. Synthetic samples were generated to address class imbalance. Using an algorithm that combines noise suppression with spatial clustering, we produced an ML model that outputs “Proximity Scores” (range: 0-200) for predicting whether Stage 3 T1D will occur within 2 years.
records.results: Of 603 participants with ≥2 AAbs (median age, 10 [IQR 8] years; 45.8% female; 77.3% non-Hispanic White), 205 (34.0%) progressed to Stage 3 T1D within 2 years. Top predictors included metabolic measures (e.g., HbA1c) and T1D risk scores (e.g., Index60). Using a fixed decision threshold of 140 facilitated prioritization of specificity and positive predictive value (PPV) as performance metrics. Mean specificity was 0.89 (±0.05), PPV 0.71 (±0.07), sensitivity 0.50 (±0.13), and balance between PPV and sensitivity (F1 score) 0.58 (±0.09).
records.conclusion: Our results demonstrate consistent, modest discriminative performance for predicting progression to Stage 3 T1D within 2 years in PTP participants with ≥2 AAbs. These findings highlight the potential for ML-based risk models to aid early identification and guide therapeutic interventions.

records.introduction_objective: People with mental illness have excess mortality from somatic comorbidities including T2D due to delayed diagnosis and undertreatment. The objective was to develop a machine learning (ML) model to predict the development of T2D in people with mental illness from data routinely collected in the Epic electronic health record (EHR).
records.methods: On a per-visit basis, all adult patients under the purview of the psychiatric hospital service of the Capital Region of Denmark with an index date (hospital discharge or outpatient visit) between June 30, 2018, and Dec. 31, 2021, were included in the training set. The validation set included patients under the purview of the adjacent Region Zealand. Prevalent cases were excluded (diagnosed T2D, use of antidiabetic medication, or ≥2 diagnostic glucose values). The outcome was T2D within 1, 2, or 3 years after index date based on WHO diagnostic criteria, censoring at death or end of follow-up. Model features included demographic and clinical factors such as ICD-10 diagnoses, lab values, medications, number of admissions, and lifestyle factors captured in the EHR. Two model types were used (1) logistic regression with elastic net regularization and (2) XGBoost.
records.results: The training set included 2.31 M visits on 62 K patients; the validation set 622 K visits on 24 K patients. The 3-year incidence of T2D was 2.8%. The selected model achieved an AUROC of 0.90 (95% CI 0.88, 0.92). Among those whose calculated risk was in the top 5%, 28% developed T2D and 53% of cases were identified. Among the top 1%, 55% developed T2D and 21% of cases were identified. Thus, patients identified by the model had 10-20 times increased risk of T2D. The most strongly contributing factors were HbA1c, BMI, triglycerides, age, and plasma glucose.
records.conclusion: The ability of this ML-developed model to identify those at high risk for T2D among people with mental disease will allow targeted testing of established and novel, mental disease-specific T2D prevention modalities in this underserved group.

records.introduction_objective: Cardiovascular-kidney-liver-metabolic (CKLM) disease reflects an interconnected network of metabolic organ dysfunction. Traditional risk models often yield miscalibrated or unstable predictions, particularly in data-sparse regions. We aimed to integrate clinical biomarkers and large-scale plasma proteomics to develop an uncertainty-aware CKLM risk prediction framework and identify key risk factors using machine learning with conformal inference.
records.methods: We analyzed 49,312 UK Biobank participants with proteomic profiling. The primary CKLM outcome was the first occurrence of chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. We used an 80/20 stratified split, selected top clinical and proteomic predictors via cross-validated random forest, benchmarked multiple classifiers, and applied J+aB conformal inference for uncertainty-calibrated risk prediction. Cox models estimated hazard ratios for top proteins, supplemented by pathway enrichment and correlation analyses.
records.results: Over a median 12.3-year follow-up, 9,787 participants developed CKLM. The final model achieved an area under the ROC curve of 0.78 and an average precision of 0.52, with consistent performance across sex, age, and ethnicity (AUC range 0.74-0.82). At 90% nominal confidence, prediction intervals showed 89.6% empirical coverage with a mean width of 0.085. Key clinical predictors included HbA1c, cystatin C, and waist-to-hip ratio; top proteomic predictors included GDF15, HAVCR1, and EDA2R. All selected proteins except PON3 were positively associated with CKLM risk, and enrichment analyses implicated inflammatory, and metabolic pathways.
records.conclusion: Integrating clinical and proteomic data with J+aB conformal inference provides accurate, uncertainty-calibrated CKLM risk estimates and mechanistic insights, supporting earlier identification of high-risk individuals and advancing precision prevention.

records.introduction_objective: Although diabetes heterogeneity is marked by non-linear, multivariate trajectories of biomarkers, comorbidities, and their interactions, most studies are limited to one timepoint. Our objective is to capture heterogeneity before diabetes diagnosis using deep learning and study the risks of complications (cardiovascular disease [CVD], dementia).

Long Short-Term Memory Networks were used to characterize patient representations before the index date (Panel A). Embeddings were clustered using Gaussian Mixture Models, and associations with complications were studied using Cox regressions adjusted for socio-demographic and clinical covariates. Biomarker trajectories were then explored using natural splines.
records.results: The analytic sample (n = 71,522; 64 years [SD: 11], 49% female, 33 kg/m2 [SD: 6.5]), was classified into three clusters (97.2%, 0.2%, 2.6%). Clusters were similar in rates of CVD. records.conclusion: Deep representation learning can incorporate longitudinal patient data for risk stratification. Embedding clusters provided limited prognostic information for CVD but may be beneficial for dementia.

records.introduction_objective: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) causes multisystem complications, but comprehensive multi-omics analyses across diverse clinical outcomes remain limited. We aimed to comprehensively construct the proteomic and metabolomic atlas of major T2D outcomes and to identify predictive panels that balance performance and cost-effectiveness.
records.methods: This study integrates UK Biobank proteomic and metabolomic data and combines cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses to construct an atlas of plasma proteins and metabolites associated with major T2D-related clinical outcomes. We developed LASSO-based predictive models, benchmarked them against SCORE2-Diabetes, and evaluated performance using Harrell’s C-index, net reclassification improvement, and integrated discrimination improvement.
records.results: The study identified molecular signals that consistently exhibited positive or negative associations across multiple T2D outcomes, revealing shared biological pathways. We also uncovered heterogeneous and outcome-specific molecules across diseases. Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses enabled the identification of state markers and early predictive biomarkers. Furthermore, protein-based models substantially outperform clinical models, and combined models achieve the best performance with consistent improvements in reclassification metrics (median delta C-index = 0.117; range: 0.060-0.213), whereas metabolites provide only modest incremental gains. Evaluation across varying selection thresholds identifies a simplified panel of 200 proteins that maintains robust predictive performance.
records.conclusion: This large-scale multi-omics study systematically constructs the molecular atlas of T2D complications, providing new insights into disease biology and potential therapeutic targets. It further defines the predictive value of proteomic and metabolomic profiles and proposes a clinically feasible and practical framework for predicting the risk of T2D complications.

We aimed to comprehensively construct the proteomic and metabolomic atlas of major T2D outcomes and to identify predictive panels that balance performance and cost-effectiveness.

Methods: This study integrates UK Biobank proteomic and metabolomic data and combines cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses to construct an atlas of plasma proteins and metabolites associated with major T2D-related clinical outcomes. We developed LASSO-based predictive models, benchmarked them against SCORE2-Diabetes, and evaluated performance using Harrell’s C-index, net reclassification improvement, and integrated discrimination improvement.

Results: The study identified molecular signals that consistently exhibited positive or negative associations across multiple T2D outcomes, revealing shared biological pathways. We also uncovered heterogeneous and outcome-specific molecules across diseases. Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses enabled the identification of state markers and early predictive biomarkers. Furthermore, protein-based models substantially outperform clinical models, and combined models achieve the best performance with consistent improvements in reclassification metrics (median delta C-index = 0.117; range: 0.060-0.213), whereas metabolites provide only modest incremental gains. Evaluation across varying selection thresholds identifies a simplified panel of 200 proteins that maintains robust predictive performance.

Conclusion: This large-scale multi-omics study systematically constructs the molecular atlas of T2D complications, providing new insights into disease biology and potential therapeutic targets. It further defines the predictive value of proteomic and metabolomic profiles and proposes a clinically feasible and practical framework for predicting the risk of T2D complications.

Introduction and Objective: ATS Insubria, the local health authority in Como and Varese, using data from “OKkio alla Salute” a nutritioral surveillance system in primary school, developed a predictive model to estimate the probability of children falling into different weight categories. The model studied associations with potential risk factors like parental BMI, dietary habits and physical activity.

Methods: The children were categorised according to their BMI as normal weight, overweight or obese. A cumulative logit (proportional odds) regression model was estimated for ordinal outcomes. The coefficients were interpreted as odds, thereby providing insight into how each factor influences the risk of having a BMI in the higher range.

Results: The use of AIC in model selection has led to the identification of parental BMI, sex, the number of days per week on which the child partakes in a minimum of one hour of active play outside of school and the frequency of vegetable consumption (excluding potatoes) as explanatory variables. The results of the estimation process are reported in Table 1.

Conclusion: Children whose lifestyle does not adhere to CREA guidelines for healthy eating and exercise, as well as having at least an overweight parent, are more likely to be at least overweight themselves. Prevention strategies should focus on improving urban health through nutrition, movement, and environmental changes to combat chronic diseases, as proposed by “Cities for Better Health” program.

records.introduction_objective: AI-based meal logging in wearables offers a scalable way to capture daily dietary intake for research, but the quality and utility of these data are uncertain. This study sought to characterize users’ nutrient intake distributions with and without Type 2 Diabetes (T2D).
records.methods: We analyzed de-identified data from 10,378 Oura Ring users (74.4% female; age 18-90 years; BMI: 25.6 ± 5.7 kg/m²; 1.7% self-reported T2D) who logged ≥1 breakfast, lunch, and dinner on ≥5 days during Jan-Nov 2025 using the Oura App. Dietary outcomes (Fig. 1), provided by AI, included carbohydrates, added sugar, fiber, protein, and fat. Differences in dietary patterns between individuals with and without T2D were assessed using Mann-Whitney U tests.
records.results: AI-based nutritional data produced normally distributed intakes across the main macronutrient categories. T2D status was associated with lower carbohydrate (−37.4 g/day; P < .001) and added sugar intakes (−10.1 g/day; P < .001), higher energy shares from fat (2.8%; P < .001) and protein (1.4%; P < .001), and lower total fiber intake (−3.7 g/day; P < .001). All values represent mean differences (T2D - non-T2D).
records.conclusion: In this study, individuals with T2D logged meals consistent with a lower carbohydrate and added sugar, higher fat dietary pattern, but also with less fiber. This difference suggests that AI-based meal logging can capture meaningful variation in everyday dietary behavior.

records.introduction_objective: Over 60% of U.S. adults have risk factors for T2DM, complicating scale-up and sustainability of evidence-based prevention efforts. We developed an EHR-based T2DM prediction model to facilitate real-world implementation.
records.methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study among adults aged 18-70 years receiving care at Kaiser Permanente Northern California from 2012-2024, followed until T2DM onset, death, disenrollment, or Dec 31, 2024. The cohort (N=3,365,464) was randomly split 70:30 for training and validation. We applied a hazard-based Super Learning approach to predict 1-, 3-, and 10-year risk. Incident T2DM was defined using diagnosis codes, glycemic test values, or T2DM medication fills; adults prescribed only metformin, SGLT2, or GLP-1s without a diagnosis code, lab or another T2DM medication were not classified as T2DM. Predictors included demographics, clinical measures, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, prescriptions, utilization, and novel predictors (MASLD and neighborhood-level measures of SES, walkability, and food environment).
records.results: Median age was 39 years (IQR: 28-53), and 55% were female. During a median follow-up of 5.4 years, T2DM incidence was 10.7/1,000 person-years. Within 1-year follow-up, the predictive model achieved an AUC of 0.886 (95% CI: 0.883-0.888) in training and 0.883 (95% CI: 0.880-0.886) in validation, with near-ideal calibration (mean predicted risk 1.03% vs observed 1.01%; slope 1.26). At the optimal cut-point (>1.2% risk) identifying the top two deciles of high risk, sensitivity was 80%, specificity 81%, and number needed to evaluate 25. Results were consistent for 3-, and 10-year follow-up.
records.conclusion: This EHR-based prediction model, developed and validated in over 3 million adults, demonstrated excellent discrimination and calibration. It can support clinicians in identifying patients for T2DM prevention programs, pharmacologic interventions, and enable efficient recruitment for intervention studies. Current work focuses on external validation and future integration into clinical workflows.

Introduction and Objective: Over 60% of U.S. adults have risk factors for T2DM, complicating scale-up and sustainability of evidence-based prevention efforts. We developed an EHR-based T2DM prediction model to facilitate real-world implementation.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study among adults aged 18-70 years receiving care at Kaiser Permanente Northern California from 2012-2024, followed until T2DM onset, death, disenrollment, or Dec 31, 2024. The cohort (N=3,365,464) was randomly split 70:30 for training and validation. We applied a hazard-based Super Learning approach to predict 1-, 3-, and 10-year risk. Incident T2DM was defined using diagnosis codes, glycemic test values, or T2DM medication fills; adults prescribed only metformin, SGLT2, or GLP-1s without a diagnosis code, lab or another T2DM medication were not classified as T2DM. Predictors included demographics, clinical measures, lifestyle factors, comorbidities, prescriptions, utilization, and novel predictors (MASLD and neighborhood-level measures of SES, walkability, and food environment).

Results: Median age was 39 years (IQR: 28-53), and 55% were female. During a median follow-up of 5.4 years, T2DM incidence was 10.7/1,000 person-years. Within 1-year follow-up, the predictive model achieved an AUC of 0.886 (95% CI: 0.883-0.888) in training and 0.883 (95% CI: 0.880-0.886) in validation, with near-ideal calibration (mean predicted risk 1.03% vs observed 1.01%; slope 1.26). At the optimal cut-point (>1.2% risk) identifying the top two deciles of high risk, sensitivity was 80%, specificity 81%, and number needed to evaluate 25. Results were consistent for 3-, and 10-year follow-up.

Conclusion: This EHR-based prediction model, developed and validated in over 3 million adults, demonstrated excellent discrimination and calibration. It can support clinicians in identifying patients for T2DM prevention programs, pharmacologic interventions, and enable efficient recruitment for intervention studies. Current work focuses on external validation and future integration into clinical workflows.

Introduction and Objective: Patients with T2D can be clustered into distinct etiologic subgroups, but it is not clear if the same is true for those with prediabetes (preDM). As metabolites mark the onset of T2D prior to clinical thresholds, we clustered individuals with preDM by preDM-related metabolites and examined subgroups for long-term T2D risk.

Methods: Data were included from N=5567 participants, N=2003 of whom had preDM (100≤fasting glucose<126 mg/dL). Machine learning was used to select baseline metabolites that distinguished preDM from normoglycemia. Those with preDM were clustered into subgroups by their values of the selected compounds, and chi-squared tests quantified baseline subgroup differences. Cox-proportional hazards models, controlling for demographics, and fasting glucose and insulin, examined subgroup differences in T2D risk over 20 years follow-up.

Results: N=31 metabolites discriminated preDM from normoglycemia (AUC=0.96;fig1A). Clustering individuals by these compounds identified 3 subgroups (fig1B). Fasting glucose and insulin did not differ between subgroups (p<.001;fig1C), but the likelihood of developing T2D did (P=.03;fig1C &1D).

Conclusion: Individuals with preDM represent discrete metabolome-based subgroups, informative for T2D progression. Future analyses will include validation in additional DEFINE-T2D cohorts.

records.introduction_objective: Older breast cancer (BC) survivors have a high rates of type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality. The UKPDS Outcomes model 2 (OM2) is a widely used DM microsimulation model to predict health outcomes. Though validated in US populations, OM2 applicability to BC survivors, who have distinct mortality and CV risk, is unknown. As accurate risk prediction is critical for DM clinical decision making in BC survivors, we compared OM2-predicted with observed mortality in BC survivors and calibrated OM2 to improve mortality prediction.
records.methods: We identified women ≥66 years with Stage II-III BC and DM from 2008-2019 US Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) data linked to Medicare. Model inputs were derived from claims; missing biometric variables were imputed with predictive means matching from NHANES. Using published OM2 equations, we predicted 10-year overall mortality and compared estimates to SEER-Medicare rates using Kaplan-Meier curves. Calibration iteratively scaled baseline hazards (time-dependent mortality risk) by BC stage to align predicted and observed survival curves, for which goodness of fit was assessed with observed expected (O/E) ratios.
records.results: Among 5938 survivors (77% Stage II), median age was 75 years (interquartile range 70-81), and 40% had preexisting CVD. Observed 10-year mortality was 64% (95% confidence interval [CI] 61%-66%) for Stage II and 76% (95% CI 72%-80%) for Stage III survivors. Uncalibrated OM2 underestimated 10-year mortality, predicting 60% [95% CI 58%-61%] for Stage II (O/E 1.1) and 60% [95% CI 57%-63%] for Stage III BC (O/E 1.3). After calibration, O/E ratios were 1.0 and predicted and observed mortality aligned across age groups.
records.conclusion: A widely used DM model substantially underestimated mortality in older BC survivors, with implications for DM clinical decision making. Calibration improved accuracy, highlighting the need to adapt T2DM models in cancer survivors.

After calibration, O/E ratios were 1.0 and predicted and observed mortality aligned across age groups.

Conclusion: A widely used DM model substantially underestimated mortality in older BC survivors, with implications for DM clinical decision making. Calibration improved accuracy, highlighting the need to adapt T2DM models in cancer survivors.

records.introduction_objective: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) exhibits substantial heterogeneity, yet the key clinical phenotypes remain unclear. We applied DDRTree machine learning to identify the key phenotype characterizing T1D heterogeneity and validate the existence of age-related endotypes.
records.methods: We performed DDRTree dimensionality reduction analysis using data on 13 phenotypes (age at onset, BMI, blood pressure, ALT, HbA1c, creatinine, triglycerides, HDL-C, total cholesterol, GADA, IA-2A, ZnT8A) from 879 patients with T1D to identify the most important clinical phenotype. We then evaluated the rationality of classifying patients into age-related endotypes (<7, 7-13, ≥13 years) and compared clinical, immunological, and genetic profiles across groups to confirm the presence of age-related endotypes. Finally, we validated the existence of these endotypes in an external UK Biobank cohort and investigated longitudinal cardiovascular outcomes associated with age-at-onset phenotypes.
records.results: Age at onset emerged as the most important phenotype for T1D heterogeneity, explaining 64.6% of the variance in the DDRTree dimensionality reduction. Classification into age-related endotypes showed significant differences in DDRTree dimensional coordinates (p = 1.61×10-54), supporting the rationality of this grouping. Autoantibody positivity (IA-2A, ZnT8A: p < 0.001), HLA genetic risk (p < 0.001), and metabolic characteristics differed significantly, further confirming age-related endotypes. Moreover, phenotypic heterogeneity by onset age attenuated with disease duration in both the internal and UK Biobank cohorts. Regarding long-term outcomes, older-onset T1D patients exhibited higher cardiovascular risk (sHR = 2.93, 95% CI: 1.49-5.78 for ≥13 vs. <7 years).
records.conclusion: DDRTree analysis identified age at onset as the key phenotype of T1D heterogeneity. Dimensionality reduction demonstrated excellent discriminative performance, supporting the existence of age-related endotypes.

records.introduction_objective: No studies to date have predicted functional pancreatic beta cell depletion in type 1 diabetes (T1D) via machine learning. The aim of this study was to develop a prediction model using machine learning to stratify patients by depletion risk.
records.methods: Records for 293 patients with T1D (180 with acute-onset T1D [AT1D] and 113 with slowly-progressive T1D [SPT1D]) were obtained from the TIDE-J multicenter longitudinal database of Japanese T1D patients. We identified clinical factors associated with functional beta cell depletion, which was defined as C-peptide [CPR] level below detection limit, using a Cox proportional hazards model. We also applied Random Survival Forest (RSF)-based survival analysis to predict functional beta cell depletion. The RSF-derived case-wise similarity matrix was visualized using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), followed by k-means clustering based on depletion risk.
records.results: In Cox analysis, ZnT8 antibodies (FDR-adjusted P = 0.001), IA-2 antibodies (P = 0.020), and BMI (P = 0.027) were associated with functional beta cell depletion. The RSF model also identified urinary ketone bodies, body weight, weight loss, and GAD antibodies as significant predictors. Patients were clustered into four groups (Clusters 1-4). In confirmation of clustering using a decision tree, body weight, weight loss, and ZnT8 antibodies (cutoff: 205 U/mL) were identified as the determinants of cluster assignment. All cluster 1 individuals retained measurable CPR for more than 6 years, while 50% of cluster 4 patients progressed to functional beta cell depletion within 4 years. Both, AT1D and SPT1D were distributed across all clusters.
records.conclusion: Machine learning approaches enable prediction of functional beta cell exhaustion across T1D subtypes using limited clinical indicators.

records.introduction_objective: Environmental factors such as the gut microbiota may play distinct roles in the pathogenesis of type 1 diabetes (T1D) presenting with or without diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) at onset. This study aimed to employ a deep learning model to identify multi-omics signatures in patients with DKA-onset T1D and to investigate the underlying mechanisms.
records.methods: Newly diagnosed T1D patients (n=69) were randomly enrolled and stratified into two groups: DKA and Non-DKA, based on the presence of ketoacidosis at onset. A deep learning model, Multi-Omics Variational Autoencoders (MOVE), was utilized to assess the importance of features from gut microbiome, serum metabolome, lipidome, and proteome profiles between the groups. Key microbiota and their potential associations with metabolic or protein features were screened through model perturbation analysis.
records.results: The MOVE model demonstrated strong capability in processing T1D multi-omics data (loss value = 0.9403). Analysis revealed distinct multi-omics signatures between the groups. The DKA group was characterized by elevated levels of s__Bacteroides clarus, 2-Arachidonyl Glycerol ether, and Phosphatidylcholine (PC) (36:2). In contrast, the Non-DKA group featured a higher abundance of f__Burkholderiaceae, along with increased levels of D-(+)-Proline, LPC (16:0), and the protein CCL28. Integrated importance evaluation of clinical, gut microbiome, metabolome, lipidome, and proteome signatures highlighted the significant role of gut microbiota in DKA onset. Perturbation-based analysis using MOVE suggested that s__Lachnospira sp000437735 might ameliorate ketoacidosis occurrence at T1D onset by facilitating the metabolism of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde.
records.conclusion: The application of a deep learning model provides novel molecular insights and potential therapeutic targets for elucidating the heterogeneity of T1D onset and for exploring individualized prevention and treatment strategies.

records.introduction_objective: Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) is a lifelong autoimmune disease with major impacts on health, quality of life, and healthcare systems worldwide. Despite decades of research, progress is often slowed by fragmented knowledge spread across isolated databases, publications, and experimental platforms. These resources are rich but heterogeneous, making it difficult to connect genetic, molecular, cellular, clinical, and imaging evidence into a coherent view.
records.methods: Here we present PanKgraph, a comprehensive knowledge graph for Type 1 Diabetes that integrates diverse data types into a unified, machine-readable framework. Unlike traditional databases, which store data in fixed schemas and silos, a knowledge graph explicitly represents entities and their relationships, enabling flexible integration of multi-modal experimental data, biomedical literature, and curated domain knowledge. This structure supports cross-scale reasoning, hypothesis generation, and discovery of non-obvious connections across biological systems.
records.results: To serve the broader research community, we provide an open, web-based, question-driven interface that allows users to explore T1D knowledge through interactive graphs, concise textual summaries, and visual representations linked to underlying experimental evidence. We further expose an application programming interface (API) designed for large language models, enabling joint analysis of scientific images, publications, and raw experimental data.
records.conclusion: By lowering barriers to data integration and interpretation, PanKgraph aims to shift T1D research beyond single-axis thinking, foster collaboration across disciplines, and accelerate innovative, systems-level insights into disease mechanisms and therapies.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) is a lifelong autoimmune disease with major impacts on health, quality of life, and healthcare systems worldwide. Despite decades of research, progress is often slowed by fragmented knowledge spread across isolated databases, publications, and experimental platforms. These resources are rich but heterogeneous, making it difficult to connect genetic, molecular, cellular, clinical, and imaging evidence into a coherent view.

Methods: Here we present PanKgraph, a comprehensive knowledge graph for Type 1 Diabetes that integrates diverse data types into a unified, machine-readable framework. Unlike traditional databases, which store data in fixed schemas and silos, a knowledge graph explicitly represents entities and their relationships, enabling flexible integration of multi-modal experimental data, biomedical literature, and curated domain knowledge. This structure supports cross-scale reasoning, hypothesis generation, and discovery of non-obvious connections across biological systems.

Results: To serve the broader research community, we provide an open, web-based, question-driven interface that allows users to explore T1D knowledge through interactive graphs, concise textual summaries, and visual representations linked to underlying experimental evidence. We further expose an application programming interface (API) designed for large language models, enabling joint analysis of scientific images, publications, and raw experimental data.

Conclusion: By lowering barriers to data integration and interpretation, PanKgraph aims to shift T1D research beyond single-axis thinking, foster collaboration across disciplines, and accelerate innovative, systems-level insights into disease mechanisms and therapies.

records.introduction_objective: Health research has historically conflated genetic ancestry with race and ethnicity, limiting precision in risk prediction for multifactorial conditions like type 2 diabetes (T2D). MicroRNAs (miRs) are dynamic molecular regulators that respond to environmental and behavioral exposures, potentially capturing extrinsic risk. The objective of this study was to determine whether miR expression patterns vary by genetic ancestry in individuals with prediabetes.
records.methods: We included genetic and miR data derived from plasma samples collected at the baseline visit for the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) (n=854). We also used a previously established miR risk score derived from random forest and lasso models. Genetic ancestry was estimated using the 1KG reference populations using k-means clustering. Logistic regression was used to determine the odds of developing T2D after 2 years based on ancestral group, miR risk score, or a combination of these two predictors.
records.results: Seven ancestral groups were selected based on cross-validation stability. Participants exhibited admixed ancestry, with a predominant European component followed by African. Ancestral composition was not associated with the odds of developing T2D. In contrast, the miR risk score was associated with increased odds (1.24, p<0.05). When the miR risk score and ancestral group were both included as predictors, the magnitude of the odds ratios increased for all ancestral groups.
records.conclusion: These findings suggest that integrating ancestry-informed genetic measures with miRs may improve precision in distinguishing intrinsic genetic risk from extrinsic social, behavioral and environmental influences. This combined approach may enhance risk prediction and inform targeted prevention strategies. Further studies are needed to determine if there are distinct sets of miRs that predict risk within ancestral groups and race and ethnic groups.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Health research has historically conflated genetic ancestry with race and ethnicity, limiting precision in risk prediction for multifactorial conditions like type 2 diabetes (T2D). MicroRNAs (miRs) are dynamic molecular regulators that respond to environmental and behavioral exposures, potentially capturing extrinsic risk. The objective of this study was to determine whether miR expression patterns vary by genetic ancestry in individuals with prediabetes.

Methods: We included genetic and miR data derived from plasma samples collected at the baseline visit for the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) (n=854). We also used a previously established miR risk score derived from random forest and lasso models. Genetic ancestry was estimated using the 1KG reference populations using k-means clustering. Logistic regression was used to determine the odds of developing T2D after 2 years based on ancestral group, miR risk score, or a combination of these two predictors.

Results: Seven ancestral groups were selected based on cross-validation stability. Participants exhibited admixed ancestry, with a predominant European component followed by African. Ancestral composition was not associated with the odds of developing T2D. In contrast, the miR risk score was associated with increased odds (1.24, p<0.05). When the miR risk score and ancestral group were both included as predictors, the magnitude of the odds ratios increased for all ancestral groups.

Conclusion: These findings suggest that integrating ancestry-informed genetic measures with miRs may improve precision in distinguishing intrinsic genetic risk from extrinsic social, behavioral and environmental influences. This combined approach may enhance risk prediction and inform targeted prevention strategies. Further studies are needed to determine if there are distinct sets of miRs that predict risk within ancestral groups and race and ethnic groups.

records.introduction_objective: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) exhibits age-dependent heterogeneity in disease progression, with younger children (<7 years) typically experiencing more aggressive β-cell destruction than adolescents (>15 years). Despite this clinical heterogeneity, the immunological and metabolic mechanisms underlying divergent progression patterns remain unclear. We hypothesized that circulating plasma factors drive age-dependent signaling pathway activation in immune cells.
records.methods: Healthy individual PBMCs were stimulated with plasma from young recent-onset T1D (RO7, n=13; age <7 years), older recent-onset T1D (RO15, n=9; age >15 years), and age/HLA-matched healthy controls (HR7, n=10; HR15, n=10), followed by microarray analysis to identify differentially expressed genes. Gene signatures were integrated with TEDDY (The Environmental Determinants of Diabetes in the Young) metabolomics data (n=113-294; age <7) and validated using Seahorse XF assays.
records.results: RO7 and RO15 plasma induced 1,719 differentially expressed genes (FDR <0.1). Integration with TEDDY metabolomics revealed elevated TCA cycle metabolites (fumaric and malic acid; FDR <0.2) in the RO7 group. Consistently, RO7 plasma induced mitochondrial metabolic gene signatures (4.6-fold TCA cycle, 2-fold OXPHOS; p<0.05). LASSO, a machine learning algorithm, identified RTK-PI3K signaling as a key discriminator between RO7 and RO15 (misclassification score = 0). Seahorse assays showed that RO15 plasma suppressed mitochondrial potential in healthy PBMCs, limiting energy availability for immune activation.
records.conclusion: Age-specific plasma factors drive distinct signaling and metabolic programs in immune cells. In RO7, PI3K signaling enhances mitochondrial bioenergetics, while suppressive factors in RO15 plasma restrict metabolic capacity. These findings provide a mechanistic link between age-dependent signaling, immune metabolism, and heterogeneous disease progression in T1D.
