Introduction and Objective: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) exhibits age-dependent heterogeneity in disease progression, with younger children (<7 years) typically experiencing more aggressive β-cell destruction than adolescents (>15 years). Despite this clinical heterogeneity, the immunological and metabolic mechanisms underlying divergent progression patterns remain unclear. We hypothesized that circulating plasma factors drive age-dependent signaling pathway activation in immune cells.

Methods: Healthy individual PBMCs were stimulated with plasma from young recent-onset T1D (RO7, n=13; age <7 years), older recent-onset T1D (RO15, n=9; age >15 years), and age/HLA-matched healthy controls (HR7, n=10; HR15, n=10), followed by microarray analysis to identify differentially expressed genes. Gene signatures were integrated with TEDDY (The Environmental Determinants of Diabetes in the Young) metabolomics data (n=113-294; age <7) and validated using Seahorse XF assays.

Results: RO7 and RO15 plasma induced 1,719 differentially expressed genes (FDR <0.1). Integration with TEDDY metabolomics revealed elevated TCA cycle metabolites (fumaric and malic acid; FDR <0.2) in the RO7 group. Consistently, RO7 plasma induced mitochondrial metabolic gene signatures (4.6-fold TCA cycle, 2-fold OXPHOS; p<0.05). LASSO, a machine learning algorithm, identified RTK-PI3K signaling as a key discriminator between RO7 and RO15 (misclassification score = 0). Seahorse assays showed that RO15 plasma suppressed mitochondrial potential in healthy PBMCs, limiting energy availability for immune activation.

Conclusion: Age-specific plasma factors drive distinct signaling and metabolic programs in immune cells. In RO7, PI3K signaling enhances mitochondrial bioenergetics, while suppressive factors in RO15 plasma restrict metabolic capacity. These findings provide a mechanistic link between age-dependent signaling, immune metabolism, and heterogeneous disease progression in T1D.

records.introduction_objective: Insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor (IGF-1R) inhibitor has been developed as an effective therapy for thyroid eye disease (TED). However, treatment-associated hyperglycemia remains a clinical concern. We aimed to examine whether early glycemic deterioration during IGF-1R inhibitor therapy is associated with subsequent glycemic trajectories and to develop and validate a risk prediction model.
records.methods: We analyzed data from three independent randomized clinical trials of the IGF-1R inhibitor IBI311 for TED, including 129 participants treated with IBI311. Two trials served as training cohort (n=76), and the remaining trial served as an independent validation cohort (n=53). Early glycemic deterioration was defined as a ≥0.5% increase in HbA1c by week 6 or initiation/intensification of glucose-lowering therapy within 6 weeks. Associations between early deterioration and glycemic outcomes at treatment completion (24 weeks) were examined in training cohort. A prediction model was developed using baseline metabolic variables with elastic net-regularized logistic regression and externally validated.
records.results: Early glycemic deterioration occurred in 18.6% (14/129) of participants. Individuals with early deterioration experienced greater increases in HbA1c (1.13% ± 0.55% vs. 0.17% ± 0.33%; P=0.001) and FBG (1.86 ± 1.79 mmol/L vs. 0.16 ± 0.61 mmol/L; P=0.021) at 24 weeks. At baseline, participants with early deterioration had higher FBG, blood pressure, lower HDL-c, and greater metabolic syndrome (MetS) score. An elastic net model incorporating baseline FBG (standard β=0.25) and MetS score (standard β=0.20) demonstrated good discrimination for early deterioration (external AUC 0.80, 95% CI 0.63-0.94).
records.conclusion: Early glycemic deterioration during IGF-1R inhibitor therapy is associated with subsequent hyperglycemia. A simple baseline model using routinely available metabolic measures may enable early risk stratification.

records.introduction_objective: Recent data from the BELIEVE and COURAGE trials validate activin type II receptor (ActR2) pathway inhibition for high-quality weight loss (fat reduction with lean mass gain). Ligand blocking monotherapy in COURAGE showed submaximal efficacy, with worsening AEs in combination. Bimagrumab in BELIEVE was not optimized for convenient, subcutaneous (s.c.) dosing, and low affinity for ActR2A limits fat mass efficacy at lower doses. These limitations underscore the need for fully optimized molecules that comprehensively and conveniently inhibit the ActR2 pathway for obesity.
records.methods: We leveraged our machine-learning platform for multi-parameter optimization to design ActR2A/B antagonists. The pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic profile was characterized in mice and non-human primates (NHP). Efficacy was evaluated in B6 lean mice and DIO mice in combination with semaglutide. Manufacturability was assessed under stressed conditions.
records.results: FBL-140 has balanced, high-affinity binding to both ActR2A and ActR2B, resulting in greater potency vs bimagrumab in human primary skeletal muscle cells and adipocytes. Superior thermostability, reduced self-interaction and lower polyreactivity deliver best-in-class drug properties. Stress tests and high concentration studies demonstrate compatibility with s.c. dosing and long shelf-life. Introduction and Objective: Recent data from the BELIEVE and COURAGE trials validate activin type II receptor (ActR2) pathway inhibition for high-quality weight loss (fat reduction with lean mass gain). Methods: We leveraged our machine-learning platform for multi-parameter optimization to design ActR2A/B antagonists. Introduction and Objective: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) plays a key role in non-shivering thermogenesis and is strongly implicated in obesity and metabolic disease, and may offer an alternative therapeutic strategy for treating obesity and its related comorbidities.

Methods: Starting from a BAT-ML (an in-house machine learning (ML)-derived BAT phenotype) GWAS, we investigated the relevance of these genetic signals in vitro using human adipocyte cell models and in vivo in HFD obese mice.

Results: At least 1 target identified through BAT-ML was found to reduce body weight and fat mass AND increased BAT/beige-like character in vivo.

Conclusion: Here, we present the first BAT-ML GWAS and prosecution of the genetic insights in adipocyte cell models through in vivo validation in support of targeting BAT for potentially treating obesity and its related comorbidities.

records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: GLP-1 RAs are increasingly used for WL, yet little is known about how PwO experience and personalize treatment in everyday life. This mixed-method study aimed to elucidate the dynamics shaping treatment experiences and dosing practices of PwO using GLP-1 RA in the US.

Methods: Public user-generated content from Reddit (N>250,000 posts) and YouTube (N=2,000 video transcripts, >56,700 comments) GLP-1 RA user forums (2019-2025) was analyzed by natural language processing (NLP) for key themes. Lived experiences and GLP-1 RA dose personalization practices of PwO were explored in 2-hour F2F ethnographic in-home interviews.

Results: NLP analysis of social data identified key health-related (behavioral considerations, medical guidance, side effects, effectiveness), psychosocial (interpersonal relationships, identity), and practical (cost and access) person-centric themes influencing GLP-1 RA use for WL. F2F interviews (N=25; age 25-65 years; 64% female; 64% White, 24% Black, 12% Hispanic) identified evolving dynamics shaping WL GLP-1 RA treatment among PwO, including experiences, goals, and dosing practices (Table 1).

Conclusion: The dynamics shaping GLP-1 RA treatment for WL highlight actionable priorities for person-centered education and support for GLP-1 RA treatment personalization.

records.introduction_objective: This study assessed the efficacy and safety of MDR-001, a novel oral GLP-1 RA, in Chinese participants (pts) with overweight or obesity without diabetes.
records.methods: In this randomized, double-blind, phase 2b study, 317 adults with obesity (BMI ≥28 kg/m2) or overweight (BMI, 24 to <28 kg/m2) were randomized 1:1:1:1:1 to BID doses of MDR-001 at 90, 120, 150, 180 mg or placebo (PBO) for 24 weeks (W). Primary endpoint was the percentage change from baseline in body weight (BW) at W24.
records.results: At baseline, mean BW was 90.1 kg; BMI was 32.3 kg/m²; 53.5% were female. At W24, least-squares mean (LSM) percentage changes in BW were -8.0%, -9.1%, -9.6%, -9.3% with MDR-001 90, 120, 150, and 180 mg, respectively, vs -2.6% with PBO (all P<.0001) (Figure A). The proportion of pts achieving ≥5%, ≥10%, and ≥15% weight loss target, reduction in WC, BMI, FPG, and ALT were significantly greater with all MDR-001 doses vs PBO (all P<.01) (Figures B, C, D). Most TEAEs were GIAEs (pooled MDR-001: nausea, 44.5%; vomiting, 37.6%; diarrhea 22.0%; constipation, 4.7%), mostly mild to moderate; occurred mainly in dose escalation phase. Only 0.8% of pts discontinued MDR-001due to TEAEs. No drug-related serious AEs occurred.
records.conclusion: MDR-001 significantly reduced BW and improved metabolic measures at W24; with consistent safety profile as other GLP-1 RAs. These promising data support further development of MDR-001 as a convenient oral therapy for obesity.

records.introduction_objective: Obesity is a chronic disease associated with increased cardiometabolic risk. Digital health interventions integrating continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and personalized feedback may support scalable behavior change. This study evaluated whether higher engagement with the Signos System, an artificial intelligence-enabled CGM platform, is associated with greater weight loss among adults with obesity without diabetes.
records.methods: This open-label, retrospective study included adults (≥18 years) with BMI ≥30 kg/m2, without diabetes, who enrolled in the Signos System between January 2022 and June 2024. The intervention combines CGM with an artificial intelligence-enabled mobile application providing personalized behavioral guidance based on glucose responses, dietary intake, physical activity, and self-reported data. Engagement was defined as Total Meaningful Actions per Day (TMAPD). Weight change was assessed as total body weight loss (TBWL%) using longitudinal within-subject comparisons and a cross-sectional analysis at 180 days.
records.results: Longitudinal analyses included 3,007 subjects. Mean daily weight loss was greater during periods of higher versus lower engagement (0.167 ± 0.006% vs 0.063 ± 0.004%; P<0.001). Higher TMAPD was associated with increased physical activity, with exercise duration increasing from 10.0 ± 0.2 to 23.1 ± 0.4 minutes per day and energy expenditure from 48.4 ± 1.3 to 106.5 ± 2.3 kcal/day (both P<0.001). In a cross-sectional cohort of 1,147 subjects, engagement correlated with TBWL% (r=0.179, P<0.001). Participants with higher engagement (TMAPD ≥1.02) achieved 5.90 ± 0.25% TBWL at 180 days.
records.conclusion: Greater engagement with the Signos System was associated with increased weight loss and physical activity among adults with obesity. Six-month weight loss exceeded 5% TBWL, a clinically meaningful threshold, supporting the role of personalized, artificial intelligence-enabled digital interventions in obesity management.

records.introduction_objective: Health risks associated with excess body weight vary based on race and ethnicity. As such, standard analytics may underestimate disparities in referral to weight management treatments (WMTs). The objective of this study was to compare standard vs. risk-based estimates of disparities in WMT referral.

We calculated propensity score weights with gradient boosting models to achieve age, sex, weight-related condition, and obesity class covariate balance for standard (Non-Hispanic single-race and Hispanic categories with uniform obesity classes) and risk-based (includes multiracial patients and Asian-specific obesity classes) analyses for Black, Asian, Hispanic, and Non-Hispanic White patients. records.results: Compared to standard analyses (N=36,522), risk-based analyses (N=38,847) revealed deep disparities for Asian patients, who were 43% less likely than Black patients [RR (95% CI): 0.57( 0.51-0.63); p<0.001], 42% less likely than Hispanic patients [RR (95% CI): 0.58 (0.52-0.66) ; p<0.001], and 36% less likely than White patients [RR (95% CI): 0.64 (0.59-0.70); p<0.001] to be referred to any WMT. records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Visceral and ectopic fat deposition are implicated in post-pancreatitis diabetes mellitus (PPDM-A). This study aimed to identify associated protein biomarkers and develop a novel prediction model by integrating cohort and proteomic data.

Methods: We conducted an integrated analysis of clinical, imaging (CT-derived), and proteomic data from a Chinese cohort and the UK Biobank. A Lipid Metabolic Score (LMS) was constructed from several lipid metrics. Model performance was assessed by AUC. Causal inference for the lead protein (STC1) was evaluated via two-sample Mendelian randomization.

Results: The LMS and recurrent pancreatitis were independent predictors of PPDM-A in the Chinese cohort. In the UK Biobank, a model combining baseline LMS and HbA1c achieved an AUC of 0.802 for PPDM-A prediction. Incorporating the protein STC1 enhanced the AUC to 0.861. Genetically elevated STC1 levels were causally associated with increased pancreas fat (OR = 1.09; P = 0.011).

Conclusion: PPDM-A is driven by recurrent pancreatitis, dysglycemia, and lipid metabolism disorders mediated by visceral and ectopic fat. The proposed clinical-proteomic model, featuring STC1, significantly improves risk stratification and offers a potentially practical tool for early identification of high-risk patients.

records.introduction_objective: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) for obesity are a promising tool for obesity risk prediction, yet their performance may vary across populations and individual-level contexts. While racial/ethnic differences in PRS performance are well documented, less is known about how demographic, lifestyle, and cardiometabolic factors influence PRS performance within and across populations.
records.methods: We constructed PRS for body mass index (BMI) using genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from the Genetic Investigation of Anthropometric Traits (GIANT) consortium (N≈1.95M; independent of target samples). PRS were constructed using pruning-and-thresholding (P+T) and Bayesian approaches (PRS-CS and PRS-CSx). Prediction performance was evaluated in the Population Architecture using Genomics and Epidemiology (PAGE) study and eight additional cohorts and biobanks (Max N=501,247). Context-specific performance was examined across strata defined by race/ethnicity, age, sex, smoking status, physical activity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), and hypertension.
records.results: Across all racial/ethnic groups in PAGE, Bayesian PRS methods outperformed P+T, with PRS-CS showing the most consistent performance (overall R²=9.0% vs. 6.6%). PRS performance varied substantially by race/ethnicity, with higher R² in non-Hispanic White participants (14.0%) compared with non-Hispanic Black participants (7.1%). Beyond race/ethnicity, significant heterogeneity in PRS performance was observed across demographic, lifestyle, and clinical contexts. Prediction accuracy was generally lower among males, older individuals, current smokers, and participants with T2D, with consistent patterns across cohorts.
records.conclusion: Bayesian PRS methods substantially improve obesity risk prediction; however, PRS performance varies across populations and individual-level contexts. These findings underscore the importance of context-specific evaluation to support equitable and clinically appropriate application of obesity PRS.

records.introduction_objective: Mechanistic studies suggest that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) modulate appetite and may reduce compulsive eating behaviors through centrally mediated mechanisms involving hypothalamic and mesolimbic pathways. However, clinical evidence remains limited. We therefore aimed to evaluate the association between GLP-1RA use and clinical outcomes among patients with coexisting obesity and binge eating disorders.
records.methods: In this retrospective cohort study, we used 2015-2024 OneFlorida+ electronic health record data to identify individuals with obesity and coexisting binge eating disorder or binge-eating-associated bulimia nervosa. Using a target trial emulation framework, we compared the risks of emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalization between GLP-1RA users and non-users. An innovative machine-learning-based, time-conditional 1:1 propensity score matching was applied to balance baseline confounders between groups, followed by Cox proportional hazards models to estimate outcome risks.
records.results: After 1:1 propensity score matching, 448 matched pairs were included. In the overall cohort, there were no significant differences in the risks of ED visits (hazard ratio [HR], 1.02; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.75-1.35) or hospitalization (HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.60-1.10) between GLP-1RA users and non-users. In stratified analyses, GLP-1RA use was associated with a significantly lower risk of ED visits (HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.49-0.65) and hospitalization (HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.76-0.88) among patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), but not among those without T2D.
records.conclusion: GLP-1RA use was associated with a significantly lower risk of ED visits and hospitalization among patients with binge eating disorders who also have T2D, whereas no such association was observed in patients without T2D
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Mechanistic studies suggest that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) modulate appetite and may reduce compulsive eating behaviors through centrally mediated mechanisms involving hypothalamic and mesolimbic pathways. However, clinical evidence remains limited. We therefore aimed to evaluate the association between GLP-1RA use and clinical outcomes among patients with coexisting obesity and binge eating disorders.

Methods: In this retrospective cohort study, we used 2015-2024 OneFlorida+ electronic health record data to identify individuals with obesity and coexisting binge eating disorder or binge-eating-associated bulimia nervosa. Using a target trial emulation framework, we compared the risks of emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalization between GLP-1RA users and non-users. An innovative machine-learning-based, time-conditional 1:1 propensity score matching was applied to balance baseline confounders between groups, followed by Cox proportional hazards models to estimate outcome risks.

Results: After 1:1 propensity score matching, 448 matched pairs were included. In the overall cohort, there were no significant differences in the risks of ED visits (hazard ratio [HR], 1.02; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.75-1.35) or hospitalization (HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.60-1.10) between GLP-1RA users and non-users. In stratified analyses, GLP-1RA use was associated with a significantly lower risk of ED visits (HR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.49-0.65) and hospitalization (HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.76-0.88) among patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), but not among those without T2D.

Conclusion: GLP-1RA use was associated with a significantly lower risk of ED visits and hospitalization among patients with binge eating disorders who also have T2D, whereas no such association was observed in patients without T2D

Introduction and Objective: Some individuals with T2D have islet autoantibodies (aab). To determine if the presence of autoantibodies represents a form of islet-directed autoimmunity, we integrated and compared serologic, functional, genetic, and histologic data from HPAP-T2D donors with (T2Daab+, n=6) or without (T2Daab-, n=47) aab, and donors with no diabetes (ND, N=96).

Methods: Donor clinical and demographic data, islet perifusion results, genetic risk scores (GRS), and multiplex immunofluorescent images (CODEX) are available on the HPAP website, PancDB. Immunofluorescent images were quantified using AI-assisted segmentation and classification algorithms in QuPath software. Statistical significance (p<0.05) was tested by ANOVA.

Results: Compared to ND donors, T2D donors had higher BMI and T2D-GRS, lower residual C-peptide, but no difference in relative pancreas weight (RPW). Compared to T2Daab-, T2Daab+ (4 GADA+, 2 IA2+) individuals were similar in age, BMI, disease duration, T1D-GRS, and T2D-GRS. T2Daab+ individuals had reduced islet function, with lower C-peptide levels (1.2±0.3 vs 3.7±0.5 ng/mL, p=0.001), lower glucose-stimulated insulin release from isolated islets (1.2±0.1 vs 1.6±0.2 stimulation index, p=0.07), and higher HbA1c (8.8±0.5 vs 7.4±0.3 %, p=0.03) than T2Daab-. RPW of T2Daab+ individuals was intermediate between T2Daab- and HPAP-T1D donors (0.86±0.08 vs 1.03±0.07 vs 0.68±0.04 g/kg, p=0.001). In pancreatic sections, the T cell/islet cell ratio was higher in T2Daab+ than in ND controls (0.38±0.09 vs 0.11±0.02; p=0.03), but was not different between T2Daab- and controls. Sections from one of six T2Daab+ donors was amyloid positive, compared to 24/41 T2Daab- donors being amyloid positive.

Conclusion: Among T2D donors, the presence of islet autoantibodies was associated with histologic evidence of latent autoimmunity, reduced islet function, and decreased pancreas size, suggesting that autoimmune processes play a role in their diabetes.

records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: We applied an AI-driven clustering approach to clamp responses to determine whether integrated symptom and physiological responses can more objectively distinguish individuals with Impaired awareness of hypoglycemia (IAH) .

Methods: 19 individuals with T1D underwent a stepped clamp with glucose sequentially lowered to 90, 65, 55, and 45 mg/dL. K-means clustering was applied using symptoms alone, physiological responses alone, and combined responses. Clustering performance was evaluated using both absolute responses and response changes

Results: Clustering using response changes separated participants into two groups consistent with preserved hypoglycemia awareness (n=10) and impaired awareness (n=9). Analysis using responses at 45 mg/dL produced a nearly identical partition (11 vs 8), with 18 of 19 individuals assigned consistently across models. Symptom responses were the primary drivers of cluster separation. The Δ90→45 analysis captures the fold change and produces the clearest overall separation of awareness phenotypes when using all responses (Figure 1).

Conclusion: AI-based clustering of hypoglycemic clamp responses identifies awareness status in T1D using integrated physiological and symptom signals. Compared with questionnaire-based approaches such as the GOLD score, AI-driven phenotyping provides an objective framework that may more accurately distinguish individuals with IAH.

records.introduction_objective: Effective collaboration between primary care and ophthalmology is critical to improving diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening access. AEYE Health was piloted across Emory Healthcare primary care sites in collaboration with ophthalmology. This Phase 1 study evaluated implementation from April to December 2025 for workflow efficiency, AI usage guidelines, and appropriate ophthalmology scheduling.
records.methods: Patients screened using AEYE Health across Emory Healthcare primary care sites were included. Ophthalmology verified findings per ETDRS criteria. Collected data included scheduling status, time to appointment, and referral adherence. Eye care providers conducted site visits at three of four clinics, and monthly stakeholder meetings reviewed access, scheduling, and workflow. Fisher's exact test, Pearson's Chi-squared test, and Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test explored associations between diabetic retinopathy and positive status.
records.results: Phase 1 included 1,635 total screening attempts and 771 screening encounters. AEYE Health identified 108 patients with more than mild DR; 114 patients with a negative result were reviewed from April to June 2025. Both groups underwent human-grade review, identifying false positives and glaucoma concerns. Most patients requiring referral had ophthalmology follow-up scheduled (56.14%, n=64), with delays from patient factors (78%), clinic error (6.5%), or outside provider care (6.5%). Glaucoma concerns appeared in positive (12.96%) and negative (23.68%) groups.
records.conclusion: AEYE Health strengthened connectivity between Emory Healthcare primary care and ophthalmology, improving eye health access and potentially reducing vision loss. Limitations included glaucoma and comorbid conditions, photography reliance, imaging staff learning curves, technical issues, and workflow integration considerations.

records.authors: JULIE OKIRO, KELLIE FORTUNE, EIMEAR DALY, CLIVE M. KILGALLEN, FABIO QUONDAMATTEO, SEAMUS SREENAN, Navan, Ireland, Dublin, Ireland, Moycullen, Ireland

records.introduction_objective: There is a need to identify additional tools to enhance risk stratification of people with Diabetic Foot Ulcers (DFU). This study aimed to evaluate the potential of material debrided from DFU to predict ulcer outcome.
records.methods: Fifty-three consecutively presenting patients with DFU were recruited and underwent conventional DFU treatment including debridement, where appropriate. Debrided material was collected, processed, and examined histologically. Patients were categorised as healed (complete re-epithelialisation in 12 weeks, n=26). Histological samples were scored by a blinded pathologist for seven histological parameters: presence of squamous cells; presence of epithelial cells; % volume of epithelium; hyperkeratosis; parakeratosis; fibrin; inflammation. Principle component analysis identified three clusters of variables which were used to generate wound healing indices: Structural Index (SI; parakeratosis, hyperkeratosis, presence of squamous and epithelial cells); Inflammatory Index (II; fibrin and inflammation); Epithelial Index (EI; % volume of epithelium).
records.results: No single histological variable could differentiate between healed and non-healed wounds. When clustered into indices, the SI differentiated between healed and non-healed DFUs (OR 10.04, 95% CI; 1.06 to 263, p = 0.044). Combining the three indices into a composite Wound Healing Prediction Score (WHPS), a significant difference between healed and non-healed wounds was found (ROC AUC 0.7, p = 0.016). An exploratory subgroup analysis of only non-infected wounds (n= 29, 15 healed, 14 non-healed) further improved the predictive performance of the WHPS (ROC AUC 0.764, p = 0.015).
records.conclusion: These preliminary results suggest that the WHPS generated by histological assessment of debrided material may help predict DFU outcome facilitating more aggressive intervention in earlier stages in those unlikely to heal.

records.introduction_objective: Generative AI (Gen AI) platforms are increasingly used for health information, yet the alignment of their outputs with culturally specific diabetes dietary guidelines remains unclear. This study evaluates the extent to which AI-generated dietary guidelines align with established guidelines from the Hong Kong Health Bureau (HK) and the ADA for the older, low-income Chinese population with T2DM.
records.methods: Six Gen AI platforms were prompted with 10 common diabetes diet-related questions tailored to this demographic group. Reference responses were generated from HK and ADA guidelines using NotebookLM to convert guideline content into structured answers, serving as the gold standard. AI-generated responses were then compared to the guideline-based reference answers using semantic similarity (SS) analysis. Scores (between 0 and 1) were averaged across three trials per question.
records.results: AI-generated responses demonstrated SS average scores ranging from 0.747 to 0.806 across platforms.
records.conclusion: Results suggest substantial overlap with established diabetes dietary guidelines. Variability across platforms underscores the need for structured evaluation frameworks to systemically assess the alignment, reliability, and cultural relevance of Gen AI health information. records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Generative AI (Gen AI) platforms are increasingly used for health information, yet the alignment of their outputs with culturally specific diabetes dietary guidelines remains unclear. This study evaluates the extent to which AI-generated dietary guidelines align with established guidelines from the Hong Kong Health Bureau (HK) and the ADA for the older, low-income Chinese population with T2DM.

Methods: Six Gen AI platforms were prompted with 10 common diabetes diet-related questions tailored to this demographic group. Reference responses were generated from HK and ADA guidelines using NotebookLM to convert guideline content into structured answers, serving as the gold standard. AI-generated responses were then compared to the guideline-based reference answers using semantic similarity (SS) analysis. Scores (between 0 and 1) were averaged across three trials per question.

Results: AI-generated responses demonstrated SS average scores ranging from 0.747 to 0.806 across platforms.

Conclusion: Results suggest substantial overlap with established diabetes dietary guidelines. Variability across platforms underscores the need for structured evaluation frameworks to systemically assess the alignment, reliability, and cultural relevance of Gen AI health information. Until such validated frameworks are established, Gen AI tools should not be relied upon as the sole source of dietary guidelines in this population.

records.introduction_objective: Mobile app-based weight management programmes using artificial intelligence (AI) coaching are increasingly used to support lifestyle change in people with type 2 diabetes (T2D), but real-world outcomes remain limited. The aim of this study was to evaluate weight loss among adults with T2D using an AI-enabled weight management app, and to examine whether AI coaching chat engagement was associated with weight loss at 12 and 26 weeks.
records.methods: This retrospective observational study included adults with T2D enrolled in a digital weight management app. Weight loss (%) was assessed at 12 and 26 weeks. AI coach engagement was defined as mean days/week of chat use and categorised as 0, 1-3, or 4-7 days/week. The multivariable linear regression model was adjusted for age, sex, baseline BMI, and other in-app activity (days/week).
records.results: At 12 weeks (n=444), users were 73.2% female, mean age 54.4 (SD 14.6) years, BMI 36.2 (SD 6.9) kg/m2. Mean weight loss was 3.63 (SD 4.16) %. At 26 weeks (n=263), mean weight loss was 4.54 (SD 6.20) %. In unadjusted analyses, users engaging with AI chat 4-7 days/week achieved greater mean weight loss than those with lower engagement at both 12 weeks (4.69% vs 3.05% and 2.23%) and 26 weeks (6.70% vs 3.99% and 3.87%) (pairwise Mann-Whitney U with Holm-Bonferroni correction; adjusted p < 0.05). In the regression model adjusted for other weight loss predictors, AI chat engagement was no longer associated with weight loss.
records.conclusion: Adults with T2D achieved meaningful weight loss at 12 and 26 weeks using an AI-enabled weight management mobile app. Higher AI chat engagement was associated with greater weight loss in unadjusted analyses but not after adjustment for overall programme activity and other factors, suggesting AI chat reflects broader user engagement.

Introduction and Objective: We evaluated whether a newly developed community health worker co-produced CGM-informed digital education intervention, My Control!, improves glycemic control to a clinically meaningful degree in Latino adults with prediabetes.

Methods: In the Trial 1 (NCT06472297) intervention development study, N=20 Latino community health workers with prediabetes risk self-monitored with a CGM for 20 days. High glucose alerts were set at 140mg/dL and low alerts were disabled. Participants received real-time feedback and submitted daily smartphone video reflections prompted by high glucose excursions. AI-assisted transcription and editing supported development of fourteen educational videos. In Trial 2 (NCT06883812), N=30 adults with lab confirmed prediabetes completed an experimental AB design with a 10-day masked CGM followed by a 10-day unmasked phase paired with daily My Control! videos sent by text. Glucose profile outcomes included mean glucose and time above range (TAR) 140mg/dL, and Wilcoxon tests were applied to study phase contrasts.

Results: In Trial 1, all participants completed CGM wear yielding 95% valid CGM data on at least 83% of study days. A total of 723 minutes of video were generated to produce 14 videos comprising My Control!. In Trial 2, masked to unmasked contrast showed decreased TAR with 52% (14 of 27) achieving greater than the 5% criterion reduction and median change of -6.4% (Q1 -11.6, Q3 1.4; p=.02). Mean glucose also decreased with median change of -3.7mg/dL (Q1 -10.6, Q3 3.6; p=.049).

Conclusion: My Control! is a community health worker-supported CGM intervention demonstrating feasible implementation and plausible clinically meaningful improvements in glycemic metrics among Latino adults with prediabetes. This biosensor-informed behavioral model positions CGM as an engaging tool to support early glycemic self-regulation in prediabetes.

records.introduction_objective: This project aimed to evaluate LLMs' recommendations for pharmacotherapy in the management of type 2 diabetes (T2D) in alignment with the 2026 American Diabetes Association’s (ADA) Standards of Care. The findings provide insights into the feasibility and reliability of integrating generative artificial intelligence with T2D and cardio-kidney-metabolic care.
records.methods: Four LLMs were used: ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Copilot 365, and Claude Opus 4.6. Each LLM generated five rounds of outputs using a published case of T2D with CKD. Three clinical pharmacists with CDCES used a 37-question binary rubric to evaluate LLM responses. Logistic regression was used to estimate high concordance (Overall Score ≥ 80%, Safety Domain ≥ 80%, and no critical errors). Percentage scores were compared across LLMs using the Kruskal-Wallis test. When statistically significant, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons were performed.
records.results: There is variability in multiple measures between LLM models, but there was initial concordance with ADA standards.
records.conclusion: Significant inter-model variability was observed in Safety, Dosing, and Overall performance. These findings signal domain-specific differences of LLMs in recommending diabetes pharmacotherapy. Further investigation is needed to critically evaluate LLM recommendations in broader T2D care and to more precisely delineate inter-model differences.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: This project aimed to evaluate LLMs' recommendations for pharmacotherapy in the management of type 2 diabetes (T2D) in alignment with the 2026 American Diabetes Association’s (ADA) Standards of Care. The findings provide insights into the feasibility and reliability of integrating generative artificial intelligence with T2D and cardio-kidney-metabolic care.

Methods: Four LLMs were used: ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Copilot 365, and Claude Opus 4.6. Each LLM generated five rounds of outputs using a published case of T2D with CKD. Three clinical pharmacists with CDCES used a 37-question binary rubric to evaluate LLM responses. Logistic regression was used to estimate high concordance (Overall Score ≥ 80%, Safety Domain ≥ 80%, and no critical errors). Percentage scores were compared across LLMs using the Kruskal-Wallis test. When statistically significant, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons were performed.

Results: There is variability in multiple measures between LLM models, but there was initial concordance with ADA standards.

Conclusion: Significant inter-model variability was observed in Safety, Dosing, and Overall performance. These findings signal domain-specific differences of LLMs in recommending diabetes pharmacotherapy. Further investigation is needed to critically evaluate LLM recommendations in broader T2D care and to more precisely delineate inter-model differences.

records.introduction_objective: FCL transcends reducing the burden of carbohydrate counting. FCL eliminates the need for meal management by the person with diabetes and restores the normal manner in which people without diabetes interact with food. That is a true freedom that people with diabetes have never known. A novel MiniMed™ FCL algorithm featuring personalized glucose prediction and automated meal detection was developed using a MiniMed™ simulator under in silico conditions. We sought to validate the predictive accuracy of this simulation environment by comparing its results against clinical outcomes from real patients (RP) using the FCL system.
records.methods: The FCL algorithm was developed using a simulator containing ~20,000 virtual patients (VPs) with diverse demographics (age, gender, BMI) and real-life scenarios derived from CareLink™ data. To manifest simulator fidelity, 24 RPs (ages 20-71) were matched to 24 VPs based on age, gender, total daily insulin (TDI), daily CHO intake, and study hardware (sensor and pump specific models). RPs underwent two 3-week phases: fully announced meals (FA) and fully unannounced meals (UA). Glycemic metrics (time in [TIR, 70-180 mg/dL] and below [TBR, <70 mg/dL]) range and mean sensor glucose (SG) were compared between virtual and clinical cohorts.
records.results: In the FA phase, VP vs. RP results showed high alignment: TIR (83.5±7.5% vs. 82.1±7.5%, p=0.5), TBR (2.3±1.2% vs. 2.0±1.2%, p=0.4), and average CGM (135±9 vs. 137±8 mg/dL, p=0.4). In the UA phase, the system remained effective: TIR (76.7±15.7% vs. 73.9±7.5%, p=0.4), TBR (1.4±0.9% vs. 1.2±0.9%, p=0.5), and average CGM (149±29 vs. 150±9 mg/dL, p=0.4).
records.conclusion: The MiniMed™ FCL algorithm demonstrated groundbreaking clinical performance without meal announcements, exceeding a TIR of >70% as recommended by the ADA, successfully reducing user burden without increasing hypoglycemia risk. The high correlation between virtual and clinical results confirms the simulator's utility in predicting outcomes across diverse populations and therapy settings.

records.methods: Utilizing a machine learning tool that detects meals based on sensor glucose, we analysed 389,796 meals from 18,513 users (EMEA region, JAN2023-FEB2026). First, 4-hour postprandial glycaemic control was assessed for meals by time of day based on user age (<16y/16-28y/29-42y/43-55y/>55y), bolusing type (BT: on-time bolus within 15 minutes, OTB/ late bolus of 15-90 minute delay, LB ) and carbohydrate input (CI: ≤26g/26-45g/>45g). records.results: OTB meals showed a 5-6% higher TIR(pp) than LB meals. In age groups, highest TIR(pp) was observed for OTB meals in users >55yr (62.15%). In CI groups, OTB meals of ≤26g carbohydrates showed highest TIR(pp) (60.05%, Table). In the second analysis, a 30-minute bolus delay for LB meals reduced TIR(pp) by ~4% in all age groups. Bolusing 30 minutes earlier for OTB meals had minimal impact. For both LB and OTB meals, higher CI was associated with lower TIR(pp).

records.authors: MOHAMMED E. AL-SOFIANI, SAHAR K. ALHARTHI, MOHAMMED ABUSAMAAN, SULTAN A. MEO, DAVID KLONOFF, Baltimore, MD, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, San Francisco, CA

records.summary: This innovative CGM-based prediction model identifies PWD at risk of fasting glycemic complications and provides a simple, scalable, and practical tool for real-world risk stratification and personalized counseling.
records.introduction_objective: Over 116 million Muslims with diabetes fast during Ramadan each year, placing them at risk of dysglycemia and acute complications. Current pre-Ramadan risk assessment relies largely on complex expert consensus-based tools without quantitative predictive tools. We aimed to develop and internally validate the first CGM-based model to predict fasting glycemic complications
records.methods: We analyzed data from 550 individuals with diabetes who fasted during Ramadan and used CGM during Ramadan and the preceding month. Candidate predictors included demographic and clinical variables and pre-Ramadan CGM metrics: time in range (TIR), time below range (TBR), glycemia risk index (GRI), and coefficient of variation (CV). The primary outcome was fasting glycemic complications during Ramadan: defined as DKA, an ED visit, fasting interruption on >2 days due to dysglycemia, or Ramadan TIR <70%. A multivariable logistic regression model was developed. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and internal validation used 10-fold cross-validation
records.results: The median age was 27 years [IQR 19-42]; 60.0% were female; 77.1% had type 1 diabetes. Overall, 410 (74.5%) experienced fasting glycemic complications. Lower pre-Ramadan TIR, higher GRI, diabetes treatment modality, and longer diabetes duration were strong predictors of fasting glycemic complications. A prediction model based solely on pre-Ramadan CGM metrics demonstrated excellent discrimination (AUC of 0.91, 95% CI 0.89-0.94) and maintained performance after internal validation (cross-validated AUC of 0.89; 95% CI 0.87-0.92), comparable to models incorporating an extensive list of demographic and clinical variables
records.conclusion: This innovative CGM-based prediction model identifies PWD at risk of fasting glycemic complications and provides a simple, scalable, and practical tool for real-world risk stratification and personalized counseling.

records.authors: STEPHANI DRIVER, REBECCA SKOTEK, LIA SKALKOS, LARA SMITH, JULIA J. AXELBAUM, TROY RUSSELL, FLORENCIA HALPERIN, TEJASWI D. KOMPALA, Boston, MA, Sharon, MA

records.introduction_objective: Multidisciplinary obesity and diabetes care requires coordination across providers and multiple data sources, often involving extensive time on documentation and chart review. We evaluated whether implementation of a real-time, AI-generated structured patient summary could improve clinician efficiency and satisfaction.
records.methods: In a large nationwide virtual obesity clinic, we conducted a pre-post evaluation of a newly launched clinician facing summary feature. Using an iterative development process with clinical stakeholder input, we deployed a large language model-based system that synthesized structured electronic health record data and unstructured visit notes into a standardized, workflow-integrated summary. RDs underwent a time-stamp assessment of minutes per patient spent on previsit chart preparation, pre and post implementation. The primary outcome was clinician efficiency, as measured by previsit chart preparation time spent. Secondary outcomes included provider satisfaction.
records.results: The AI generated structured patient summary displays relevant information from recent provider interactions, including outstanding action items, recent labs, medication changes, dietary recall and nutritional goals. Primary outcome: Preimplementation of the new summary tool, RDs spent an average of 125.5 mins/week on previsit charting. In post-intervention assessment, this was significantly reduced to 78.7 mins/week per clinician (p <0.05). Of surveyed RDs, 84% reported the intervention decreased perceived time spent on previsit charting. Qualitative outcomes: Clinicians reported ‘satisfied’ (32%) or ‘very satisfied’ (61%) with the new tool. Constructive feedback was used for iterative retraining of the AI model.
records.conclusion: Implementation of a real-time, AI generated patient summary was associated with documentation efficiency gains and had high acceptability by clinicians in a large virtual obesity practice.

records.introduction_objective: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) limits quality of life and survival and its accelerated course in type 1 diabetes (T1D) may challenge standard risk prediction models. We assessed the 10-yr CVD risk performance of the Framingham Risk Score (FRS), ASCVD Risk Estimator Plus (ASCVD), AHA PREVENT, and Steno Type 1 Risk Engine (ST1RE) prediction models over 30 yrs in a T1D population, and evaluated the role of coronary artery calcification (CAC) and HbA1c as risk enhancers.
records.methods: Analysis included 1311 participants followed for 30 yrs during the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) study. Model-predicted CVD risk calculated at EDIC Years 1, 10, and 20 was compared to observed CVD incidence during subsequent intervals (Years 1-10, 10-20, and 20-30); calibration and c-statistics were assessed for each period.
records.results: At EDIC Year 20, the 10-yr observed CVD risk in this population was 1.43 (95% CI 1.36-1.49) times higher than predicted by FRS, >2-fold higher than predicted by ASCVD and PREVENT (RR 2.69, 95% CI 2.55-2.86 and 2.40, 95% CI 2.30-2.51, respectively), and lower than predicted by ST1RE (RR 0.61-0.87 at all timepoints). ASCVD and PREVENT underpredicted risk in both sexes. All models except ST1RE underpredicted risk in females. Discrimination was modest (c-statistic 0.54-0.64) across models, with the strongest performance by PREVENT. Among individuals classified as low or moderate predicted risk, those with CAC ≥100 Agatston units had an observed risk comparable to the high-risk category; those with CAC=0 had an observed risk comparable to the low-risk category. Risk reclassification based on CAC score modestly improved discrimination (maximal c-statistic increased to 0.68). HbA1c similarly enhanced risk of CVD.
records.conclusion: In T1D, traditional CVD risk prediction models have limited performance. Risk enhancers improved risk classification. More accurate, tailored risk estimation is needed to identify early risk mitigation interventions in T1D.

records.introduction_objective: Adiposity reflects heterogeneous biological processes that are not fully captured by body mass index (BMI). Proteomic profiling may better distinguish metabolic health. We aimed to derive a proteomics-based BMI (ProtBMI) using machine learning and assess its relevance for type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk in UK and Chinese adults.
records.methods: ProtBMI was developed in UK Biobank (n=45,226) using 2,923 Olink proteins and a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model. Boruta feature selection and recursive feature elimination identified a 30-protein signature predicting BMI (R²=0.78), which was externally validated in China Kadoorie Biobank (n=3,997; R² = 0.57). Association of ProtBMI and BMI with metabolic traits were assessed using linear regression, and with incident T2D using Cox regression adjusted for confounders. Risk prediction models were evaluated using the C-statistic, and net reclassification index (NRI).
records.results: Among UKB participants, ProtBMI (mean 27.4 [SD 4.2] kg/m²) showed stronger associations than BMI (mean 27.4 [4.8] kg/m²) with glycaemic, lipid, and inflammatory biomarkers. ProtBMI was more strongly associated with incident T2D (1,054 events) than BMI (HR per SD: 2.07 [95% CI 1.95-2.18] vs. 1.83 [1.73-1.93]). T2D risk increased across ProtBMI categories within BMI strata, with up to a ~9-fold difference among individuals with BMI 25-30 kg/m² and ~2-fold differences among those with BMI ≥30 kg/m². Within the normal BMI range (22.5-24.9 kg/m²), ProtBMI ≥25 was associated with 2.5-fold higher T2D risk compared with ProtBMI <25. Adding ProtBMI to a conventional risk prediction model improved the C-index from 0.821 (0.808-0.834) to 0.833 (0.820-0.845) and NRI by 34.8%. Findings were directionally consistent in CKB (mean BMI 23.9 [SD 3.6] kg/m²).
records.conclusion: ProtBMI captures metabolic variation beyond BMI, identifies individuals at higher T2D risk within BMI strata, including within the “normal” range, and modestly improves T2D risk prediction across diverse populations.

records.authors: MARIA P. SANTOS, ARON CULOTTA, KATHERINE THEALL, SYLVIA H. LEY, Boston, MA, New Orleans, LA

records.introduction_objective: Acute hyperglycemia is common and linked to higher mortality. Community healthy food access may shape this risk and how discharge risk-prediction tools classify patients. The objective of this study was to evaluate the fairness of a machine learning (ML) model for predicting long-term mortality among hospitalized patients with acute hyperglycemia, across strata of community-level food access.
records.methods: A retrospective cohort of 4,627,091 U.S. hospital patients without baseline diabetes from the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative was used to evaluate whether a Gradient Boosting Machine was fair by community-level food access in predicting all-cause mortality >30 days after discharge (median follow-up: 3.3 years). Acute hyperglycemia was defined as two or more glucose readings ≥180 mg/dL during hospitalization. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality >30 days post-discharge. Community-level food access was categorized using the modified Retail Food Environment Index: (1) No Healthy Access (0-5), (2) Limited Healthy Access (5.1-10), (3) Enhanced Healthy Access (10.1-37.5), and (4) Balanced Healthy Access (37.6-100). Discrimination (AUC), calibration, and group fairness metrics were compared across food access groups.
records.results: The ML model’s sensitivity and specificity were similar across food access strata, with true positive rates ranging of 68%-72% and false positive rates of 7.5%-10.4%, suggesting modest accuracy loss in disadvantaged communities. Patients from “No Healthy Access” areas were more often flagged as high risk (19.1%, 95% CI: 18.5%-19.6%) than those from “Enhanced Healthy Access” areas (15.0%, 95% CI: 14.4%-15.6%). The resulting disparate impact ratio was 0.78 (95% CI: 0.76-0.80), falling below the 0.80 threshold and signaling a significant disparity.
records.conclusion: Sensitivity and specificity were comparable across strata, but high-risk flagging was higher in the stratum with lowest healthy food access.

records.introduction_objective: Area indices used to assess SDOH’s impact on diabetes outcomes collapse many SDOH dimensions and flatten address-level variation, complicating study of SDOH pathways. We use machine learning on discrete address-level SDOH measures to identify pathways for diabetes prevalence.
records.methods:
We used GPS-Health, a complete geolocated Maryland land parcel dataset (n=2369365) with 1317 features from calculating routing, distance, and count density of geocoded discrete SDOH resources (e.g. schools) and hazards (e.g. pollution sites), plus ancillary data (e.g. school quality).
We trained a gradient boosted model (LightGBM) using all features (training sample n=1653482 parcels, testing sample n= 413371) on tract-level diabetes prevalence in CDC PLACES. We ranked top 30 features by importance. We also compared the model’s adjusted R2 and RMSE against OLS of area deprivation index (ADI) on diabetes prevalence.
records.results:
The model had a training-sample adjusted R2 of 0.949, MAE 0.480, Spearman 0.967, and RMSE 0.667; and testing-sample adjusted R2 of 0.948, MAE 0.482, Spearman 0.967, and RMSE 0.671. Of the top 30 features by importance, 8 were related to local economic value, 8 proximity to hospitals, 6 local school performance, and 4 proximity to gun violence. The remaining 4 included proximity to food pantries, gyms, pollution sites, and FQHCs.
OLS on diabetes prevalence using ADI had an adjusted R2 of 0.381 and RMSE of 2.51.
records.conclusion:
Address-level discrete SDOH explain much of the variation in census tract diabetes prevalence in Maryland. The model’s adjusted R2 and RMSE suggested a better fit than ADI for diabetes prevalence.
Our study is limited by cross-sectional analysis: future work could leverage differences in open dates for SDOH sites.
Top features suggest local economic resources, geographic accessibility to healthcare, accessibility to educational quality, and exposure to violence are important potential predictors of diabetes prevalence.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Area indices used to assess SDOH’s impact on diabetes outcomes collapse many SDOH dimensions and flatten address-level variation, complicating study of SDOH pathways. We use machine learning on discrete address-level SDOH measures to identify pathways for diabetes prevalence.

Methods: We used GPS-Health, a complete geolocated Maryland land parcel dataset (n=2369365) with 1317 features from calculating routing, distance, and count density of geocoded discrete SDOH resources (e.g. schools) and hazards (e.g. pollution sites), plus ancillary data (e.g. school quality).
We trained a gradient boosted model (LightGBM) using all features (training sample n=1653482 parcels, testing sample n= 413371) on tract-level diabetes prevalence in CDC PLACES. We ranked top 30 features by importance. We also compared the model’s adjusted R2 and RMSE against OLS of area deprivation index (ADI) on diabetes prevalence.

Results: The model had a training-sample adjusted R2 of 0.949, MAE 0.480, Spearman 0.967, and RMSE 0.667; and testing-sample adjusted R2 of 0.948, MAE 0.482, Spearman 0.967, and RMSE 0.671. Of the top 30 features by importance, 8 were related to local economic value, 8 proximity to hospitals, 6 local school performance, and 4 proximity to gun violence. The remaining 4 included proximity to food pantries, gyms, pollution sites, and FQHCs.
OLS on diabetes prevalence using ADI had an adjusted R2 of 0.381 and RMSE of 2.51.

Conclusion: Address-level discrete SDOH explain much of the variation in census tract diabetes prevalence in Maryland. The model’s adjusted R2 and RMSE suggested a better fit than ADI for diabetes prevalence.
Our study is limited by cross-sectional analysis: future work could leverage differences in open dates for SDOH sites.
Top features suggest local economic resources, geographic accessibility to healthcare, accessibility to educational quality, and exposure to violence are important potential predictors of diabetes prevalence.

records.introduction_objective: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is characterized by immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic β cells, progressing from autoantibody (AAB) positivity to insulin deficiency and islet failure. We integrated genotype, chromatin accessibility, transcriptomic, proteomic, and spatial profiling of human pancreatic tissue using three AI foundation models to define how regulatory variation, cell-state transitions, and microenvironmental context change across progression.
records.methods: Our models were initially trained on large-scale publicly available datasets, then applied to pancreatic datasets from the Human Pancreas Analysis Program (HPAP) and validated using longitudinal samples from the TEDDY cohort, enabling cross-cohort evaluation of disease-associated regulatory, cellular, and spatial changes.
records.results: First, we developed a genomic foundation model integrating whole-genome sequencing and ATAC-seq to predict gene expression by linking risk variants to cell type-specific regulatory elements and target genes. Many variants localized to β-cell-active enhancers and were connected to genes governing β-cell identity and stress responses, suggesting inherited variation reshapes regulatory networks in these cells. Second, a single-cell foundation model integrating scATAC-seq, scRNA-seq, and CITE-seq resolved endocrine cell states across T1D progression. Beyond canonical α and β cells, we identified β-cell subpopulations marked by stress activation, reduced maturity signatures, and metabolic reprogramming. Third, a spatial foundation model characterized islet architecture and cellular neighborhoods. We observed progressive disruption of islet organization, with immune cells enriched near stress-associated β-cell states and local inflammatory signaling, alongside diminished α-β spatial coupling, as discovered via the Pancreatlas Platform.
records.conclusion: Together, these findings integrate genetic risk, regulatory remodeling, cellular plasticity, and spatial reorganization to provide a unified view of T1D progression.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is characterized by immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic β cells, progressing from autoantibody (AAB) positivity to insulin deficiency and islet failure. We integrated genotype, chromatin accessibility, transcriptomic, proteomic, and spatial profiling of human pancreatic tissue using three AI foundation models to define how regulatory variation, cell-state transitions, and microenvironmental context change across progression.

Methods: Our models were initially trained on large-scale publicly available datasets, then applied to pancreatic datasets from the Human Pancreas Analysis Program (HPAP) and validated using longitudinal samples from the TEDDY cohort, enabling cross-cohort evaluation of disease-associated regulatory, cellular, and spatial changes.

Results: First, we developed a genomic foundation model integrating whole-genome sequencing and ATAC-seq to predict gene expression by linking risk variants to cell type-specific regulatory elements and target genes. Many variants localized to β-cell-active enhancers and were connected to genes governing β-cell identity and stress responses, suggesting inherited variation reshapes regulatory networks in these cells. Second, a single-cell foundation model integrating scATAC-seq, scRNA-seq, and CITE-seq resolved endocrine cell states across T1D progression. Beyond canonical α and β cells, we identified β-cell subpopulations marked by stress activation, reduced maturity signatures, and metabolic reprogramming. Third, a spatial foundation model characterized islet architecture and cellular neighborhoods. We observed progressive disruption of islet organization, with immune cells enriched near stress-associated β-cell states and local inflammatory signaling, alongside diminished α-β spatial coupling, as discovered via the Pancreatlas Platform.

Conclusion: Together, these findings integrate genetic risk, regulatory remodeling, cellular plasticity, and spatial reorganization to provide a unified view of T1D progression.

records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Improved definition of endotypes for type 1 diabetes (T1D) can facilitate the development of targeted therapies and improve clinical management of disease. We recently discovered four distinct sub-groups of T1D derived from a machine learning-based genetic risk score, which had significant differences in clinical parameters such as T1D age of onset and rate of T1D complications. Here we further expanded on the characterization and evaluation of these sub-groups as potential endotypes of T1D.

Methods: We mapped 29,746 T1D and non-diabetic individuals of European Ancestry to four genetic sub-groups using our machine learning method, and performed association testing, allele frequency enrichment, gene and pathway enrichment and risk scoring for related autoimmune diseases for each sub-group.

Results: Genetic sub-clusters demonstrated biologically and clinically significant differences in genetic features and autoimmune predisposition (Figure 1), which supports that they represent endotypes of T1D.

Conclusion: Sub-grouping of individuals based on genetic risk profiles revealed endotypes of T1D with distinct clinical and mechanistic properties. Analyses in patient cohorts will further validate the clinical and therapeutic value of these endotypes.

records.introduction_objective: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and mechanistic analyses of insulin resistance (IR) have largely focused on the fasting state, leaving fed-state mechanisms poorly understood. The C2CD4A/B locus harbors a type 2 diabetes (T2D) GWAS signal that colocalizes with an insulin fold change (IFC) signal, an index of fed-state IR. We previously identified a chromatin accessibility QTL (caQTL) at this locus in skeletal muscle, where the T2D risk allele is associated with reduced accessibility at a putative enhancer; the caQTL colocalizes with the T2D and IFC signals. Here, we functionally characterize this variant to elucidate the mechanism underlying the GWAS association.
records.methods: Luciferase assays were performed in LHCN-M2 human myotubes using constructs centered on the risk or non-risk allele; data were analyzed using a mixed-effects model. Candidate regulatory factors at the caQTL were identified by FIMO motif scan, and an interaction QTL analysis was performed in type 1 fibers. We applied an enhancer-gene linking deep learning model and nominated VPS13C as the effector gene. siRNA-mediated VPS13C knockdown in LHCN-M2 myotubes was assessed by insulin-stimulated glucose uptake (ISGU) assays.
records.results: Concordant with the caQTL, constructs carrying the risk allele showed reduced reporter activity relative to the non-risk allele (p = 0.004). The interaction QTL revealed that the effect of genotype on chromatin accessibility is modulated by MEF2D expression (βgi = −0.181, p = 0.003), suggesting that the risk allele disrupts MEF2D-dependent enhancer activation in a dose-dependent manner. ISGU assays showed decreased glucose uptake of VPS13C knockdown relative to controls.
records.conclusion: We provide functional evidence that the C2CD4A/B T2D risk variant reduces enhancer activity through a MEF2D-dependent mechanism in skeletal muscle, and that VPS13C plays a role in ISGU. Collectively, this work advances our understanding of the context-specific mechanisms linking the C2CD4A/B locus to T2D and fed-state IR.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and mechanistic analyses of insulin resistance (IR) have largely focused on the fasting state, leaving fed-state mechanisms poorly understood. The C2CD4A/B locus harbors a type 2 diabetes (T2D) GWAS signal that colocalizes with an insulin fold change (IFC) signal, an index of fed-state IR. We previously identified a chromatin accessibility QTL (caQTL) at this locus in skeletal muscle, where the T2D risk allele is associated with reduced accessibility at a putative enhancer; the caQTL colocalizes with the T2D and IFC signals. Here, we functionally characterize this variant to elucidate the mechanism underlying the GWAS association.

Methods: Luciferase assays were performed in LHCN-M2 human myotubes using constructs centered on the risk or non-risk allele; data were analyzed using a mixed-effects model. Candidate regulatory factors at the caQTL were identified by FIMO motif scan, and an interaction QTL analysis was performed in type 1 fibers. We applied an enhancer-gene linking deep learning model and nominated VPS13C as the effector gene. siRNA-mediated VPS13C knockdown in LHCN-M2 myotubes was assessed by insulin-stimulated glucose uptake (ISGU) assays.

Results: Concordant with the caQTL, constructs carrying the risk allele showed reduced reporter activity relative to the non-risk allele (p = 0.004). The interaction QTL revealed that the effect of genotype on chromatin accessibility is modulated by MEF2D expression (βgi = −0.181, p = 0.003), suggesting that the risk allele disrupts MEF2D-dependent enhancer activation in a dose-dependent manner. ISGU assays showed decreased glucose uptake of VPS13C knockdown relative to controls.

Conclusion: We provide functional evidence that the C2CD4A/B T2D risk variant reduces enhancer activity through a MEF2D-dependent mechanism in skeletal muscle, and that VPS13C plays a role in ISGU. Collectively, this work advances our understanding of the context-specific mechanisms linking the C2CD4A/B locus to T2D and fed-state IR.

records.introduction_objective: The dysfunction of beta cells in pancreatic islets is a driving force of Type 2 diabetes (T2D) pathogenesis. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have revealed that numerous T2D-associated SNPs (genetic variants) located in non-coding regions, suggesting a crucial role for distal cis-elements in regulating gene expression. However, a major challenge remains in defining the specific tissues and cell types through which these diabetes-associated variants exert their effects.
records.methods: In this study, we performed epigenomic profiling of the enhancer mark H3K4me1 in human islet cells isolated from healthy and T2D subjects using Paired-Tag, a multiomic approach which profiles the chromatin modification and RNA from same single cells.
records.results: We defined cell type-specific histone modification landscapes in human pancreatic islets, revealing distinct active enhancer states and transcription factor motifs across islet cell types. We integrated genome-wide association study (GWAS) data with Paired-Tag epigenomic profiles to identify type 2 diabetes-associated SNPs residing in enhancers and assess their functional relevance. To further identify the putative function variants, we applied machine learning to predict and interpret functional noncoding variants associated with type 2 diabetes, revealing islet cell type-specific effects on chromatin accessibility. We identified a small cohort of T2D-associated H3K4me1+ enhancer SNPs which potentially determine transcription factor binding and regulate gene expression. Taken together, this work evaluates the putative mechanism of T2D-associated SNPs in modulating activity of pancreatic enhancers at single cell level.
records.conclusion: Our results highlighted the functional importance of T2D variants in regulating enhancer activity measured by H3K4me1, which may yield novel insights into the pathogenesis of T2D.
records.abstract_text:
Introduction and Objective: The dysfunction of beta cells in pancreatic islets is a driving force of Type 2 diabetes (T2D) pathogenesis. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have revealed that numerous T2D-associated SNPs (genetic variants) located in non-coding regions, suggesting a crucial role for distal cis-elements in regulating gene expression. However, a major challenge remains in defining the specific tissues and cell types through which these diabetes-associated variants exert their effects.

Methods: In this study, we performed epigenomic profiling of the enhancer mark H3K4me1 in human islet cells isolated from healthy and T2D subjects using Paired-Tag, a multiomic approach which profiles the chromatin modification and RNA from same single cells.

Results: We defined cell type-specific histone modification landscapes in human pancreatic islets, revealing distinct active enhancer states and transcription factor motifs across islet cell types. We integrated genome-wide association study (GWAS) data with Paired-Tag epigenomic profiles to identify type 2 diabetes-associated SNPs residing in enhancers and assess their functional relevance. To further identify the putative function variants, we applied machine learning to predict and interpret functional noncoding variants associated with type 2 diabetes, revealing islet cell type-specific effects on chromatin accessibility. We identified a small cohort of T2D-associated H3K4me1+ enhancer SNPs which potentially determine transcription factor binding and regulate gene expression. Taken together, this work evaluates the putative mechanism of T2D-associated SNPs in modulating activity of pancreatic enhancers at single cell level.

Conclusion: Our results highlighted the functional importance of T2D variants in regulating enhancer activity measured by H3K4me1, which may yield novel insights into the pathogenesis of T2D.

records.introduction_objective: The genetic architecture of complex traits has largely been studied using additive GWAS models that assume a linear allele effect. However, this can miss recessive signals, where increased risk is observed only among individuals homozygous for the minor allele. We aimed to identify novel loci associated with T2D under a recessive model using largest and most diverse GWAS meta-analysis.
records.methods: We meta-analyzed 13 T2D recessive GWAS including 300k cases and 1.2M controls (35.8% non-European ancestry). Variants were considered recessive if they showed a two-fold larger effect size or greater statistical significance under recessive model compared to additive.
records.results: We identified 129 independent associations with stronger statistical evidence under the recessive model, compared to additive, including 28 novel signals. Among them, a novel variant rs3862269 showed effect only in homozygous individuals (OR = 1.07, P = 6 × 10-9) and is the lead eQTL for ELAVL4 in pancreatic islets, a gene implicated in beta cell function. We also identified ancestry-specific recessive signals, such as rs12712928 near SIX3, enriched in East Asians, which showed a significant recessive effect (OR = 1.08, P = 2 × 10-13) with no effect in heterozygous (OR = 1.01, P = 0.8), which may explain the ancestry heterogeneity in allelic effects due to much lower frequency of homozygous outside East Asians. We show that approximately 3% of known loci demonstrated recessive effects. For example, at HNF1A locus, the strongest signal was a common missense variant (rs1169288) with stronger recessive association (OR = 1.11, P = 1 × 10-52; additive OR = 1.05, P = 3 × 10-41) and only effect in homozygous carriers (OR = 1.15, P = 1 × 10-15), but not in heterozygous.
records.conclusion: This study highlights the importance of recessive effects in T2D, identifying novel and ancestry specific associations missed by additive models, which may impact risk prediction models and explain ancestry related heterogeneity.

Among them, a novel variant rs3862269 showed effect only in homozygous individuals (OR = 1.07, P = 6 × 10-9) and is the lead eQTL for ELAVL4 in pancreatic islets, a gene implicated in beta cell function. records.summary: These results demonstrate that systematic harmonization of pancreatic and immune datasets is feasible and produces a traceable multimodal resource, enabling cross-system investigation of pancreatic-immune interactions in T1D and providing an AI-ready foundation for future scalable discovery in diabetes research.
records.introduction_objective: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) research requires linking pancreatic molecular phenotypes with immune and longitudinal data, yet these datasets remain siloed across repositories, limiting systematic and AI-driven analysis. We evaluated whether curating and harmonizing multimodal T1D datasets from major public resources into a unified, interoperable framework could enable cross-cohort data linkage and support scalable AI model development.
records.methods: Datasets were curated from the Human Pancreas Analysis Program (HPAP v4.0.0), ImmPort, and the TEDDY NCC1 cohort. Inclusion required donor-level data availability and interoperability with standardized molecular or longitudinal formats. Data were harmonized into interoperable structures and integrated at the donor level. A knowledge graph framework recorded data provenance and lineage, enabling traceable cross-cohort linkage and standardized integration. Integration completeness and cross-modal linkage coverage were assessed as primary outcomes.
records.results: The integrated resource includes 193 donors and 17 molecular modalities, encompassing more than 4,000 experiments from HPAP v4.0.0. Six ImmPort immunology studies related to T1D immune responses were harmonized. The TEDDY NCC1 cohort contributed 27 data assets with over 39,000 entries and longitudinal data from more than 800 children at risk for T1D. Cross-cohort linkage across pancreatic, immune, and longitudinal data layers enables donor-level analysis connecting pancreatic molecular states with immune and longitudinal datasets across stages of T1D progression. Knowledge graph integration confirmed complete provenance traceability across datasets.
records.conclusion: These results demonstrate that systematic harmonization of pancreatic and immune datasets is feasible and produces a traceable multimodal resource, enabling cross-system investigation of pancreatic-immune interactions in T1D and providing an AI-ready foundation for future scalable discovery in diabetes research.

Conclusion: These results demonstrate that systematic harmonization of pancreatic and immune datasets is feasible and produces a traceable multimodal resource, enabling cross-system investigation of pancreatic-immune interactions in T1D and providing an AI-ready foundation for future scalable discovery in diabetes research.

Introduction and Objective: Recent evidence suggests that extra-pancreatic tissues, including the stomach, may also express insulin. The aim of this study was to investigate whether the human stomach expresses insulin and key β-cell-associated transcriptional markers, and to characterize the cellular and spatial context of such expression.

Methods: Gastric biopsies were obtained from 15 human subjects undergoing gastric sleeve or gastric bypass surgery. Insulin (INS) and PDX1 mRNA analysis were performed and samples were processed for histological analysis using immunohistochemistry. Spatial transcriptomic data set from the human stomach were obtained from public available data. Data were processed and normalized scaled with SCTransform() function. Cell types were assigned based on the paired stomach scRNA-seq dataset with provided cell type annotation using Seurat prediction model.

Results: Here, we report identification of insulin-positive cells in stomach biopsies obtained from 15 patients undergoing bariatric surgery. Detection of insulin expression varied regionally between corpus (80% of patients), antrum (73%) and the fundus (46%). To assess whether gastric cells transcribe INS, we analyzed spatial transcriptomics data using the NanoStrings Platform and identified INS mRNA positive cells. Similarly, cells positive for the transcription factor PDX1, which controls the expression of INS, were identified in stomach biopsies. Across patient cohorts, gastric INS mRNA levels correlated significantly with the inflammatory marker hsCRP (C-reactive protein).

Conclusion: These findings reveal region-specific insulin and PDX1 expression and active INS transcription in the human stomach. These findings raise the possibility that gastric insulin contributes to metabolic regulation, especially in metabolically unhealthy states. The presence of insulin-producing cells suggests a potential endocrine reservoir that could be leveraged for innovative regenerative or reprogramming approaches for treating diabetes.

Introduction and Objective: A goal of UGMF is to identify unexpected flux alterations in disease or genetic variation. Current UGMF methods introduce tracers at a specific metabolic location. This biases global results and introduces complications. The exception is 2H2O, which distributes universally and enters covalent C-H bonds through well described reactions, revealing metabolic history.

Methods: We present a UGMF technique with 2H2O and combinatorial analysis and apply this to CD, a monogenic disorder of aspartate:glutamate mitochondrial transporter. CD and WT mice were injected with 2H2O for 24 hr. Liver extracts were analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Inaccuracy of isotope ratios was corrected by machine learning. Pathway contributions were inferred from number of C-H bonds exchanging with 2H2O.

Results: Significant differences were found for many metabolites, including lower gluconeogenic input in CD. An unexpected result was highly significant (p < 10-5) differences in source of urea cycle (UC) intermediates ornithine (Orn) and citrulline (Ctln): 40 - 50% from de novo synthesis in CD versus 15% in WT (Fig)

Conclusion: 2H2O UGMF revealed a novel change in metabolic source of UC intermediates in CD. Greater input from de novo synthesis may represent compensatory increase in extrahepatic Orn/Ctln synthesis or slowing of Arginase flux, and may be a biomarker of ammonia toxicity

records.introduction_objective: Skeletal muscle loss and weakness are clinically important complications of type 2 diabetes (T2D) that worsen insulin resistance and functional decline. Current therapies improve glycemia but do not directly address muscle health. JUV-161 is a novel biologic identified using a machine learning multi-omics platform with predicted insulin-sensitizing and muscle protective activity.
records.methods: Male db/db mice (9 weeks; n=12-15/group) received vehicle (HSA), JUV-161 (48mg/kg), semaglutide (6 nmol/kg), or combination once daily SC for 21 days. Fasting glucose and body composition (EchoMRI) were measured. ITT, glucose challenge, grip strength, and in vivo gastrocnemius (GC) force testing (AURORA) were performed. TA/GC weights, serum chemistry, and HbA1c were assessed at takedown.
records.results: JUV-161 improved glycemic control as monotherapy, with greater benefit in combination therapy. HbA1c decreased from 8.3% (vehicle) to 7.2% (JUV-161), 7.4% (semaglutide), and 6.3% (combination). ITT showed improved glucose disposal with JUV-161, strongest in combination. JUV-161 reduced serum glucose, creatinine, and creatine kinase; triglycerides and VLDL decreased only with combination therapy. JUV-161 improved forelimb and all-limb grip strength and enhanced GC twitch force and force-frequency response. TA and GC muscle weights increased with preservation of lean mass.
records.conclusion: JUV-161 improves glycemic control while increasing skeletal muscle mass and restoring muscle strength and contractile performance in db/db mice, with additive benefit in combination therapy. By addressing both hyperglycemia and diabetes-associated functional muscle decline, JUV-161 has strong translational potential as a differentiated therapy to reduce frailty risk and improve mobility-related outcomes in patients with T2D.
