Introduction and Objective: Skeletal muscle loss and weakness are clinically important complications of type 2 diabetes (T2D) that worsen insulin resistance and functional decline. Current therapies improve glycemia but do not directly address muscle health. JUV-161 is a novel biologic identified using a machine learning multi-omics platform with predicted insulin-sensitizing and muscle protective activity.

Methods: Male db/db mice (9 weeks; n=12-15/group) received vehicle (HSA), JUV-161 (48mg/kg), semaglutide (6 nmol/kg), or combination once daily SC for 21 days. Fasting glucose and body composition (EchoMRI) were measured. ITT, glucose challenge, grip strength, and in vivo gastrocnemius (GC) force testing (AURORA) were performed. TA/GC weights, serum chemistry, and HbA1c were assessed at takedown.

Results: JUV-161 improved glycemic control as monotherapy, with greater benefit in combination therapy. HbA1c decreased from 8.3% (vehicle) to 7.2% (JUV-161), 7.4% (semaglutide), and 6.3% (combination). ITT showed improved glucose disposal with JUV-161, strongest in combination. JUV-161 reduced serum glucose, creatinine, and creatine kinase; triglycerides and VLDL decreased only with combination therapy. JUV-161 improved forelimb and all-limb grip strength and enhanced GC twitch force and force-frequency response. TA and GC muscle weights increased with preservation of lean mass.

Conclusion: JUV-161 improves glycemic control while increasing skeletal muscle mass and restoring muscle strength and contractile performance in db/db mice, with additive benefit in combination therapy. By addressing both hyperglycemia and diabetes-associated functional muscle decline, JUV-161 has strong translational potential as a differentiated therapy to reduce frailty risk and improve mobility-related outcomes in patients with T2D.

records.introduction_objective: GDF8 and activin A signal through the activin typeII receptor ActRIIA and ActRIIB to limit muscle growth. However, the specific role of each ActRII at regulating muscle mass remains to be elucidated. Here we pharmacologically interrogate the function of ActRIIA and ActRIIB using human myoblast differentiation model which is highly predictive of muscle growth in humans.
records.methods: Binding affinity of antibodies was determined via Biacore 8K and biochemical activity was measured using HTRF. Human primary skeletal muscle cells were cultured on Matrigel in growth medium (ATCC, PCS-500-030). Then myogenic differentiation was initiated by changing to the differentiation medium (ATCC, PCS-950-050). Myoblasts differentiated for 4-6 days with GDF8 or activin A alone or in the presence of anti-ActRIIA, anti-ActRIIB and dual anti-ActRIIA/IIB Bimagrumab antibodies. Following differentiation, cells were stained for MyHC and with Hoechst. Images were acquired using Opera Phenix Plus high-content system and analyzed with AI.
records.results: The anti-ActRIIA antibody LA01 specifically inhibited ActRIIA with a KD of 67 pM and an IC50 of 0.2 nM. The anti-ActRIIB antibody 17G05 specifically inhibited ActRIIB with a KD of 509 pM and an IC50 of 0.26 nM. Each antibody had no detectable binding to the other activin type II receptor. GDF8 or activin A treatment induced markedly atrophy of human myotube cultures. This atrophy was completely prevented by LA01, which resulted in a significant increase in myotube number, width and differentiation index. The recovery magnitude by the anti-ActRIIA antibody was comparable to that treated with bimagrumab. In contrast, 17G05 failed to relieve GDF8-induced inhibition of differentiation and showed only a moderate effect on the inhibition induced by activin A.
records.conclusion: These results indicate that ActRIIA plays a more prominent role than ActRIIB in the differentiation of human myoblasts. This provides a strong rationale for more presicse targeting ActRII receptors to preserve muscle in obesity treatment.

Methods: Binding affinity of antibodies was determined via Biacore 8K and biochemical activity was measured using HTRF. Human primary skeletal muscle cells were cultured on Matrigel in growth medium (ATCC, PCS-500-030). Then myogenic differentiation was initiated by changing to the differentiation medium (ATCC, PCS-950-050). Myoblasts differentiated for 4-6 days with GDF8 or activin A alone or in the presence of anti-ActRIIA, anti-ActRIIB and dual anti-ActRIIA/IIB Bimagrumab antibodies. Following differentiation, cells were stained for MyHC and with Hoechst. Images were acquired using Opera Phenix Plus high-content system and analyzed with AI.

Results: The anti-ActRIIA antibody LA01 specifically inhibited ActRIIA with a KD of 67 pM and an IC50 of 0.2 nM. The anti-ActRIIB antibody 17G05 specifically inhibited ActRIIB with a KD of 509 pM and an IC50 of 0.26 nM. Each antibody had no detectable binding to the other activin type II receptor. GDF8 or activin A treatment induced markedly atrophy of human myotube cultures. This atrophy was completely prevented by LA01, which resulted in a significant increase in myotube number, width and differentiation index. The recovery magnitude by the anti-ActRIIA antibody was comparable to that treated with bimagrumab. In contrast, 17G05 failed to relieve GDF8-induced inhibition of differentiation and showed only a moderate effect on the inhibition induced by activin A.

Conclusion: These results indicate that ActRIIA plays a more prominent role than ActRIIB in the differentiation of human myoblasts. This provides a strong rationale for more presicse targeting ActRII receptors to preserve muscle in obesity treatment.

Introduction and Objective: Pancreatic fat infiltration plays a significant role in the progression of diabetic microvascular complications (DMCs).

Methods: Data were derived from a type 2 diabetes cohort study, including 666 patients from China, aged 70.9±7.7 years. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) was used to measure glycemic fluctuations.

Pancreatic fat infiltration was significantly associated with diabetic kidney disease (OR = 1.05, P = 0.02) and diabetic foot (OR = 1.04, P = 0.03). These associations were mediated by insulin resistance, with mediation effects of 29.8% and 5.3%, respectively. Excessive pancreatic fat was association with increased time of hypoglycemia, as measured by CGM. GWAS identified 9 significant SNPs associated with pancreatic fat deposition, including loci in MORC1, SDK1, and EYA1, which are involved in fat metabolism and vascular dysfunction.

Conclusion: Pancreatic fat infiltration was associated with diabetic kidney disease, diabetic foot and time of hypoglycemia. Genetic loci associated with pancreatic fat provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms.
